div.p: 731 Gramm. cod. Darmstad. in Act. Monac. II p. 515 ἔστι δὲ τὸ φενακίζειν εἰπεῖν καὶ περὶ τοὺς φήληκας· Σοφοκλῆς ἐν Ἰάμβῃ· καὶ φήληκας δὲ φαμὲν πλανῶντας (πλανῶνας cod.: corr. Werfer) τὴν ὄψιν ὡς πεπείρους.

Welcker, p. 73, discredited the title of the play on the ground that the story of Iambe is entirely undramatic, and he has been generally followed. Thus Hermann conjectured ἐν Νιόβῃ, and Nauck ἐν Ἀμύκῳ. But I believe that Hartung discovered the right solution, in assigning the fragment to the Triptolemus, and that this must be added to the list of examples where a quotation has been fixed by reference not to the title of a play but to some character or episode represented in it: see Introduction, § 1. It is scarcely likely that Iambe was a character in the Triptolemus: rather we should suppose that it became relevant to describe her success in cheering Demeter, for which see Hom. h. Dem. 202 ff. As an inmate of the house of Celeus (Apollod. 1. 30), it was natural to mention her in connexion with the story of Triptolemus.

The grammarian states that Sophocles applied φενακίζειν to the deceptive appearance of a certain kind of wild fig which looked edible while still unripe. But it is not clear whether he also attributes to Sophocles the use of the word φήληξ. For the fact cf. schol. Ar. Pac. 1166 φήληκα] τὸν ὄλινθον (l. ὄλυνθον). λέγει δὲ αὐτὰ ὁ Καλλίστρατος. κυρίως μὲν οὖν ὁ ἤδη σκληρὸς καὶ πάρωρος. ὁ ὄψιν μὲν πεπάνσεως ἔχων, ἄωρος δὲ ὤν. καὶ μήποτε φήληξ τίς ἐστιν ὁ ἀπατεὼν καὶ ψευδόμενος τῇ ὄψει εἰς βρῶσιν. Etym. M. p. 791, 33 φήληξ τὸ ἠρέμα (vix) πεπανθὲν σῦκον· καὶ φήληκας δὲ φαμὲν τὰ διαπατῶντα τὰς ὄψεις σῦκα ὡς εἴη πέπειρα. Phryn. (Bekk. anecd.) p. 71, 4 [p. 123, 8 de B.] φήληκες· τῶν σύκων τὰ δόξαν παρέχοντα ὡς ἤδη πέπονα καὶ ἐδώδιμα, ἄωρα δέ ἐστι (δὲ ὄντα de B.).
732 Hesych. I p. 134 ἄλυτον· ἀκατάλυτον, ἀκατάπαυστον. Σοφοκλῆς ἰνεῖ.

The mutilated or corrupt ἰνεῖ was altered to Ἰνοῖ by Musurus, and Αἰγεῖ was conjectured by Blomfield, Οἰνεῖ by Dindorf (fr. 416), Ἴωνι by Nauck, and Φινεῖ by Wecklein. Of these restorations Dindorf's is the best, if we could be certain that Sophocles wrote an Oeneus (II p. 120). See the evidence of constant confusion between Ἰνοῖ and Οἰνεῖ referred to by Nauck, TGF p. 536. Meineke substituted Ἠλέκτρᾳ, on the assumption that El. 230 is referred to.

ἄλυτος means unending also in El. 230 τάδε γὰρ ἄλυτα κεκλήσεται, where schol. L has τὸ θρηνεῖν τὸν πατέρα ἄλυτόν μοι ἔσται ὅ ἐστιν οὐδέποτε παύσομαι ἀλλ' ἀεὶ ἐν τῷ θρηνεῖν ἔσομαι, agreeing exactly with Hesych. Jebb's incurable, or irremediable, suggests that ἄλυτος had the same range as λύειν.
733 φίλου et πράξαντος schol. Aristid. (bis)

733 Schol. Aristid. p. 85 Σοφοκλέους ὂν ἐν Οἰδίποδι τοῦτο εἰς παροιμίαν ἐπεκράτησε, τὸ ‘φίλου κακῶς πράξαντος ἐκποδὼν φίλοι.’ ibid. p. 681 ὥσπερ καὶ τὸ ‘φίλου... φίλοι’ Σοφοκλέους ὂν παροιμιῶδες γέγονε. The verse is quoted without name of poet or play, but always with the reading ἀνδρός, by schol. Soph. El. 188, schol. Eur. Andr. 976, Zenob. 1. 90, Diogen. 1. 79, Greg. Cypr. 1. 60, Macar. 2. 6, Menand. mon. 32, Suid. s.vv. ἀνδρὸς γέροντος, ἐκποδών, οἰκονομῶ, ὑπερίσταται. Michael. Acomin. II p. 85, 1. It is evident that the schol. Aristid. has quoted from memory, and that his reading φίλου, as well as πράξαντος, was suggested by the text of Aristides I p. 112, 5 Jebb (I 180 Dind.) οὐ γὰρ ἐκποδὼν εἶναι κατέδειξε φίλου κακῶς πράξαντος, ibid. p. 268, 11 (436) τὸ παλαιὸν ῥῆμα ἐξηλέγχθη ψευδῶς ἔχον, τὸ κακῶς πραξάντων λήθην εἶναι παρὰ τοῖς φίλοις. But the scholiast's memory has played him false still further, when he ascribes the verse to the Oedipus of Sophocles. Unger (Parad. Theb. p. 374) corrected the reference by substituting the Oedipus of Euripides. It must, however, be regarded as extremely doubtful whether we ought to pay any regard to the scholiast at all, when we find schol. Eur. Phoen. 402 quoting the verse after the introductory words παρὰ τὸ Φιλοκτήτου. Wecklein infers that it occurred in the Philoctetes of Euripides, and the balance of probability is somewhat against the authorship of Sophocles.

The first appearance of this well-worn maxim is in Theogn. 209 οὐκ ἔστιν φεύγοντι φίλος καὶ πιστὸς ἑταῖρος, | τῆς δὲ φυγῆς ἐστιν τοῦτ’ ἀνιηρότερον. He is followed by Euripides, who repeats the thought in several passages: Her. 305 ὡς τὰ ξένων πρόσωπα φεύγουσιν φίλοις | ἓν ἦμαρ ἡδὺ βλέμμ’ ἔχειν φασὶν μόνον. ib. 559 φίλοι γάρ εἰσιν ἀνδρὶ δυστυχεῖ τίνες; Or. 1096 νῦν δ’ οὐκέτ’ εἰμὶ δυστυχοῦντί σοι φίλος; El. 605 οὐδεὶς δυστυχοῦντί σοι φίλος. ib. 1131 πένητας οὐδεὶς βούλεται κτᾶσθαι φίλους. Phoen. 403 εὖ πράσσε· τὰ φίλων δ’ οὐδέν, ἤν τι δυστυχῇς. Med. 561 πένητα φεύγει πᾶς τις ἐκποδὼν φίλος. Nothing of the kind is found in Aeschylus or Sophocles, and the fact that Euripides harps on the theme, and the coincidence of ἐκποδών with Med. l.c., may be taken somewhat to favour his authorship. Cf. Ov. Trist. 1. 5. 29 at simul intonuit, fugiunt; nec noscitur ulli, | agminibus comitum qui modo cinctus erat. ib. 1. 9. 5 donec eris felix, multos numerabis amicos; | tempora si fuerint nubila, solus eris. Campbell quotes Milton, Samson Agonistes 191 ff. ‘In prosperous days they swarm, but in adverse withdraw their head, not to be found, though sought.’

734 Pollux 6. 83 ἔστι μέντοι καὶ τὸ τῆς μαγίδος ὄνομα παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ ἐν χρήσει ‘τὰς Ἑκαταίας μαγίδας δόρπων.’ id. 10. 81 ὡς παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ εἴρηται ‘τὰς... δόρπων.’ Helladius in Phot. bibl. p. 533b 10 ἡ μαγίς ἀντὶ τῆς τραπέζης Αἰγύπτιον δόξει καὶ παντελῶς ἔκθεσμον· Ἐπίχαρμος δὲ ὁ Δωριεὺς (fr. 118 K.) καὶ Κερκίδας ὁ μελοποιὸς (fr. 8) ἐπὶ τῆς αὐτῆς διανοίας ἐχρήσαντο τῇ λέξει, καὶ μὴν καὶ ὁ Ἀττικὸς Σοφοκλῆς.

It is assumed that χρήσει is corrupt, and that it has displaced the name of the play: Brunck conjectured Κρίσει, and Dindorf Χρύσῃ (fr. 651). If Dindorf is right, the reference would be to the service of the Tauric Artemis. Iphigenia was sometimes identified with Hecate (Hes. fr. 123, Stesich. fr. 38), and for Artemis-Hecate see on Eur. Phoen. 110. But the words are quite common with the grammarians' sense 'in use,' and seem to be unobjectionable. Helladius clearly represents the attempt of an Atticist—possibly Irenaeus, one might guess—to
show that μαγίς, which was in use at Alexandria for a tray (Poll. 6. 83, schol. Ar. Nub. 669), rested on good Attic authority. It was also interpreted (1) as μάκτρα or τράπεζα in connexion with ritual (Pollux, l.c.). This seems to be the explanation of Athen. 173 A, where the Delians are said to have been called Μαγίδες and Γογγύλοι, because they acted as μάγειροι and τραπεζοποιοί to foreign worshippers. (2) As μᾶζαι, but here also with a particular limitation to sacred cakes. Thus the μελιτοῦττα carried by the devotee who descended into the cave of Trophonius at Lebadea was called μαγίς: Hesych. III p. 61, Etym. M. p. 573, 2 (who also testify to its use in ceremonial ablution). In the same way it was applied to 'Hecate's supper': Phot. lex. p. 240, 5 μαγίδες· μᾶζαι, καὶ τὰ τῇ Ἑκάτῃ συντελούμενα δεῖπνα. οὕτως Ἀριστοφάνης (fr. 813, I 579 K.). Cohn (Jahrb. f. Philol. Suppl. XII 296) regarded this as a reference to the present passage, and wished to substitute Σοφοκλῆς for Ἀριστοφάνης: he claimed that, since οὕτως always precedes the citation of a classical author, the reference could not be to Aristophanes of Byzantium, although he is known to have dealt with this word (Eustath. Od. p. 1761, 34). But the new Photius proves that Cohn's assumption was incorrect, and Strecker (Hermes XXVI 277) may have been right in holding that Helladius derived ultimately from Arist. Byz. through Phrynichus or some other. Probably μαγίς was originally a cook's tray, and like our dish was subsequently employed to describe the food served on it. Athen. 663 B refers to ἡ παρὰ Κυπρίοις καλουμένη μαγίς as derived from μάττειν.

'Hecate's Supper' was offered monthly at the cross-roads where the ghosts collect, and was eagerly awaited by the beggars of the neighbourhood: see schol. Ar. Plut. 594 κατὰ δὲ νουμηνίαν οἱ πλούσιοι ἔπεμπον δεῖπνον ἑσπέρας, ὥσπερ θυσίαν τῇ Ἑκάτῃ ἐν ταῖς τριόδοις, οἱ δὲ πένητες ἤρχοντο πεινῶντες καὶ ἤσθιον αὐτὰ καὶ ἔλεγον ὅτι ἡ Ἑκάτη ἔφαγεν αὐτά. Dem. 54. 39, attributing to certain disreputable people τὰ Ἑκαταῖα κατεσθίειν. Theophr. char. 28 J.: the superstitious man purifies himself, if he sees any one feasting on the garlic at the cross-roads. Plut. qu. conv. 7. 6 p. 709 A comments on the absurdity of those who make such offerings, but have nothing for themselves.

The phrase furnishes a good example of the purely stylistic device by which the adjective is transferred to the less appropriate noun. In the case of proper names its artificial character is especially obvious: Hom. E 741 Γοργείην κεφαλὴν δεινοῖο πελώρου, and Lucr. 5. 24 Nemeaeus magnus hiatus ille leonis are among the most familiar of the examples collected by Headlam in C.R. XVI 434. For Sophocles see Jebb on Ant. 794.

lg.l: πίνειν ἴσον πέφυκε τῷ διψῆν κακόν.

div.p: 735. 2 ἴσον κακὸν πέφυκε τῷ διψῆν βίᾳ A: corr. Meineke, κακόν delebat Bothe
735 Athen. 428 A καὶ ὁ Σοφοκλῆς δὲ ἐν σατυρικῷ φησὶν ὡς ἄρα ‘τὸ πρὸς... βίᾳ.’

Meineke's correction was accepted by Dindorf and Nauck, and is superior to the alternative suggested by Bothe, which Campbell adopts. The qualification of διψῆν by βίᾳ gives a false antithesis, since thirst through whatever cause it arises is equally hard to bear. Hence Nauck remarks that, if Bothe's view is approved, βίᾳ must be changed to ἄγαν or λίαν (F. W. Schmidt). It is not impossible that βίᾳ was a gloss on πρὸς βίαν: for, though I cannot find an identical example in the scholia, schol. rec. Aesch. Prom. 369 has πρὸς βίαν χειρούμενον] βιαίως πιεζόμενον, and so schol. Eur. Hec. 406 πρὸς βίαν ὠθουμένη] βιαίως ἐκκρουομένη, and Suid. s.v. πρὸς βίαν· βιαίως (Brunck on O.T. 805), and schol. Ant. 94 says ἡμεῖς ἔτι φαμὲν ἐν τῇ συνηθείᾳ βίᾳ ἀντὶ βιαίως. Now observe schol. Eur. Med. 1216 εἰ δὲ πρὸς βίαν ἄγοι] ὅτε δὲ φησὶν αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν ἐβούλετο ἀναστῆσαι βίᾳ. On the other hand κακός is sometimes interpolated: see Cobet, N.L. p. 424.

For πρὸς βίαν πίνειν, ‘to drink under compulsion,’ see Alcae. fr. 20 νῦν χρὴ μεθύσθην καί τινα πρὸς βίαν | πώνην, ἐπειδὴ κάτθανε Μύρσιλος, Ar. Ach. 73 ξενιζόμενοι δὲ πρὸς βίαν ἐπίνομεν. For similar uses of πρός in Sophocles cf. πρὸς χάριν (fr. 28 n.), πρὸς ἡδονήν, πρὸς ὀργήν (El. 369), πρὸς εὐσέβειαν (ib. 464).
736 Hesych. I p. 289 ἀρραγὲς ὄμμα· οὐ δακρῦον. ᾧ τρόπῳ φαμέν ‘κατερράγη μου δάκρυον.’ Σοφοκλῆς σατυρίκῳ (Σατυρίσκῳ Musurus, σατυρικῷ Casaubon, Τυροῖ βῳ conj. Μ. Schmidt).

The thought is that the eyes present a barrier which may yield to the pressure of an excessive emotion, when it can no longer be controlled. Cf. Ant. 802 ἴσχειν δ’ | οὐκέτι πηγὰς δύναμαι δακρύων, Aesch. Ag. 214 δάκρυ μὴ κατασχεῖν, Eur. Her. 449 δακρύων ὡς οὐ δύναμαι κατέχειν | γραίας ὄσσων ἔτι πηγάς, Ι. Α. 888 δάκρυον ὄμματ’ οὐκέτι στέγει, Aesch. Cho. 184 ἐξ ὀμμάτων δὲ δίψιοι πίπτουσί μοι | σταγόνες ἄφρακτοι δυσχίμου πλημμυρίδος. But in Apoll. Rhod. 3. 805 τὰ δ’ ἔρρεεν ἀστεγὲς αὔτως the best texts have ἀσταγές and there is no authority for ἀστεγές. Hence tears are said to ‘burst forth’: Trach. 852 ἔρρωγεν παγὰ δακρύων, ibid. 919 καὶ δακρύων ῥήξασα θερμὰ νάματα, Eur. Alc. 1068 ἐκ δ’ ὀμμάτων πηγαὶ κατερρώγασιν. Α.Ρ. 7. 434 δάκρυα δ’ οὐκ ἔρρηξ’ ἐπὶ πένθεσιν, ib. 7. 10 ἔρρηξαν Μοῦσαι δάκρυα Πιερίδες. I suspect, however, that in Plut. Pericl. 36 ῥῆξαι κλαυθμόν follows the analogy of ῥῆξαι φωνήν.
737 περισκοπῶν V: περισκοπεῖ Μ
737 Achill. Isag. ad Arat. Phaen. (Petav. Uranol. p. 121 Α) p. 27, 1 Maass ‘μισῶ . . . περισκοπῶν,’ φησὶν ὁ Σοφοκλῆς.

The contrasting clause must have been to the effect ‘and neglects what is close at hand.’ The sentiment was familiar, and was employed to some purpose against the μετεωροσοφισταί (Adam on Plat. rep. 488 Ε). Cf. Ο.Τ. 130 τὰ πρὸς ποσὶ σκοπεῖν | μεθέντας ἡμᾶς τἀφανῆ προσήγετο, Pind. Isth. 8(7). 13 τὸ δὲ πρὸ ποδὸς ἄρειον ἀεὶ <σκοπεῖν> χρῆμα πάν. [Eur.] Rhes. 482 μὴ νυν τὰ πόρρω τἀγγύθεν μεθεὶς σκόπει. Nauck quotes Enn. Iphig. fr. VIII quod est ante pedes, noenu spectat: caeli scrutatur plagas. Eupolis fr. 146, 1 297 K. (of Protagoras) ἀλαζονεύεται μὲν ἁλιτήριος | περὶ τῶν μετεώρων, τὰ δὲ χαμᾶθεν ἐσθίει. Aristoph. fr. 672, 1 557 K. ὂς τὰ μὲν ἀφανῆ μεριμνᾷ, τὰ δὲ χαμᾶθεν ἐσθίει. Plat. Theaet. 174 A ὥσπερ καὶ Θαλῆν ἀστρονομοῦντα, ὦ Θεόδωρε, καὶ ἄνω βλέποντα, πεσόντα εἰς φρέαρ Θρᾷττά τις ἐμμελὴς καὶ χαρίεσσα θεραπαινὶς ἀποσκῶψαι λέγεται, ὡς τὰ μὲν ἐν οὐρανῷ προθυμοῖτο εἰδέναι, τὰ δ’ ἔμπροσθεν αὐτοῦ καὶ παρὰ πόδας λανθάνοι αὐτόν. Antipat. Sidon. Α. Ρ. 7. 172 ἴδ’ ὡς τὰ κατ’ αἰθέρα λεύσσων | τοὐν ποσὶν οὐκ ἐδάην πῆμα κυλινδόμενον. The lesson is enforced by the use of περισκοπεῖν, to consider a thing in all its bearings, and so to consider curiously (like Prometheus, who was ἀκριβῶς περισσόφρων Aesch. Prom. 344). The suggestion involved is that of a pedantic and over-subtle mind: so περιφρονῶ in Ar. Nub. 225 ἀεροβατῶ καὶ περιφρονῶ τὸν ἥλιον, ib. 741 σχάσας τὴν φροντίδα | λεπτὴν κατὰ μικρὸν περιφρόνει τὰ πράγματα. Cf. Eudorus ap. Stob. ecl. 2. 7. 2 (p. 42, 18 W.) ἡ θεωρία δ’ ἐστὶ περίσκεψις τοῦ πράγματος καὶ οἷον ἐπίκρισις κατὰ τὸν περὶ αὐτοῦ λογισμόν. — H. points out that μέν appears to be out of its logical order, which would require ὅστις τὰ μὲν ἀφανῆ . . . τὰ δ’ ἐν ποσίν . . ., and refers to Aesch. Theb. 21. See his note on Aesch. Ag. 8, and Jebb on Phil. 279 ὁρῶντα μὲν ναῦς . . . ἄνδρα δ’ οὐδέν’ ἔντοπον, Ai. 372. But here of course the context may have given another complexion to the structure, especially if περισκοπῶν (cr. n.) is the right reading.

lg.l: κἀνταῦθα . . . πᾶς προσκυνεῖ δὲ τὸν στρέφοντα κύκλον ἡλίου

div.p: 738 κἀνταῦθα om. M | ἡλίου κύκλον V
738 Achill. Isag. ad Arat. Phaen. (Petav. Uranol. p. 122 E) p. 28, 17 Maass Σοφοκλῆς δὲ εἰς Ἀτρέα τὴν εὕρεσιν (τῆς ἀστρονομίας) ἀναφέρει λέγων ‘κἀνταῦθα . . . ἡλίου.’

J. writes: ‘The current legend was as follows. Atreus and Thyestes were contending for the sovereignty of Mycenae. Hermes gave to Atreus a golden lamb, and this τέρας (Eur. Or. 995) was hailed as a sign that he was to be king (regni stabilimen mei, Accius Atreus fr. VIII R.). Then Thyestes seduced Aerope, the wife of Atreus, and with her aid stole the lamb. Hereupon Zeus wrought a fresh portent; he changed the course of the sun, causing it to rise in the east, and not (as it was said to have done pre- viously) in the west. See Plat. polit. 268E τὸ περὶ τῆς χρυσέας ἀρνὸς σημεῖον, 269 A μαρτυρήσας ἄρα ὁ θεὸς Ἀτρεῖ μετέβαλεν (the course of sun and stars) ἐπὶ τὸ νῦν σχῆμα. So (1) Eur. El. 727 ἄστρων μετέβασ’ ὁδοὺς | Ζεὺς καὶ φέγγος ἀελίου, (2) Eur. I. T. 192 ff. and 816 ἡλίου μετάστασιν, (3) Ovid Trist. 2. 391 si non Aeropen frater sceleratus amasset, | aversos Solis non legeremus equos. Hence τὸν στρέφοντα κύκλον ἡλίου ought to mean, “Zeus, who makes the orb of the sun change its course.”

But Achilles Tatius quotes the verse to show that Sophocles ascribed the invention of astronomy to Atreus. By τὸν στρέφοντα then he understood Atreus. In this he seems to have been mistaken; but, if so, the source of his error is evident. There was another legend which represented Atreus as vindicating his claim against Thyestes by proclaiming an astronomical discovery of his own, — viz. that the sun moved in a direction opposite to that in which the sky revolved with the stars. See Eur. fr. 861 (from his Thyestes ? Nauck, p. 639), where Atreus is probably the speaker: δείξας γὰρ ἄστρων τὴν ἐναντίαν ὁδὸν | δήμους τ’ ἔσῳσα καὶ τύραννος ἱζόμην. Here τὴν ἐναντίαν means τῇ τοῦ ἡλίου. Cf. Strabo 23 (from Polybius) Ἀτρέα δὲ (sc. παραδείξαντα) τοῦ ἡλίου τὸν ὑπεναντίον τῷ οὐρανῷ δρόμον. Eustathius (Od. p. 1645, 56) quotes these words from Strabo. Welcker (p. 361) thinks — though doubtfully — that Sophocles may have meant this. The words would then signify, “every one now does homage to the man (Atreus) who reversed the course of the sun's orb” (i.e., who made this discovery). But this is to strain τὸν στρέφοντα.

One thing, however, is clear. Achilles Tatius cannot have been mistaken in stating that the verse had some connexion with Atreus. It is certain then that one or another form of the legend about the sun is referred to, and that στρέφοντα is sound. Nauck cannot be right in conjecturing τρέφοντα, nor Blaydes in proposing φλογωπόν or πυρωπόν.’

I think it is possible to fix the allusion more exactly. In the first place, we must not be misled by the speculations of Stoics and other rationalizers into supposing that the scientific discoveries of astronomy have any more connexion with the plays of Sophocles than they have with the heroic age itself. Achilles is only repeating what he has derived — through intermediate sources — from Posidonius, and Polybius (in Strabo) belongs to the same school of thought. Eur. fr. 861 need not mean anything more than this: ‘I saved the townships and became king by displaying the stars moving in a new (or contrary) direction.’ That is to say, it expresses exactly the same thing as is referred to in El. 727 and Or. 1001 ff.

We must next enquire what form of the story is contemplated by the present extract from Sophocles. The various ramifications of the Atreus-legend may be conveniently studied in Escher's article on Atreus in Pauly-Wissowa I 2139-2144; and there can be no doubt that we are concerned with the version preserved by Apollod. epit. 2. 10 ff., according to which, after Thyestes had succeeded in obtaining the sovereignty through the theft of the lamb, he was ultimately deposed in consequence of the miracle which Atreus was permitted to accomplish: Ζεὺς δὲ Ἑρμῆν πέμπει πρὸς Ἀτρέα καὶ λέγει συνθέσθαι πρὸς Θυέστην περὶ τοῦ βασιλεῦσαι Ἀτρέα, εἰ τὴν ἐναντίαν ὁδεύσει ὁ
Ἥλιος· Θυέστου δὲ συνθεμένου τὴν δύσιν εἰς ἀνατολὰς ὁ Ἥλιος ἐποιήσατο· ὅθεν ἐκμαρτυρήσαντος τοῦ δαίμονος τὴν Θυέστου πλεονεξίαν, τὴν βασιλείαν Ἀτρεὺς παρέλαβε καὶ Θυέστην ἐφυγάδευσεν (Apollod. l.c. 12). So schol. Eur. Or. 998: Atreus would have lost his kingdom, εἰ μὴ ὡς ἂν φιλόσοφος ἀπέδειξεν αὐτοὺς ἀσεβοῦντας, εἰ Θυέστην βασιλέα ἕλωνται, τεκμήριον δὲ τῆς ἀσεβείας τὸν Ἥλιον καὶ τὰς Πλειάδας ἐκ δύσεως ἀνίσχοντας. . . τινὲς δέ φασι τὸν Δία πρὸς χάριν Ἀτρέως ποιῆσαι τὸν Ἥλιον καὶ τὰς Πλειάδας ἐκ δύσεως ἀνατεῖλαι μεταστρέψαντα τὴν τάξιν ἐν μιᾷ ἡμέρᾳ . . . ἀλλ’ ὕστερον πάλιν ὁ Ἀτρεύς, φιλονεικίᾳ τῇ πρὸς τοῦτον, προσελθὼν ἐπηγγέλλετο δεῖξαι τὸν ἥλιον ἐκ δυσμῶν εἰς ἀνατολὰς τὴν πορείαν ποιούμενον, καὶ τὴν Πλειάδα ὁμοίως εἰς ἀνατολὴν ὁρῶσαν. This is precisely the situation which the present fragment depicts; and Euripides seems to have followed the same form of the legend in the wellknown choruses of the Electra and Orestes, as has been pointed out by Wedd in his note on Or. 1001 ff. τὸν στρέφοντα is of course Atreus, who is saluted with divine honours in virtue of his achievement (Phil. 657, Plat. rep. 398 A); but whether these lines come from the Atreus or from some other play must remain uncertain for want of evidence. Although there is some reason to think that Sophocles in that play gave another account of the sun's altered course (I p. 93), the evidence of the tragic texts themselves, so far as they are preserved, rather indicates that Sophocles and Euripides both related the story in substantially the same form as that in which it is given by Apollodorus. This inference is entirely consistent with Plato's allusion, but requires us to impeach the accuracy of Statyllius Flaccus, who may have been obsessed by the later version. There is nothing by which we can gauge his trustworthiness as a witness to the actual tradition.

It should be observed that the words as they stand are unmetrical, and the quotation has probably been garbled by the omission of what is irrelevant to the immediate purpose (e.g. πᾶς τις ἡλίου κύκλον | ἔφριξ’ ἰδὼν δὲ τὸν στρέφοντα προσκυνεῖ). Headlam bracketed ἡλίου without giving any reason (C.R. XIII 4). Before the appearance of Maass's edition it was not known that κἀνταῦθα formed part of the quotation, and, if the text is sound, some words must have been omitted between it and πᾶς. Hence Maass conjectured προσκυνεῖ σε τὸν κτἑ., but the metrical difficulty would remain unsolved. Weil suggested that the text should be reconstructed thus: τὸν <προσημήνανθ’ ὁδοὺς | ἰδὼν πάλιν> στρέφοντα, but στρέφοντα is much more forcible as applied to Atreus (see on fr. 620). Murray suggests that the metre may have been iambic tetrameter as in fr. 314. 291 ff.

lg.l: πῶς ἂν οὐκ ἂν ἐν δίκῃ

div.p: 739 Bekk. anecd. p. 128, 28 σημειωτέον δὲ ὅτι καὶ δὶς καὶ τρὶς χρῶνται αὐτῷ (sc. τῷ ἄν) ἐν μιᾷ συντάξει, ὡς παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ εὕρηται ‘πῶς ἂν . . . θάνοιμ’ ἄν;’

Dindorf conjectured πῶς ἄῤ, but there is no objection to the triple ἂν. Cf. Eur. Andr. 934 οὐκ ἂν ἔν γ’ ἐμοῖς δόμοις | βλέπουσ’ ἂν αὐγὰς τἄμ’ ἐκαρποῦτ’ ἂν λέχη. Tro. 1244 ἀφανεῖς ἂν ὄντες οὐκ ἂν ὑμνήθημεν ἄν. The purpose of the repetition is to throw rhetorical emphasis on any word which it is desired to accentuate, apart from the ἂν which regularly follows the conditional verb: see Kuehner-Gerth I 247, Goodwin § 223, Gildersleeve § 467. The words are echoed in Eur. Tro. 961 πῶς οὖν ἔτ’ ἂν θνῇσκοιμ’ ἂν ἐνδίκως, πόσι.
740 Phot.ed. Reitz. p. 36, 13 (= Bekk. anecd. p. 347, 25) ἀείζων . . . Σοφοκλῆς δὲ τὴν εὐθεῖαν εἶπεν ‘ἀείζως γενεά.’

The grammarian is illustrating the contraction of ἀείζωος to ἀείζως parallel to ἀείνως: ἀένναος (Moeris p. 188, 17). The source was Phrynichus: see Bekk. anecd. p. 22, 16 (praep. soph. p. 37, 10 de B.). The gods (μακάρων γένος αἰὲν ἐόντων) are probably meant.

741 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 36, 18 (Phryn. fr. 93 de Β.) ἀείζων πένθος ἐρεῖς, ὡς Σοφοκλῆς, καὶ ἀείζωον (ἀείζων Burges) ἕλκος. The same occurs in Bekk. anecd. p. 347, 30, but with the accidental omission of καί. The critics were misled in consequence and supposed that ἀείζων ἕλκος was the quotation from Sophocles.

There is a similar phrase in Aesch. Suppl. 999 χώρᾳ τ᾽ ἄχθος ἀείζων πέλοι, referring to the undying curse proceeding ἀείνως : ἀένναος (Moeris p. 188, 17). The source was Phrynichus: see Bekk. anecd. p. 22, 16 (praep. soph. p. 37, 10 de B.). The gods (μακάρων γένος αἰὲν ἐόντων) are probably meant. πένθος from the death of a suppliant. So in identical circumstances, but with weaker sense (note σοί), Eur. Hel. 987 ἀθάνατον ἄλγος σοί, ψόγος δὲ σῷ πατρί. Cf. Eur. fr. 799 οὕτω προσήκει μηδὲ τὴν ὀργὴν ἔχειν | ἀθάνατον. Tr. fr. adesp. 79 ἀθάνατον ὀργὴν μὴ φύλασσε θνητὸς ὤν. Reitzenstein, comparing Lucr. 1. 34 aeterno vulnere amoris, suggests that ἀείζων ἕλκος <ἔρωτος> may be drawn from an Alexandrian source. For ἕλκος see on fr. 614.
742 Bekk. anecd. p. 353, 5 ἀθέμιστα καὶ ἀνόσια δρᾶν Δείναρχος (fr. 89. 4 S.) εἶπε καὶ Σοφοκλῆς.

The words are not metrical, and Nauck suggests that the order was ἀνόσια κἀθέμιστα δρᾶν. But a doubt is thrown on the evidence by Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 39, 27, where the same extract occurs, but Ξενοφῶν appears in place of Σοφοκλῆς. Reitzenstein thinks that the mention of Sophocles in Bekker's codex may be merely an error. But, even if this is not so, the most we can infer is that Sophocles used ἀθέμιστος : the words quoted belong to Dinarchus alone.

743 Bekk. anecd. p. 362, 22 αἱματορρόφον. Σοφοκλῆς ῾τίσω δ᾽ ἄνωθεν ἐστὶν ἢ αἱματορρόφος.' σημαίνει δὲ.... The verse was restored as above by Bekker, and his corrections are now partly confirmed by Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 53, 13 αἱματορρόφος· Ἄρχιππος εἶπε. σημαίνει δὲ... <Σοφοκλῆς δέ> 'τίσις> δ᾽ ἄνωθεν εἶσιν αἱματορρόφος.'

τίσις αἱματορρόφος implies the conception of the Erinys as a blood-sucking vampire. Aeschylus provides ample illustration: Ag. 1187 καὶ μὴν πεπωκώς γ', ὡς θρασύνεσθαι πλέον, | βρότειον αἷμα κῶμος ... συγγόνων Ἐρινύων. Cho. 575 φόνου δ' Ἐρινὺς οὐχ ὑπεσπανισμένη | ἄκρατον αἷμα πίεται τρίτην πόσιν. Eum. 264 ἀλλ᾽ ἀντιδοῦναι δεῖ σ᾽ ἀπὸ ζῶντος
ῥοφεῖν | ἐρυθρὸν ἐκ μελέων πέλανον. In Ag. 1479 ἔρως αἱματολοιχός is traced to the working of the τριπάχυντος δαίμων of the Pelopidae. The Erinyes were represented in the form of snakes (Eur. I.T. 286, etc.), and the snake was also a drinker of blood (Ar. Eq. 198 δράκοντα ...αἱματοπώτην). Miss J. E. Harrison, Proleg. p. 2152, points out that the Townley schol. gives a variant εἰαροπῶτις = 'blood-drinking' in Hom. I 571 for the vulgate ἠεροφοῖτις Ἐρινύς. It is perhaps worth remarking that this trait might be used as an argument in favour of the view, strongly combated by Gruppe (Bursians Jahresb. CXXXVII 492), that the Erinyes were originally the souls of the departed.—In place of ἄνωθεν Burges (on Aesch. Eum. 263) conjectured ἔνερθεν, not without a certain speciousness, although the corruption is unlikely. But the images of Sophocles are not traced with the same consistent vigour which Aeschylus applied to the portrayal of his demonic agencies. αἱματορρόφος merely suggests the ghoulish avengers, and ἄνωθεν is correctly used to mark the ultimate responsibility of Zeus. So Aesch. Ag. 1578 ff. φαίην ἂν ἤδη νῦν βροτῶν τιμαόρους | θεοὺς ἄνωθεν γῆς ἐποπτεύειν ἄχη, | ἰδὼν ὑφαντοῖς ἐν πέπλοις Ἐρινύων κτέ.
744 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 62, 1 (= Bekk. anecd. p. 367, 20) ἀκόλαστος ὄχλος Εὐριπίδης (Hec. 607) εἶπεν, ἀκόλαστον δὲ σῶμα Σοφοκλῆς.

Cobet (N.L. p. 428) conjectured that Sophocles wrote ἀκόλαστον στόμα, comparing Eur. Or. 10 ἀκόλαστον ἔσχε γλῶσσαν. [He adds Bacch. 386, substituting by a slip of memory ἀκολάστων for ἀχαλίνων.] Gomperz (Nachlese, p. 44) defended σῶμα as expressing, like our 'body' and the Gk δέμας, κάρα, etc., merely the personality addressed or described: see also n. on Eur. Hclid. 528. But I see no reason why ἀκόλαστον σῶμα should not be applied to one whose bodily appetites are uncontrolled: Arist. eth. N. 7. 4. 1148a 5 τῶν περὶ τὰς σωματικὰς ἀπολαύσεις, περὶ ἃς λέγομεν τὸν σώφρονα καὶ ἀκόλαστον. There is more than a periphrasis here, even if we choose to speak of the adjective as transferred.

lg.l: σπουδὴ γὰρ ἡ κατ' οἶκον ἐγκεκρυμμένη

app.rdg: Brunck : προσθυραῖον cod. Bekk., πρὸς θυραιον cod. Phot.

div.p: 745 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 65, 16 (= Bekk. anecd. p. 373, 1) ἀκουσίμη· ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀκουστή. Σοφοκλῆς ‘σπουδὴ...ἀκουσίμη.” δύναται δὲ καὶ ἡ φωνὴ ἀκουσίμη λέγεσθαι. The source was Phrynichus (fr. 13 de B.).

Welcker (p. 149) assigns these verses to Odysseus speaking with Antenor in the Λάκαιναι (II p. 34) of a secret compact concluded with the Greeks; and Hartung, reading σπονδή, which he wrongly translates Einverständnisz, takes a similar view.

1 σπουδή. Brunck edited σπονδή without remark, and F. W. Schmidt conjectured κραυγή. Nauck formerly proposed ποῦ δή. But σπουδή, 'heat,' may quite well be right, as in O.T. 778. Blaydes well remarks: 'dicitur, ni fallor, vehementia sermonis rixosa'; but his conjecture εὖ κεκρυμμένη is not required.

2 Wecklein conjectured ἡ for οὐ.—ἀκουσίμη is wrongly rendered audible by L. and S., but the gloss ἀκουστή is practically correct, since Sophocles uses ἀκούσιμος and ἀκουστός indifferently in the sense of 'fit to be heard': see on fr. 357, and cf. O. T. 1312 ἐς δεινόν, οὐδ᾽ ἀκουστόν, οὐδ᾽ ἐπόψιμον, where the terminations -τος and -ιμος are obviously parallel. On the other hand, in O.C. 27 ἐξοικήσιμος does not mean 'habitable' but 'inhabited,' as is sufficiently shown by the reply ἀλλ'
ἐστὶ μὴν οἰκητός, and by the requirement of the sense. The force of the suffix is originally quite vague, but in usage gradually tends to become specialized: cf. the use of λεύσιμος and ἁλώσιμος. For the formation see Brugmann, Comp. Gr. II p. 174 E. tr., who shows that these adjectives were secondary derivatives from -σι stems, and that ἄλκιμος, νόμιμος and the like were modelled on them. Lobeck, Phryn. p. 227, pointed out that ἀρώσιμοι in Ant. 569 is contrary to analogy, which requires ἀρόσιμος.
746 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 66, 2 (= Bekk. anecd. p. 373, 14) ἀκουσία· τὸ πρᾶγμα. Σοφοκλῆς ‘ἐξαίρετον...ἀκουσίαν.’ It is unnecessary to read τὸ <ἆκον> πρᾶγμα, as Ellendt and others have proposed.

ἀκουσία does not seem to occur elsewhere, and Lobeck (Phryn. p. 4) suggested that γνώμην or the like was to be supplied from the context. ‘I make an exception of the unwitting deed’: Campbell well compares fr. 665. For ἐξαίρετον cf. Eur. I. T. 755 ἐξαίρετόν μοι δὸς τόδ' = ‘grant me this as an exception.’ Plat. Phaedr. 242 Β Σιμμίαν Θηβαῖον ἐξαιρῶ λόγου, ‘I make an exception of Simmias.’
747 Bekk. anecd. p. 407, 12 ἀντάρης νυκτερὶς ὄψεσιν φησὶ Σοφοκλῆς. The same words are found in Suid. s.v.

I understand these words as meaning ‘the bat, hostile to men's vision’; for such is the chief characteristic of the bat, ‘dayes enimy,’ as Spenser calls him. ἀντήρης acquires the sense hostile, for which cf. Eur. Phoen. 1367, in the same manner as ἐναντίος and ἀνταῖος (fr. 334 n.). Nor should any difficulty be found in ὄψεσιν: Soph. twice uses it for ‘the eyes’ (O. T. 1328, Ant. 52), a sense which is common in the Greek of Polybius and Plutarch.

Critics have generally either given up the passage as hopeless, or indulged in wild conjectures. Thus Ellendt proposed ἀντήρης νυκτέραις ὄψεσιν, ‘face to face with visions of the night.’ Bernhardy's ἀνταυγής, and Campbell's ἀτειρής, are unsuitable as applied to the bat, which is not usually credited with keenness of sight. H. conjectures ἀνταίαισι for ἀντάρης, thinking of the bat's ill-omened aspect. Lobeck (Path. Prol. p. 267) suggested ἀμπαρής as an equivalent of ἀνάπηρος.
[νεκυομαντεῖον ἐν τῇ ἀόρνῳ λίμνῃ περὶ Τυρσηνίαν.]

748 Bekk. anecd. p. 414, 3 ἄορνος λίμνη (λιμήν cod.) περὶ Τυρσηνίαν. φησὶ δὲ καὶ ἐν Κύμῃ τῇ Χαλκιδίκῃ ἄορνον λίμνην εἶναι, περιπεφυκότων δὲ πολλῶν δένδρων μηδὲν εἰς αὐτὴν ἐμπίπτειν τῶν ἀποπιπτόντων φύλλων. εἶναι δὲ καὶ νεκυομαντεῖον ἐν τῇ Τυρσηνίᾳ λίμνῃ Σοφοκλῆς ἱστορεῖ. L. Dindorf deleted λίμνῃ, but without good cause, as will presently appear. Substantially the same extract occurs in Eustath. Od. p. 1667, 63 (Ael. et Paus. fr. 356 Schw.) and Etym. M. p. 115 ad fin., but without any reference to Sophocles.

It will be seen that Sophocles is quoted for the existence of an oracle of the dead at a certain Tyrrhenian lake; and it can hardly be doubted that he introduced the name Ἄορνος. But it may be assumed that he did not mention its proximity to Cumae; and, inasmuch as the situation of Lake Avernus subsequently became famous, the compiler, Aelius Dionysius or another, seems to have drawn the
conclusion that there was a second Avernus in Etruria. There is however no evidence of the existence of more than one Avernus on the W. coast of Italy, and Sophocles must have used the epithet Tyrrhenian in the wider sense: cf. fr. 598. Similarly Verg. Georg. 2. 164 Tyrrhenusque fretis inmittitur aestus Avernis.

Ἄορνος λίμνη is also recorded (1) near Tartessus in Spain (schol. Ar. Ran. 475): (2) in Thesprotia (Pausan. 10. 30. 6). At the latter place was a νεκυομαντεῖον, which may have been the oracle of Odysseus mentioned by Lycophr. 799. On the other hand, the νεκυομαντεῖον at the Italian Avernus (for which cf. Diod. 4. 22) was the traditional scene of the νέκυια in the Odyssey: Eustath. Od. p. 1667, 37, Max. Tyr. 14. 2, Strabo 244 ἐμύθευον δ' οἱ πρὸ ἡμῶν ἐν τῷ Ἀόρνῳ τὰ περὶ τὴν νέκυιαν τὴν Ὁμηρικήν· καὶ δὴ καὶ νεκυομαντεῖον ἱστοροῦσιν ἐνταῦθα γενέσθαι καὶ Ὀδυσσέα εἰς τοῦτ᾽ ἀφικέσθαι. Το whom does Strabo allude as οἱ πρὸ ἡμῶν? I am disposed to conjecture that the mention by Sophocles of Aornus occurred in the Ὀδυσσεὺς ἀκανθοπλήξ, in reference to the prophecy of Tiresias concerning the death of Odysseus: see fr. 453, etc., and especially II p. 108. Holzinger, however, prefers to connect it with the Euryalus.

The popular derivation of Ἄορνος from the absence of birds, which were unable to fly over the lake by reason of its mephitic vapours, has been made familiar by Lucr. 6. 740, and Verg. Aen. 6. 242. It was an entrance to the under world : thus the Thesprotian Ἄορνος near Ephyra was connected with the story of Orpheus. In all such places it was customary to invoke the spirits of the dead. The evidence relating to νεκυομαντεῖα is collected by Gruppe, Gr. Myth. p. 9359: besides Ephyra and Taenarum, Phigalia and Heraclea are mentioned as places containing such oracles. See also Frazer's Pausanias, III p. 347.

749 Cramer, anecd. Oxon. I p. 223, 11 κρίκος...ἔστι δ᾽ ὅτε καὶ ἐν ὑπερθέσει κίρκος· ‘ῥήξασα κίρκους’ παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ. This is a somewhat obscure matter. There is a trace of the same extract in Etym. M. p. 538, 41 κρίκος... ἔστι δ᾽ ὅτε καὶ ἐν ὑπερθέσει γίνεται κίρκος (so cod. Leid.), ὡς καρδία κραδία. Cf. Pollux 1. 94 (speaking of ships' furniture) ἔστι δέ τις καὶ μηχανὴ καὶ τροχὸς καὶ τροχιλία, καὶ δι᾽ ὧν οἱ κάλοι διείρονται κρίκοι· τὸ γὰρ κίρκοι ποιητικόν (Bethe quotes our passage here with Hom. Ω 272), ἴδιον δὲ τὸ κύκλοι, But this evidence is not sufficiently precise to justify the inference that Sophocles was speaking of the freeing of ships' ropes owing to the bursting of the rings through which they were passed. Hesych. 11 p. 486 κίρκοι...πάντα τὰ ἐπικαμπῆ κίρκοι λέγονται, Etym. Gud. p. 323, 7, give no further help. That κίρκος may have been a term for a particular kind of fastening seems to be indicated by κίρκωσον in Aesch. Prom. 74, (στεφάνιον) οὐκ ἔχον κίρκους οὐδὲ τοὺς δεσμούς, Dittenberger Syll.2 11 320, Wien. Stud. XXIV 133.
750 Cramer, anecd. Oxon. I p. 268, 25 τὸ παθητικὸν λέλημμαι. Σοφοκλῆς· ‘οἴμοι λέλημμαι.’

On the relation λέλημμαι : εἴλημμαι the data are not completely given in Curtius, Verb, p. 361 E. tr., and his explanation is obsolete. The facts seem to indicate that εἴλημμαι < *σέσλημμαι was the original form, and that λέλημμαι, produced later by analogy, established itself particularly in the Ionic dialect: see Smyth, Ionic, § 585, 6, § 595, 4. Wright, Gr. Gram. § 517. G. Meyer, however (Gr. Gram. p. 625), treats εἴληφα as due to the analogy of εἴρηκα. εἴλημμαι prevails ordinarily in Attic prose and comedy, λέλημμαι in tragedy: for examples of the latter see Blaydes on Ar. Eccl. 1090, Elmsley on Eur. Bacch. 1100.
751 ἐτῆρας (γρ. εὔειρας) cod. Cram.: εὔειρας ΑΕ | θεοῖς ἔρεξ' L. Dindorf: θεοῖς ἐρέξας (vel ἐράξας) codd., θεοῖσι ῥέζ' Meineke
751 Schol. Lond. (AE) Dion. Thr. p. 541, 5 Hilg. = Cramer, anecd. Oxon. IV p. 329, 20 τὸ ἐτήρ παρὰ τὸ ἔτος· Σοφοκλῆς ‘ἐτῆρας . . . ἐπακτίοις.’ γράφεται δὲ καὶ εὔειρας (εὐῆρας conj. Schneidewin).

The occasion described may be taken to have been a thank-offering on the return home from a successful voyage or prosperous undertaking. — ἐτῆρας. The age of sacrificial victims was determined by various considerations, concisely described by Stengel, griech. Sakralaltertümer, § 82. Frequently τέλεια are required, and Hesych. s.v. states that some authorities interpret this word as equivalent to a year old. So the Homeric βοῦς ἤνις (Z 93 etc.) is traditionally explained. There was an old law at Athens, referred to by Androtion (FHG 1375) and Philochorus (FHG I 394), forbidding the slaughter of πρόβατον ἄπεκτον ἢ ἄτοκον.— θεοῖς. For the synizesis in the third foot according to Sophocles' usual practice see Jebb on At. 1129. — ἐπακτίοις shows that the sacrifice is made to the gods who protect sea-faring. Cf. ApoU. Rhod. 1. 403 νήεον αὐτόθι (at Pagasae) βωμὸν ἐπάκτιον Ἀπόλλωνος, | Ἀκτίου Ἐμβασίοιό τ’ ἐπώνυμον. Ἐπάκτιος was a title given to Hermes at Sicyon, Ἐπακταῖος to Poseidon at Samos (Hesych. 11 p. 133). Pan was worshipped as Ἄκτιος (Theocr. 5. 14) and as αἰγιαλίτης (Α. Ρ. 10. 10,1 αἰγιαλίτην | Πᾶνα τὸν εὔορμον τῇδ’ ἔφορον λιμένων); Apollo as Ἐπάκτιος at Corcyra, and as Ἄκτιος especially in Acarnania (Gruppe, Gr. Myth. p. 12252, Pauly- Wissowa I 1215).
752. 1 ἠελίοιο κτείρειε ἐμέ V: corr. Μ. Schmidt et Bergk 2 sq. ὃν οἱ add. Petau | καὶ add. Petau: πατέρα τε πάντων coni. Wagner
752. Anon. de Arati interp. (Petav. Uranol. p. 274 A) p. 28, 17 Maass οἱ δὲ Δία τὸν ἤλιον νοήσαντες λέγουσιν ὅτι καὶ Σοφοκλῆς Δία τὸν ἥλιον καλεῖ λέγων· ‘ ἠελίοιο . . . πάντων.’

Nauck's statement that the genuineness of the fragment was doubted by Bernhardy (Grundr. d. gr. Lit. 3 11 2 Ρ. 333) is an error: his remarks apply to fr. 1120. Rapp in Roscher I 2024 thinks it improbable that this fragment was written by Sophocles, on the ground that sunworship was a late development in Greek religious thought, arising from the idealization of the Sun as the source of the change of the seasons (Athen. 693 F). On the other hand, Farnell (v p. 418) holds that the poet was alluding to some religious speculation of his own age. In Ar. Pac. 410 sun-worship is attributed to the barbarians; and, except at Rhodes, there is no trace of anthropomorphism in the Hellenic cult. See also frs. 26 and 582. Blaydes conjectured οἰκτείρειέ με... ἥλιος coll. fr. 872, but without advantage. It is difficult to determine to whom Sophocles alluded as οἱ σοφοί. Possibly to Pherecydes of Syros: Lyd. de mens. 4. 3 Ἥλιος αὐτὸς (sc. Ζεύς) κατὰ Φερεκύδην (Diels, Vorsokr. 3 II 201, 29). It is less probable that he would have taken into account the speculations of the contemporary Heraclitean school, for which see on Cleanth. fr. 28. Xenophanes (Α 42 Diels), as well as other pre-Socratic thinkers, held that animal life was directly due to the action of the sun, but such views scarcely account for the present fragment. Cf. Ο. T. 660 τὸν πάντων θεῶν θεὸν πρόμον Ἅλιον, and see Jessen in Pauly-Wissowa VIII 62. For the later glorification of the sun-god see Gruppe, p. 1466 f.

lg.l: βαρὺς βαρὺς ξύνοικος, ὦ ξένοι, βαρύς.

div.p: 753 Philodem. περὶ ποιημάτων 11 3 (Herc. pap. coll. alt. iv f. 120, as restored by Hausrath in Jahrb. Philol. Suppl. XVII 239) καλῶς ἔχειν ἢ κακῶς τὸν ἦχον ποεῖν· καλῶς μὲν [ὡς] παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ βαρὺς βαρὺς <σ> ὐνοικο[σ, ὦ] ξένοι, βα[ρ]ύς, οὐ διὸ τὴν [σύ]νθεσιν, ὣς τινές [φασιν, ἐν δὲ] τῷ [βαρὺ]ς ξ<ύ> νοικος, ὦ ξένοι, βαρὺς βαρύς εἴπερ κτἑ. Philodemus was apparently discussing whether σ or ξ was the more euphonious in certain combinations, and preferred σύνοικος to ξύνοικος here.

The passage is several times referred to by grammarians and rhetoricians, but the name of the author is elsewhere omitted: see Apollonius de synt. 1. 2 ἐν οἷς δὶς τὸ αὐτὸ στοιχεῖον, παραλαμβάνεται, ἔλλαβεν ἔννεπε. . . ἀλλὰ Καὶ λέξις· ‘μῶσ’ ἄγε, μῶσα λίγεια,’ ‘ βαρὺς βαρὺς σύνοικος.’ (Η. ’s note on this passage in C.R. XIII 4 seems to be due to an oversight.) Phoebamm. ap. Walz Rhet. Gr. VIII p. 516 ἡ δὲ ἐπίζευξις τὸ αὐτὸ παρονομάζει συνημμένως, ὡς τὸ . . . ‘ βαρὺς βαρὺς σύνοικος.’ lohann. Sicel. ibid. vi p. 338 (discussing ἐπανάληψις) καὶ ἄλλως ‘ βαρὺς σύνοικος, ὦ φίλοι, βαρύς.’ Nauck points out that φίλοι in the last quotation is an example of a common error: e.g., LP give φίλῳ in Eur. Hec. 19.

The rhetorical repetition of a word or phrase is called indifferently by the grammarians ἀναδίπλωσις, ἐπανάληψις or ἐπαναφορά (Rutherford, Annotation, p. 269). ἐπίζευξις, employed by Phoebammon, is another less common term to express the same thing. Such a repetition as the above is rare in Sophocles (Ai. 620 ἔπεσ’ ἔπεσε, ib. 1205 ἐρώτων δ’ ἐρώτων, O.T. 1330 κακὰ κακά), but became a mannerism with Euripides (see on Hel. 176, Phoen. 103).

For βαρὺς ξύνοικος cf. Aesch. Suppl. 420 βαρὺν ξύνοικον θησόμεσθ’ ἀλάστορα. The metaphorical use of ξύνοικος (and πάροικος) was inherited from the lyric poets: cf. Sappho fr. 80 ὁ πλοῦτος ἄνευ τᾶς ἀρέτας οὐκ ἀσίνης πάροικος, Bacchyl. 14. 56 ὀλβίων παῖδές νιν (sc. Δίκαν) αἱρεῦνται σύνοικον, Ariphron (PLG 111 596) Ὑγίεια . . . σὺ δέ μοι πρόφρων σύνοικος εἴης. In Callim. h. Dem. 118 ἐμοὶ κακογείτονες ἐχθροί the use of κακογείτων as a nonepithetized compound is wrongly objected to by Meineke.
754 Δηὼ Casaubon: Δημήτηρ A

754 Antiphanes (fr. i, 11 12 K.) ap. Athen. 396 Β καὶ πρῶτα μὲν | αἴρω ποθεινὴν μᾶζαν, ἣν φερέσβιος | Δηὼ βροτοῖσι χάρμα δωρεῖται φίλον· | ἔπειτα πνικτὰ τακερὰ μηκάδων μέλη, | χλόην (χλόῃ Kock) καταμπέχοντα, σάρκα νεογενῆ. | —τί λέγεις;—τραγῳδίαν περαίνω [so Casaubon: παραινῶ A (cf. Eur. Hel. 1017)] Σοφοκλέους.

The verses of Antiphanes are obviously paratragoedic, and the sequel shows that they were modelled on Sophocles. It should, however, be stated that Kock thought that the younger Sophocles was referred to. Gomperz (Naehl. p. 12) rightly recognized that the spaced words were taken over in their entirety. The rest is doubtful, for the tragic vocabulary seems to have been placed in a ludicrous setting: for μηκάδων cf. fr. 509. In this connexion it is material to observe that, while the writers of the Middle Comedy were especially prone to direct parody (Athen. 482 c quotes Antiochus of Alexandria περὶ τῶν ἐν τῇ μέσῃ κωμῳδίᾳ κωμῳδουμένων ποιητῶν), they also followed with zest the practice of describing homely objects in the grandiloquent style of poetry. Thus on Ar. Plut. 515 ἢ γῆς ἀρότροις ῥήξας δάπεδον καρπὸν Δηοῦς θερίσασθαι
the schol. says: ἤδη τὸ ἔπος τοῦτο τῆς μέσης κωμῳδίας ὄζει. Antiph. fr. 52 (ΙΙ 31 K.) is a good example. The subject is treated by Meineke, FCG 1 291 ff. — Δηώ (Ant. 1121) was the hypocoristic form of Δημήτηρ, and the latter, originally a gloss, found its way into the text: see cr. n. and Hesych. I p. 484, Suid. s.v. For the language cf. Aesch. fr. 300, 7 φερέσβιον Δήμητρος . . .στάχυν.—χάρμα is a word undoubtedly borrowed from tragedy. —The language used suggests the subject of the Triptolemus.

lg.l: οὐ γάρ τι νόθος τῷδ᾿ ἀπεδείχθην,
Ζεὺς ἐμὸς ἄρΧων, θνητῶν δ᾿ οὐδείς.

div.p: 755. 1 ἀπεδείχθην Casaubon: ἀπεδείχθη vulgo 2 αὐτὸς vulgo

755 Arist. eth. Eud. 7. 10. 1242a 37 ἡ δὲ τῶν ἀδελφῶν (sc. φιλία) πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἑταιρικὴ μάλιστα ἡ κατ’ ἰσότητα. ῾ οὐ γάρ τι. . . ἄρχων.᾿ ταῦτα γὰρ ὡς τὸ ἴσον ζητούντων λέγεται. Bergk was the first to connect this passage with Philo quod omn. prob. lib. 3 II p. 448 M. τὸν ἀψευδῶς ἐλεύθερον ἀναζητῶμεν, ᾧ μόνῳ τὸ αὐτοκρατὲς πρόσεστι, καὶ ἂν μυρίοι γράφωσι δεσπότας ἑαυτούς. ἀναφθέγξεται γὰρ ἐκεῖνο τὸ Σοφόκλειον, οὐδὲν τῶν Πυθοχρήστων διαφέρον ῾ ὁ θεὸς ἐμοὶ (ἐμὸς cod. Med.) ἄρχων, θνητῶν δὲ οὐδὲ εἷς.᾿

It is usual to place a colon or a full-stop after ἐκλήθη; but in that case there is no obvious connexion between the two statements ‘ We are true brothers,’ and 'Zeus is my master’ ; and it is only the evidence of Philo which has prompted an arrangement unsuitable to the context in Aristotle. Susemihl's text has no stop. Too much importance need not be attributed to Philo; for the Stoic writer, from whom he drew, would not have hesitated to twist the quotation so as to fit his text. — Campbell ingeniously remarks that the text would suit the relation of Heracles to Iphicles. Heracles might well have been taunted with νοθεία: cf. Ar. Αν. 1650, where Poseidon says to him, νόθος γὰρ εἶ κοὐ γνήσιος. But we hear nothing to the credit of Iphicles, and the supposed friendship is at variance with the account of Hes. Scut. 88 ff.

1 οὐ γάρ τι: see on fr. 92. —τῷδ᾿ ἀπεδείχθην: ‘ he never exhibited me as....’ The sting lies in the publicity: Ο. T. 1405, Eur. Ion 879 οὓς ἀποδείξω | λέκτρων προδότας ἀχαρίστους, Ar. Ran. 1011 μοχθηροτάτους ἀπέδειξας. For the dative see Kuehner-Gerth I 422, Eur. Hclid. 39 n.

756 Athen. 23 C κατακεῖσθαι δὲ λέγεται καὶ κατακεκλίσθαι...ἔστι δὲ εὑρεῖν καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς ἐννοίας ταύτης σπανίως τὸ ἀνακεῖσθαι. σάτυρος παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ τοῦτό φησιν ἐπικαιόμενος τῷ Ἡρακλεῖ· ‘ἀνακειμένῳ...εἰσαλοίμην.’

Brunck with some probability referred the quotation to the Ἡρακλῆς ἐπὶ Ταινάρῳ; and he, as well as the editors of Athenaeus, assumed that the quotation from Sophocles began after φησιν. This involved certain metrical and other difficulties, which disappear as soon as it is recognized that ἀνακειμένῳ is the first word of the quotation. Nauck, who saw this, thought that the incident was referred to by Aristid. II p. 405 Dind., where the attack of philosophy upon rhetoric is compared to that of a satyr upon Heracles, ἤδη δέ τις καὶ σάτυρος τῶν ἐπὶ σκηνῆς κατηράσατο τῷ Ἡρακλεῖ, εἶτα γ᾽ ἔκυψε προσιόντος κάτω. It should be observed that Brunck had already connected this passage with the Ἡρακλῆς ἐπὶ Ταινάρῳ, not without reason,
although Heracles was such a common figure in the satyric drama (Wilamowitz, Eur. Her. I2 p. 98) that the chances are against his guess. But Nauck's view is impossible, and shows that the meaning of ἐπικαιόμενος has not hitherto been understood. Nauck quotes, apparently with approval, Kaibel's conjecture ἐπιμαινόμενος and must have interpreted it as 'infuriated against,' though it does not appear whether Kaibel had the same intention. Ellendt also was dissatisfied with ἐπικαιόμενος, and proposed ἐπικείμενος as 'pone accubans.' But ἐπικαιόμενος is sound, and was used, at any rate in the Hellenistic age, for 'to be inflamed with love.' Cf. schol. Ar. Lys. 221 ἐπιτυφῇ· ἐπικαυθῇ καὶ πυρωθῇ ἐπ᾿ ἐμοί. Hesych. II p. 173 ἐπιτυφῇ· ἐπικαῇ. ἐπιπυρωθῇ. Suid. s.v. ἐπιτυφῇ. With this meaning the purport of the quotation is clear enough. I have followed Kaibel in the division of the lines, although it is possible that the first line ended with μέσον.

The use of ἀνακεῖσθαι in place of κατακεῖσθαι of banqueters was treated as a solecism by the Atticists. Phryn. CXCI (p. 294 Ruth., p. 216 Lob.) ἀνάκειται μὲν γὰρ ἀνδριὰς καὶ ἀναθήματα καλῶς ἐρεῖς, ἀνάκειται δ᾽ ἐπὶ τῆς κλίνης οὐκέτι ἀλλὰ κεῖται. Similarly [Herodian.] Philetaer. (Moeris ed. Pierson, p. 441). Suid. s.v. ἀνακεῖσθαι. Ammon. p. 18. Yet, as the meaning was found in writers of repute, the grammarians were bound to explain it. Phryn. (Bekk. anecd.) p. 26, 23 ἀνακεῖσθαι· τὸ κατακεῖσθαι [violently and unnecessarily altered by de Borries (p. 46, 10)]. And Suid. continues: καὶ ἀνακεῖσθαι πολλάκις ἀντὶ τοῦ κατακεῖσθαι. But the best account is in Athen. 23 B—E, who quotes from Philippides (fr. 30, III 310 K.) the joke: ‘καὶ δειπνῶν ἀεὶ ἀνακείμενος παρ' αὐτόν.’ καὶ ἐπάγει· ‘πότερον ἀνδριάντας εἱστία;’ It is clear that κατακεῖσθαι became the fashionable term in the fourth cent. B.C., and that ἀνακεῖσθαι (and ἀναπίπτειν) were regarded as old-fashioned or 'provincial.'—εἰσαλοίμην, not εἰσαλαίμην, as Blaydes conjectured; for ἁλοίμην, ἁλέσθαι, etc. are well established beside ἡλάμην (ἡλόμην).

lg.l: ὦ γλῶσσα, σιγήσασα τὸν πολὺν χρόνον,
πῶς δῆτα τλήσῃ πρᾶγμ᾽ ἐπεξελθεῖν τόδε;
ὑφ᾽ ἧς τὸ κρυφθὲν ἐκφανεῖς ἀνακτόρων.

div.p: 757. 2 ἐπεξελθεῖν Brunck : ὑπεξελθεῖν CE, ὑπεξελεῖν Heimsoeth 4 ἀνακτόρων Grotius : ἀνάκτορον CE, ἀνάκτορι Meineke

757 Athen. 33 C 'ὦ γλῶσσα...ἀνάκτορον,' φησὶ Σοφοκλῆς. The context in Athenaeus does not assist the interpretation of the lines, which are simply the apologetic opening of a new speech. 'Welcker (p. 416) refers this frag. to the Μυσοί, supposing the verses to be spoken by an old servant of Auge, the mother of Telephus, whom the latter (not recognizing her) wishes to marry' (J.). Hartung assigns it to a messenger in the Tereus. H. with more probability thinks of Creusa.

2 ἐπεξελθεῖν is 'to relate.' 'Cp. fr. 919. Thuc. 1. 22. 2 ἀκριβείᾳ περὶ ἑκάστου ἐπεξελθών. So often in Plato. Heimsoeth's ὑπεξελεῖν = “to reveal” (as some take it in O.T. 227).' (J.) ὑπεξελθεῖν (see cr. n.), with the meaning 'to escape from,' and followed by an acc. after the analogy of ὑπεκδῦναι, ὑπεκδραμεῖν, etc. is not altogether indefensible, if we understand πρᾶγμα as the necessity of speaking rather than the secret itself.

3 ἀνάγκης. The thought is proverbial, and the words are a variant of the saying attributed to Thales, ἰσχυρότατον ἀνάγκη (Stob. ecl. 1. 4. 7a, p. 72, 1 W.). Hence Eur. Hel. 513 σοφῶν δ᾽ ἔπος, | δεινῆς ἀνάγκης οὐδὲν ἰσχύειν πλέον, Alc. 965 κρεῖσσον οὐδὲν ἀνάγκας ηὗρον, Aesch. Prom. 105 τὸ τῆς ἀνάγκης ἔστ᾽ ἀδήριτον σθένος, Eur. fr. 299 πρὸς τὴν ἀνάγκην πάντα τἄλλ᾽ ἔστ᾽ ἀσθενῆ, and other illus-
trations. So there are many echoes of Simonid. fr. 5, 21 ἀνάγκᾳ δ᾽ οὐδὲ θεοὶ μάχονται (fr. 256 n.).

4 τὸ κρυφθὲν...ἀνάκτορον was taken by Brunck and Schweighäuser as arcanum regium, — an impossible view. With ἀνακτόρων the sense is, 'the secret of (or concerning) my masters.' For the omission of the article cf. Ant. 365 τὸ μηχανόεν τέχνας, Eur. Phoen. 1097 τῷ νοσοῦντι τειχέων. Blaydes conj. ἔργον τορῶς.
758 ἔστιν coni. Herwerden
758 Athen. 40 A Σοφοκλῆς δὲ φησί ‘τὸ μεθύειν πημονῆς λυτήριον.’

Cobet (Coll. Crit. p. 201) proposed <κακὸν> τὸ μεθύειν, comparing Eur. fr. 1079. This was adopted by Nauck, but does not agree so well with the context in Athenaeus as Herwerden's addition. For the commonplace cf. Simonid. fr. 86 οἶνον ἀμύντορα δυσφροσυνάων. Alcae. fr. 41 οἶνον λαθικάδεα. Eur. Bacch. 280 βότρυος ὑγρὸν πῶμ'...ὃ παύει τοὺς ταλαιπώρους βροτοὺς | λύπης, ὅταν πλησθῶσιν ἀμπέλου ῥοῆς. ib. 772 τὴν παυσίλυπον ἄμπελον. Ar. Ran. 1321 βότρυος ἕλικα παυσίπονον. Tibull. 1. 2. 1 vinoque novos compesce dolores.
759 Athen. 52 B τὸ δὲ δένδρον καρύα παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ ‘καρύαι μελίαι τε.’

lg.l: θάρσει· μέγας σοι τοῦδ᾽ ἐγὼ φόβου μοχλός.

div.p: 760 Athen. 99 D Σοφοκλῆς δέ που ὁ ποιητὴς τὸν φύλακα μοχλὸν φόβου (που A : corr. Kaibel) ὠνόμασεν ἐν τούτοις ‘θάρσει...μοχλός.’ Eustath. Od. p. 1944, 26 copied the extract from Athenaeus.

For the metaphorical use of μοχλός (which does not occur elsewhere) see on fr. 761. The whole phrase was perhaps modelled on the Homeric ἕρκος πολέμοιο, ἕρκος ἀκόντων: for the objective genitive cf. also O. T. 1200 θανάτων πύργος. Eur. Med. 1322 ἔρυμα πολεμίας χερός. Ar. Vesp. 615 πρόβλημα κακῶν. Kuehner-Gerth I 336.

761 Athen. 99 D κἀν ἄλλοις δὲ τὴν ἄγκυραν ἰσχάδα κέκληκε (sc. Σοφοκλῆς) διὰ τὸ κατέχειν τὴν ναῦν. ῾ ναῦται . . . ἰσχάδα.’ Philodem. περὶ ποιημάτων 11 20 ed. Hausrath in Jahrb. Philol. Suppl. XVII 249 [ Herc. pap. coll. alt. iv f. 137 and VI f. 154] οἷον [ὅτα]ν ἐπὶ τοῦ [πλευσι]διᾶν Σοφοκλῆς [λέγ]ῃ ῾ ναῦτα <ι> ... [ἰσχά]δα.’

No other authority for ἰσχάς as ’an anchor’ seems to have been known to the grammarian who first made this quotation, and we may therefore assume that it was a linguistic experiment of Sophocles. It is imitated in Lucian Lexiph. 15 ἔκτοράς τινας ἀμφιστόμους καὶ
ἰσχάδας σιδηρᾶς ἀφείς. Cf. Philostr. vit. Apoll. 2. II χρυσῆν ἄγκυραν, ἣν νομίζουσιν Ἰνδοὶ κηρύκειον ἐπὶ τῷ πάντα ἴσχειν. Most of the examples in which a new sense is given to a word based on its real or supposed etymology are comic or at least fantastic : Athen. 98 c ff. gives examples from Dionysius the tyrant, who called a maiden μένανδρος and a pillar μενεκράτης. So Nicander called an asp ἰοχέαιρα; but, though Simonides (fr. 231) named Zeus ἀρίσταρχος and Aeschylus (fr. 406) gave the epithet ἀγησίλαον to Hades, the fancifulness lay rather with their imitators (Callim. Lav. Pall. 130, Α. Ρ. 7. 545). See also Starkie on Vesp. 589, who compares εὐλαβὴς λίθος, ‘a stone easy to grasp.’ Other illustrations in Arist. rhet. 3. 10. 141 Ia I ff. — νηός does not occur elsewhere in tragedy, although it is given by some MSS in Eur. Med. 523, where ναός is now read. In Eur. Ι. T. 1485 the MSS have νηῶν, but no one follows them. Here the authority for νηός, is exceptionally strong, and it would be hazardous to change it. The Doric ναός, is found in Ant. 715, Ai. 872, as well as in lyrics, and here and there in Aesch. and Eur.
762. 1 δὲ μύνδων coni. Bergk, ἐπερρεθείη L Clementis 2 σαίνοντες Brunck: σαίνουσιν AC | οὐραίαισι coni. Nauck

762 Athen. 277 B κατὰ γὰρ τὸν Σοφοκλέα ‘χορὸς . . . οὐραίοισι’ οὐ τὴν κεκτημένην ἀλλὰ τὰς λοπάδας. The first line is quoted without the name of its author by Clem. Alex. Strom. 6 Ρ. 787 χορὸς δὲ ἀναύδων ἰχθύων ἐπερρεθείη, ἡ μοῦσα ἡ τραγικὴ εἴρηκέν που.

Brunck suggested that the lines belong to the Ἀχιλλέως ἐρασταί, being a description by Peleus of the coming to land of Thetis on the occasion when he won her as his bride. He is followed by Hartung, who assigns them to the Peleus. It is quite as likely that the mistress of the band of fishes is Amphitrite: see Hom. ε 422, μ 97.

1 χορός. There is a comparison to a trained chorus singing and dancing harmoniously under the direction of the master-musician. The love of music popularly attributed to the dolphin gives a particular justification to the allusion : ps.-Arion (PLG III 80) 4 βραγχίοις περὶ δὲ σὲ πλωτοὶ | θῆρες χορεύουσι κύκλῳ, Anacreont. 55, 24 δελφῖσι χορευταῖς, Eur. El. 435 ἵν᾿ ὁ φίλαυλος ἔπαλλε δελφὶς πρῴραις κυανεμβόλοις, Hel. 1454 χοραγὲ τῶν καλλιχόρων δελφίνων, Pind. fr. 235 δελφῖνος ὑπόκρισιν· | τὸν μὲν ἀκύμονος ἐν πόντου πελάγει | αὐλῶν ἐκίνησ᾿ ἐρατὸν μέλος. The music of the chorus proceeds from the lashing of the water by their tails, so that there is an ironical oxymoron in the use after ἀναύδων of ἐπερρόθει, which suggests deliberately the combined voices of the choristers. H. quotes in this connexion Aesch. Cho. 456 στόσις δὲ πάγκοινος ἅδ᾿ ἐπιρροθεῖ, Eur. Hec. 553 λαοὶ δ᾿ ἐπερρόθησαν, Or. 901.—For Bergk's conjecture (see cr. n.) cf fr. 1072, and for ἀναύδων Ai. 1297 ἐλλοῖς ἰχθύσιν, Aesch. Pers. 580.

2 σαίνοντες οὐραίοισι. For σαίνω see on frs. 687, 885, and Blomfield’s elaborate discussion on Aesch. Theb. 379. The present passage is illustrated by two descriptions of Poseidon’s progress over the sea: Quint. 5. 93 τοὶ δ᾿ ἑκάτερθεν ἀολλέες ἀμφὶ ἄνακτα | ἀγρόμενοι δελφῖνες ἀπειρέσιον κεχάροντο, | σαίνοντες βασιλῆα. Philostr. imag. i. 8. i ἡ θάλαττα γαλήνην ἄγει παραπέμπουσα αὐτὸν αὐτοῖς ἵπποις καὶ αὐτοῖς κήτεσι· καὶ γὰρ ἐκεῖνα ἕπεται καὶ σαίνει τὸν Ποσειδῶνα. Immediately after our passage, Athen. quotes Achaeus fr. 27 πολὺς γὰρ ὅμιλος ποντίου κύκλου σοβῶν ἐνάλιος θεωρία, χραίνοντες οὐραίοισιν εὐδίαν ἁλός: the words are corrupt and mutilated, but Achaeus, who was a few years younger than Sophocles, seems to have imitated him here.— τὴν κεκτημένην. Η. writes: ‘Moeris p. 201, 9 κεκτημένη, ἡ δέσποινα, παρὰ τοῖς Ἀττικοῖς. Pollux 3. 73 δεσπότης, δεσπόζων, κύριος, κεκτημένος (Φρύνιχος γὰρ ἐν Σατύροις [fr. 48, 1 382 K.] τὸν δεσπότην κεκτημένον ὠνόμασεν), ἐωνημένος (Ar. Plut. 7), πριάμενος . . . δέσποινα, δεσπόζουσα, κεκτημένη, ἐωνημένη,
πριαμένη. Bekk. anecd. p. 102, 20 κυρίαν οὔ φασι δεῖν λέγειν, ἀλλὰ κεκτημένην· τὸν δὲ κεκτημένον μὴ λέγεσθαι ἀντὶτοῦ δεσπότου. Σατυρικοῖς κεκτημένον λέγει, Φιλήμων κυρίαν, is mutilated and corrupt. We have τίς δ᾿ ἂν φίλους ὄνοιτο τοὺς κεκτημένους; in Aesch. Suppl. 339, ὁ κεκτημένος Ar. Fhii. 4, Xen. oec. 20. 22, τῆς ἐμῆς κεκτημένης (as though a substantive) Ar. Eccl. 1126 [so Menand. Her. 37 and elsewhere], ἡ κεκτημένη Lucian II 580, 111 301, Alciphr. 3. 63. Slaves are κτήματα Eur. Med. 48, Arist. pol. 1. 4. 1253b 32. — In this sense tragedy elsewhere uses ἡ κρατοῦσα Aesch. Cho. 730, Soph. Track. 405 πρὸς τὴν κρατοῦσαν Δῃάνειραν, “ the mistress, Deianira” (rather than as Jebb, “ the royal”) ’—Brunck’s emendation (see cr. n.) seems indispensable, and is certainly preferable to σαίνουσι δ’ (adopted by Campbell from an earlier suggestion of Nauck), or ἐπιρροθῶν ἔσαινεν (Blaydes). The change is perhaps supported by the fr. of Achaeus, and the MS reading may have been due to the following dative. For the concord κατὰ σύνεσιν see Gildersleeve, § 122.

lg.l: διψῶντι γάρ τοι πάντα προσφέρων σοφὰ
οὐκ ἂν πλέον τέρψειας ἢ ᾿μπιεῖν διδούς.

div.p: 763 ἢ ᾿μπιεῖν Person: μὴ πιεῖν AC, ἢ πιεῖν Casaubon
763 Athen. 433 E τὸ δίψος γὰρ πάσιν ἰσχυρὰν ἐπιθυμίαν ἐμποιεῖ τῆς περισσῆς ἀπολαύσεως, διὸ καὶ ὁ Σοφοκλῆς φησι ‘ διψῶντι . . . διδούς.᾿

1f. ῾ Νο display of wisdom would be so welcome to a thirsty man as an offer to drink.’ For προσφέρω see on fr. 502 There is a remarkable echo of the first line in Eur. Med. 298 σκαιοῖσι μὲν γὰρ καινὰ προσφέρων σοφὰ | δόξεις ἀχρεῖος, most successfully parodied in Ar. Thesin. 1 130 σκαιοῖσι γάρ τοι καινὰ προσφέρων σοφὰ | μάτην ἀναλίσκοις ἄν. In Eur. Ι.Α. 97 πάντα προσφέρων λόγον is ‘ using every form of argument.’ Cf. Aesch. fr. 322 κάπηλα προσφέρων τεχνήματα, ῾ using knavish tricks.’ In Pind. ol. 9. 107 σοφίαι μὲν | αἰπειναί· τοῦτο δὲ προσφέρων ἄεθλον it is not always observed that τοῦτο looks back to σοφίαι, i.e. a prize of poetry. Bakhuyzen (de parodia, p. Ι35) argues that these lines really belong to a comic poet, perhaps Sophilus, who, like Aristophanes, was parodying the passage in the Medea. This is to build on a very weak foundation: it would be surprising if we did not occasionally find coincidences of language in the tragic poets even more striking than this. — — ἢ ᾿μπιεῖν. Nauck and Cobet prefer Casaubon’s reading, and Blaydes thinks that the simple verb, which has usage in its favour, is necessary: Hdt. 4. 72 ἐκ τῆς χειρὸς διδοῖ πιεῖν, Anth. Pal. 12. 34 εἷς δὲ πιεῖν ἐδίδου. But cf. Xen. Cyr. 7. 1. 1 τῷ Κύρῳ προσήνεγκαν ἐμπιεῖν καὶ φαγεῖν. Thus there is no valid objection to ἐμπιεῖν, which accounts better for the corruption of the MSS. Although ἐμπίνειν is commonly applied to convivial drinking, it is not exclusively so employed, but signifies strictly ’ to take a draught ’ of anything: cf. Hdt. 4. 64, Flut. de garrul. 14 p. 509 D. Sternbach's τι δούς for διδούς is unnecessary.

lg.l: ἣ τὰς ἀρύστεις ὧδ᾿ ἔχουσ᾿ ἐκώμασας.

div.p: 764 Athen. 783 F λέγουσι δὲ καὶ πρόχουν ἄρυστιν. Σοφοκλῆς ῾ κακῶς . . . ἐκώμασας.᾿

The colloquial character of the lines leaves little doubt that they are drawn from a satyr-play. Meineke completed the first line by adding κακή before κακῶς, and Nauck adopts his suggestion.
The addition suits the context; for the idiom κακὸς κακῶς is common in comedy, and where it occurs in serious poetry (e.g. Phil. 1369) is part of an imprecation. Still, Meineke's conjecture is hardly more than a possibility.
1 κακῶς ὀλουμένη is partly colloquial, but in comedy we should have ἀπολουμένη (e.g. Ar. Ach. 778). ’A curse upon you!’ See further on Eur. Hclid. 874 τοῦ κακῶς ὀλουμένου.

2 ἀρύστεις here means ῾ ladles ’ or ’bowls.’ It belongs to the same group as ἀρυστήρ, ἀρύταινα and ἀρύβαλλος, the two latter of which denoted the vessels used in the bath for administering a douche (Neil on Ar. Eq. 1090). The inference is that the ἄρυστις )( κύαθος was of considerable size, and even the diminutive ἀρύστιχοι could be used for voting-urns (Ar. Vesp. 855). The conclusion is fortified by Hesych. I 294 ἀρύστεις· τὰς ἀπνευστὶ πόσεις (‘bumpers’). τὸ δὲ αὐτὰ καὶ ἀρυστῆρας καὶ ἀρυστίχουσ ἐκάλουν. Hence Kaibel restores in Athen. l.c. ἐστὶ δὲ καὶ πόσις (for πόλις) Ἰώνων ἄρυστις. The word, to be compared with φύστις, ξύστις, ἄμυστις, is strictly a nomen actionis, but acquires the concrete sense by transference, like ἄροσις, βάσις, ὄψεις, and many other examples collected by Lobeck, Paralip. p. 442. Campbell’s hesitation is thus unjustifiable. — The fact that ὧδ᾿ ἔχων is generally intransitive, as in El. 789, has caused some doubt as to the meaning; but neither Hartung’s view that ἀρύστεις is a cognate ace. to be taken with ἐκώμασας (’das Becherfest'), nor Meineke’s alteration ὧδ’ ἑλοῦσ’ ἐκόμπασας, can be approved. There is no valid objection to rendering ‘ with the bowls in your hands like that,’ ὧδε being deictic. But it is much better to join ὧδ᾿ ἐκώμασας (’hast burst in hither’) giving the verb its natural complement. For the hyperbaton cf. (e.g.) Eur. Hclid. 844.
765 γὰρ ἡ seclusi

765 Athen. 592 A Σοφοκλῆς δ᾿ ὁ τραγῳδιοποιὸς ἤδη γέρων ὢν ἠράσθη Θεωρίδος τῆς ἑταίρας . . . . . τῆς δὲ Θεωρίδος μνημονεύει λέγων ἔν τινι στασίμῳ (στασίμως A: corr. Casaubon) οὕτως· ῾ φίλη γὰρ ἡ θεωρίς.᾿

The assertion of Athenaeus that Sophocles formed a connexion with a certain hetaera named Theoris is supported by Suid. s.v. Ἰοφῶν, which is practically identical with schol. V Ar. Pan. 78 φασὶ δὲ ὅτι καὶ Ἀρίστων τοῦ Σοφοκλέους νόθος υἱὸς ἐγεγόνει ἔκ τινος Θεφρίδος Σικυωνίας. See also Hermesianax ap. Athen. 598 c. From the anonymous vit.. Soph. 7 (p. Lii Blaydes) and Suid. s.v. Σοφοκλῆς we learn that Ariston had a son called Sophocles, whom his grandfather preferred to his legitimate son lophon. The comparison is prompted by the fact that lophon and the younger Sophocles were both tragic poets themselves; and the second Argument to the Oed. Col. states that that play was produced by the younger Sophocles in 402 B.C. after his grandfather's death. It should be observed that, if these facts are admitted, they tend to discount the value of Athenaeus’ statement that the connexion with Theoris belonged to the old age of Sophocles. Further in CIA II 672 there is mentioned a certain Sophocles, the son of lophon, of Colonus; and, though it is of course possible, as Haigh (Tragic Drama, p. 1325) suggests, that lophon also had a son named Sophocles, the story of Theoris and her son is highly suspicious, and has all the appearance of being nothing more than a chronique scandaleuse. However this may be, it is obvious that the detection of a reference to Theoris in the words φίλη γὰρ ἡ θεωρίς was only a foolish jest. These words appear to be part of an iambic line, although they are quoted from a chorus, and it is at least possible that they are really taken from a comic poet, who saw his opportunity in the fact that Sophocles had applied the epithet φίλῃ to θεωρίς: for these reasons I bracket γὰρ ἡ. I do not see much probability in Nauck’s suggestion that θεωρίς was used by Sophocles in the sense of βάκχη (Hesych. 11 p. 312); it is more likely that he was referring to the sacred vessel ’beloved (by Apollo)’: contrast Aesch. Theb. 842. Welcker had no sufificient ground for referring this fr. to the Triptolemus.
766 Athen. 688 Α καὶ ὁ Σοφοκλῆς δὲ τὰς ἀπολελυμένας τοῦ φόβου πεποίηκε λεγούσας· ‘θυμῷ...θυγάτηρ.’

‘Locus graviter corruptus,’ says Blaydes; but scholars have exercised themselves over the passage from the time of Casaubon without agreeing on any particular remedy. Meineke's θυμῷ δ' οὐκέτι καρδία | χορεύει τάρβους θυγάτηρ is, apart from οὐκέτι (Brunck) for οὔτι (the old vulgate, at one time reported as the reading of A), the same text which Casaubon deliberately rejected for the conclusive reason that it is not the heart itself but its throbbing which can be properly described as the daughter of Fear. The chief advantage of Bamberger's ἐλπίς for οὔτις is that it removes the difficulty of φαιδρά (v. infra), but, apart from other objections, it is decisively condemned by the context in Athenaeus, whose declared purpose is to illustrate the thesis, κατὰ τὰς ἐν τοῖς φόβοις γινομένας ἀγωνίας πάλλεσθαι τὴν καρδίαν ἐπιδηλότατα συμβαίνει (687 F). The text may be rendered: ‘No daughter of Fear dances blithely in our breasts.’ That is an extraordinarily bold figure for ‘No heart throbs tumultuously with fear,’ but may perhaps be justified in detail. (1) It is always the fear of an impending danger which begets the heart-throb. So Hom. K 93, Anaxandrides (fr. 59, II 160 Κ.), and Plat. Tim. 70 c, quoted by Athenaeus. See also Eur. Bacch. 1289 λέγ', ὡς τὸ μέλλον καρδία πήδημ' ἔχει, Soph. O. T. 153 ἐκτέταμαι φοβερὰν φρένα δείματι πάλλων, Aesch. Prom. 907 κραδία δὲ φόβῳ φρένα λακτίζει, Suppl. 793 κελαινόχρως δὲ πάλλεταί μου καρδία . . . οἴχομαι φόβῳ, Cho. 410 πέπαλται δ’ αὖτέ μοι φίλον κέαρ (with the context), ib. 166 ὀρχεῖται δὲ καρδία φόβῳ, ib. 1023, where κρότῳ is surely right. Plaut. Capt. 636 quin quiescis dierectum cor meum? ac suspende te. | tu sussultas, ego miser vix asto prae formidine. Aul. 626 (after a bad omen) continuo meum cor coepit artem facere ludicram | atque in pectus emicare. Cas. 413 f., Cist. 551. (2) This consideration will account for the boldness of the personification, which is not really stronger than that of the oracle's reply represented as the child of Hope in Ο.Τ. 157 εἰπέ μοι, ὦ χρυσέας τέκνον Ἐλπίδος, ἄμβροτε Φάμα. Our taste is more offended by Aesch. Pers. 581 παίδων τᾶς ἀμιάντου, but we must not assume that Sophocles was impeccable: cf. [Longin.] de sublim. 33. 5. (3) For θυμῷ, which is impeached by Campbell, cf. Aesch. Suppl. 575 χλωρῷ δείματι θυμὸν | πάλλοντ’ ὄψιν ἀήθη. (4) φαιδρά may be thought inconsistent with τάρβους: hence λαιδρά was conjectured by Jacobs, and Schweighäuser adopted the impossible rendering ‘openly.’ The best answer is to quote Anaxandrides l.c.: ὦ πονηρὰ καρδία, | ἐπιχαιρέκακον ὡς εἶ μόνον τοῦ σώματος· ὀρχῇ γὰρ εὐθύς, ἄν <μ'> ἴδῃς δεδοικότα. For the adverbial acc. neut. plural see on Eur. Hel. 455 ἀνάξι' ἠτιμώμεθα, and add Bacch. 435 ἄκρανθ᾿ ὡρμήσαμεν, Her. 898 ἄκραντα βακχεύσει. (5) The minor corrections of οὔτις (οὐκέτι Brunck, οὔτοι Dindorf) are unnecessary, if the text is generally sound. The multiplication of persons by the speaker does not increase the harshness of the image.
Welcker refers the lines to the Nausicaa, Hartung to the Lemnians.
767 παρασύρας Choerob. cod. V et Etym. M.: παρὰ συρὰν Choerob. codd. NC

767 Choerob. in Theod. p. 278, 27 [=267, 6 Hilgard] ἡ ἴκτινα αἰτιατικὴ... οὐκ ἔστιν ὡς ἀπὸ τῆς ἴκτιν εὐθείας,...ἀλλ᾿ ἔστιν ἴκτινος ἡ εὐθεῖα, ὡς παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ· ‘ἴκτινος...κρέας.’ Etym. M. p. 470, 103 (p. 1345 Gaisf.)=Etym. Flor. ed. Miller
p. 167, and Zonar. lex. p. 1100 ἴκτινος ἔκλαγξε (ἔκραξε cod. Haun. and Zonar.) παρασύρας κρέας.

παρασύρας expresses the swiftly swooping movement of the kite as he descends upon his food, and snatches it away without faltering. Neither L. and S.'s ‘filch,’ nor Campbell's ‘as it tears at the carrion’ is satisfactory. Ellendt's praetervolando trahere is better, but fails to give the exact force of παρασύρειν. The proper application of the word is to a river in full flood sweeping away every obstacle: see lexx. and the metaphorical use in [Longin.] de sublim. 32. 4 τῷ ῥοθίῳ τῆς φορᾶς ταυτὶ (sc. τὰ πάθη) πέφυκεν ἅπαντα τἄλλα παρασύρειν καὶ προωθεῖν. —Choerob.'s reading suggested παρασύρων to Blaydes, but the aor. is better. — For the accentuation of ἴκτινος (ἰκτῖνος) see Chandler, § 290, and for the general sense cf. Semonid. fr. 11 σπλάγχν’ ἀμφέποντες αὐτίκ’ ἰκτίνου δίκην.

lg.l: φυσᾷ γὰρ οὐ σμικροῖσιν αὐλίσκοις ἔτι,

div.p: 768 Cic. Att. 2. 16. 2 Gnaeus quidem noster iam plane quid cogitet nescio, ‘φυσᾷ γὰρ . . . ἄτερ.’ [Longinus] de subl. 3. 2 φλοιώδης γὰρ ἁνὴρ καὶ φυσῶν κατὰ τὸν Σοφοκλέα μικροῖς μὲν αὐλίσκοισι, φορβειᾶς δ’ ἄτερ.

Welcker assigned these lines to the Orithyia, and there has been a lively controversy whether Sophocles actually wrote a play with such a title. It must be observed in the first place that Longinus and Cicero do not agree, and that, if they are referring to the same passage, either Longinus is quoting inaccurately or his text is corrupt (οὐ σμικροῖς Toll, and so Wecklein). For the bearing of this on the interpretation of σμικροὶ αὐλίσκοι see below. Immisch (Rh. Mus. XLVIII 512) infers that Cicero's quotation is from a different original, and that it should be removed to the tragic adespota. But it is difficult to believe that two passages so nearly identical, and both familiar in their rhetorical application, were entirely independent of each other. Immisch has left out of account the possibility that Longinus adapted the quotation from Sophocles to suit his particular contention, that bombast is especially contemptible if coming from an inferior artist — a possibility which applies equally well, if we accept Immisch's interpretation of αὐλίσκοι and φορβειά. Marx (Wiener Stud. XX 191) for different reasons arrives at a conclusion similar to that of Immisch, that Aeschylus wrote the lines quoted by Cicero, and that Sophocles imitated them (cf. fr. 805). He is then obliged to assume that Longinus quoted the passage of Sophocles twice in a similar context, but with an entirely different purpose in either case. The assumption is improbable and gives too much weight to the precarious evidence of Iohannes Siceliota. That Sophocles compared a violent utterance to an inartistic performance by a flute-player appears to be certain. But what is there to show that he was speaking of Boreas? Or, even if so, that the quotation belonged to an Orithyia? The only direct evidence in favour of an affirmative answer is fr. 805, where see note. Some weight ought perhaps also to be attached to fr. 956. Since the allusion to Orithyia occurs not in a chorus but in an iambic narrative, it is natural to infer that it was relevant to the main action of the play in which it occurred. Buecheler in Rh. Mus. xxxix 274 agreed with Welcker, thinking that Sophocles imitated and criticized the Orithyia of Aeschylus in a play written under the same title. On the whole, I prefer to follow G. Wolff, who in Philol. XXVIII 343 argued that the existence of an Orithyia was not established, and referred fr. 956 to the Tympanistae.

φυσᾷ appears to be used here with metaphorical import, as our ‘blow’ is employed dialectically in the sense of ‘to blow one's own trumpet.’ See Headlam on Herond. 2. 32, and cf. Dem. 19. 314 τὰς γνάθους φυσῶν, describing the self-importance of Aeschines, Hyperid. fr. 91 K. (Athen. 591 F) οὐ σιωπήσῃ, μειράκιον, μεῖζον τῆς μητρὸς ἔχων τὸ φύσημα; addressed to Demeas, the son of an αὐλητρίς, who had been adopted by Demades. There was something ridiculous to the Athenians in the puffed-out cheeks of the flute-player (Plut. Alcib.
2), and this feeling contributed towards the aesthetic objection which made them speak contemptuously of the flute. Hence the epigram (Athen. 337 E): ἀνδρὶ μὲν αὐλητῆρι θεοὶ νόον οὐκ ἐνέφυσαν, | ἀλλ’ ἅμα τῷ φυσῆν χὠ νόος ἐκπέταται. This contempt was symbolized for them in the legend which represented Athena as throwing away the flute in disgust at the disfigurement which it caused (Melanippides fr. 2, 3, Telestes fr. 1, 3), and Marsyas as having subsequently picked it up; and was not the less cherished because flute-playing happened to be the favourite art of the despised Boeotians (Plut. l.c., Ar. Ach. 862 ff., Plat. rep. 399 E, Frazer on Pausan. 1. 24. 1). Here the diminutive αὐλίσκοι is significant; the plural (cf. αὐλοί) refers to the double flute: see Dict. Ant. II 840 (s.v. tibia), where also the contrivance of the φορβειά is explained. Its absence suggests that the player was not a skilled musician or properly equipped: see Ar. Vesp. 582 κἂν αὐλητής γε δίκην νικᾷ, ταύτης ἡμῖν ἐπίχειρα | ἐν φορβειᾷ τοῖσι δικασταῖς ἔξοδον ηὔλησ’ ἀπιοῦσιν. Cf. the account of its invention by Marsyas: Plut. cohib. ir. 6 p. 456 C φορβειᾷ τινι καὶ περιστομίοις τοῦ πνεύματος τὸ ῥαγδαῖον ἐγκαθεῖρξε. Ο. Immisch, however, who thinks that Cicero and Longinus are not referring to the same passage, would explain Longinus by identifying μικροὶ αὐλίσκοι with παρθένιοι (Athen. 176 E, 634 F), which owing to their extreme shrillness especially required the moderating influence of the φορβειά. Thus Cicero's poet means: ‘he blows no longer on a small flute (i.e. such as is not well adapted to a violent fortissimo, but requires the moderating influence of the mouthpiece), but a full deep note on a large flute without a mouthpiece.’ Sophocles, on the other hand, was referring to a musician who strained his delicate instrument by blowing too loud on it. See however Guhl and Koner, p. 209: it is not easy to understand why the φορβειά was any the less requisite on a more powerful instrument.
769 Clem. Alex. paedag. 3 p. 286 ἁβροδίαιτον ἐπονειδίζων νεανίαν ὁ Σοφοκλῆς λέγει ‘γυναικομίμοις . . . ἐσθήμασι.’

Bergk thinks that the reference to Sophocles was an error (Introduction, § 1), and that the passage actually intended was Eur. fr. 185, 3 γυναικομίμῳ διαπρέπεις μορφώματι, which has been recovered from Plato and Philostratus. The resemblance is close, but cf. Eur. Bacch. 978 ἐπὶ τὸν ἐν γυναικομίμῳ στολᾷ. Moreover, ἐμπρέπεις is shown to be Sophoclean by El. 1187 ὁρῶν σε πολλοῖς ἐμπρέπουσαν ἄλγεσιν, where the verb suggests by contrast the picture of Electra as a royal princess πολλαῖς χλιδαῖσιν ἐμπρέπουσαν (Kaibel). Nauck's critical note requires modification; for Stählin's edition, which has since appeared, gives ἐμπρέπεις without recording any variant.

lg.l: πρὸς δ᾿ οἷον ἥξεις δαίμον’ [ὡς Ἔρωτα] . . .
ὃς οὔτε τοὐπιεικὲς οὔτε τὴν χάριν
οἶδεν, μόνην δ’ ἔστερξε τὴν ἁπλῶς δίκην.

div.p: 770. 1 ὡς ἔρωτα delendum arbitror 3 οἶδε μόνην Plut., ᾔδει μόνον Clem. | δὲ στέρξαι Plut., δ’ ἔστεργε Clem.

770 Clem. Alex. strom. 2 p. 494 P. εὖ γοῦν ἡ τραγῳδία ἐπὶ τοῦ Ἅιδου γράφει ‘πρὸς δ’ οἷον . . . ἁπλῶς δίκην.’ καὶ γὰρ εἰ μηδέπω ποιεῖν τὰ προσταττόμενα ὑπὸ τοῦ νόμου οἷοί τέ ἐστε, ἀλλά τοι . .. τρέφειν τε καὶ αὔξειν τὸν ἔρωτα τῆς ἐλευθερίας δυνάμεθα. Plut. amat. 17. 761 F δηλοῖ τὰ περὶ Ἄλκηστιν καὶ Πρωτεσίλεων καὶ Εὐρυδίκην τὴν Ὀρφέως, ὅτι μόνῳ θεῶν ὁ Ἅιδης Ἔρωτι ποιεῖ τὸ προσταττόμενον· καίτοι πρός γε τοὺς ἄλλους, ὥς φησι Σοφοκλῆς, ἅπαντας ‘οὔτε . . . δίκην.’ vv. 2 and 3 are also quoted
by Eustath. opusc. p. 305, 11 with the introductory words: εἰ καὶ μηδεμίαν χάριν οἶδε θάνατος κατὰ τὸν τραγῳδόν.
Η. renders: ‘And what a Power is he thou 'lt come before! That knows not favour, no, nor equity, But only cares for Justice absolute.’

The general sentiment recalls the famous fragment of Aeschylus (fr. 161): μόνος θεῶν γὰρ Θάνατος οὐ δώρων ἐρᾷ | οὐδ’ ἄν τι θύων οὐδ᾿ ἐπισπένδων ἄνοις, | οὐδ’ ἔστι βωμὸς οὐδὲ παιωνίζεται· | μόνου δὲ Πειθὼ δαιμόνων ἀποστατεῖ. Cf. Propert. 4. 11. 2 panditur ad nullas ianua nigra preces.

1 ὡς Ἔρωτα. ‘The context in Plutarch l.c. might at first sight suggest that Ἔρωτα was a vestige of words in which the poet described Hades as yielding to Love, though obdurate to the other gods (e.g. εἰς Ἔρωτα < μὲν | μόνον προσηνῆ, πρὸς δὲ τοὺς ἄλλους πικρόν, > ὃς κτέ.). [Mekler has since independently suggested almost exactly the same supplement: εἰς ἔρωτα < μὲν | πρᾷον πεφυκότ᾿, εἰς δὲ τοὺς ἄλλους βαρύν >.] But the context in Clement is not equally favourable to such a conjecture. Previous suggestions are : (1) ἐξερῶ τάχα Nauck. This (or ὡς ἐρῶ τάχα) might be supported by El. 35 ὧν πεύσει τάχα— followed immediately by the statement ἄσκευον κτέ. (2) ὡς στερρόν τινα R. Enger. (3) ὡς ἀγνώμονα Blaydes. (4) ὦ γέρον, τάχα Herwerden. (5) ὡς ἐρώμενον Welcker.’ (J.) R. Ellis preferred ὡς ἔρωτ᾿ ἄγειν, ‘for estimating love.’ It is curious that there should be a reference to Ἔρως in the immediate context of both authors who cite the fragment, since Sophocles appears only to have been concerned with the inexorability of Death. H. further notices that the phrase ποιεῖν τὸ προσταττόμενον (τὰ προσταττόμενα) is also to be found in both. Whatever may be the relation of Clement to Plutarch, if we suppose that their similarity is other than accidental, I should in any case hold that, so far as the text of Sophocles is concerned, the words ὡς Ἔρωτα have displaced the original script, and are to be attributed to a commentator who thought fit to compare the inflexible power of Love with that of Death, and had in view such passages as Ant. 781 ff., Trach. 441 ff., Soph. fr. 684. That such is the way of scholiasts hardly needs proof: a typical instance may be read in the scholia on Trach. 460. The conjectures mentioned above are based on the assumption that ὡς ἔρωτα is a mutilation of the original; but, if the view I have advocated is correct, it is idle to guess at the lost words. Tucker, following the same idea that occurred to J., proposed πρὸς δ’ οἶον εἴξει δαιμόνων Ἔρωτά τι. But, if Plutarch really intended to adduce the authority of Sophocles for the purpose supposed, is it likely that he would omit the verse which contained the pith of his statement?

2 f. τοὐπιεικές is contrasted with τὴν ἁπλῶς δίκην, much as we oppose ‘equity’ — in the non-technical sense—to the ‘rigour of the law.’ J. quotes Arist. eth. N. 5. 14. 1137b 11 τὸ ἐπιεικὲς δίκαιον μέν ἐστιν, οὐ κατὰ νόμον δέ, ἀλλ᾿ ἐπανόρθωμα νομίμου δικαίου. See also his n. on Ο. C. 1127. Cf. Eur. fr. 645: if the gods show mercy in certain cases, ἤτἄρα θνητῶν εἰσιν ἀσυνετώτεροι, | ἢ τἀπιεικῆ πρόσθεν ἡγοῦνται δίκης. Valckenaer (diatr. p. 188) gave a good illustration from Plutarch’s description of the younger Cato, who, following the Stoic pattern of the wise man (Chrysipp. II 640 Arn.), refused to deviate from the strictest norm of Justice: διαφόρως τοῦ καλοῦ τὸ περὶ τὴν δικαιοσύνην ἀτενὲς καὶ ἄκαμπτον εἰς ἐπιείκειαν ἢ χάριν ὑπερηγαπηκώς (Plut. Cat. mi. 4).

lg.l: σκαιοῖς δὲ φαῦλον κἀν βραχεῖ διδάσκαλον.

div.p: 771. 2 ἐνικτῆρα . . . αἰεί L Clementis

771 Clem. Alex. strom. 5 p. 659 Σοφοκλῆς ὁ τῆς τραγῳδίας ποιητής φησί που ῾καὶ τὸν . . . διδάσκαλον,᾿ τὸ φαῦλον ἐπὶ τοῦ ἁπλοῦ τάσσων: vv. 2 and 3 are also quoted by Plut. de Pyth. or. 25 p. 406 F εὖ γὰρ εἰδέναι χρὴ τὸν θεόν, ὥς φησι Σοφοκλῆς, ῾σοφοῖς. . . διδάσκαλον.᾿

The fragment is variously interpreted.
Brunck remarked: ῾ aeque vera videretur sententia, si duabus transpositis vocibus legeretur: σκαιοῖς μὲν αἰνικτῆρα . . . σοφοῖς δὲ φαῦλον κτἑ. Sed alterum tuetur auctoritas librorum. In his nihil decerni potest, quum ignoretur a qua persona et qua occasione sententia recitata fuerit.’ It is plain that he had no clear conception of the meaning. There is little profit to be had from the older versions, and C. W. King’s rendering of the third line — ‘ to fools a bad instructor even in trifles ’—is certainly wrong. J.'s note runs as follows: ῾ σοφοῖς . . . σκαιοῖς: cp. Eur. El. 972 ὅπου δ᾿ Ἀπόλλων σκαιὸς ᾖ, τίνες σοφοί; (“foolish ”—“wise”). By αἰνικτῆρα θεσφάτων it is implied that the god wishes to exercise the understanding of the “ wise, ” and to give them subtler or deeper lessons than suit the σκαιοί—not that he wishes to keep them in the dark. φαῦλον= ἁπλοῦν (according to Clement), “ simple ” : that is, he speaks in the language of φαῦλοι, the common sort, to those who can understand nothing more subtle: Eur. Hipp. 988 οἱ γὰρ ἐν σοφοῖς | φαῦλοι παρ᾿ ὄχλῳ μουσικώτεροι λέγειν. So Thuc. 3. 37. 3 οἱ φαυλότεροι . . . πρὸς τοὺς ξυνετωτέρους.᾿ J. evidently thought that the verses express the character or purpose of Apollo, that he chooses to be enigmatical to the wise, but straightforward to the foolish. I agree, however, with H. (Proc. Camb. Phil. Soc. 1907, p. 17) that both σοφοῖς and σκαιοῖς are to be taken as datives iudicantis—a view which seems to have been anticipated by Ellendt, who remarks: ’deum dicit sapientibus obscura et ambigua, stultis intellectu facilia portendere videri.’ H. points out that the interpretation adopted by J. cannot be reconciled with the meaning either of σκαιοῖς or of φαῦλον: thus φαῦλος does not mean ’simple’ in the sense of clear, lucid (τορός), or unconfused; and σκαιός, when used in a moral sense, always implies moral obliquity, i.e. it is equivalent to ’perverse’ or ’wrong-headed.’ He quotes Aesch. Prom. 637 λέξω τορῶς σοι . . . οὐκ ἐμπλέκων αἰνίγματ᾿, ἀλλ᾿ ἁπλῷ λόγω, Suppl. 473 αἰνιγματῶδες τοὔπος· ἀλλ᾿ ἁπλῶς φράσον, adding that the contrast is different here where φαῦλος and not ἁπλοῦς is used. H. renders accordingly: ῾ to the wise a hinter of deep meaning oracles, but in the eyes of the perversely stupid only a poor and meagre teacher.’ I doubt if this gives the tone of the last line. The wise view the god as αἰνικτήρ, and seek for an interpretation; the fool regards only the surface meaning. The attitude of the σκαιοί, who think that they understand the oracle but do not, is admirably illustrated in Dio Chrys. 10. 22-32. The clown (for σκαιός see on Eur. Hclid. 458, and Starkie on Vesp. 1183) thinks there is nothing to understand; Apollo is a plain person, of few words — like himself; an expounder in brief, μὴ ἐν πολλοῖς ὀλίγα λέγων ἀλλ’ ἐν ὀλίγοις πολλά, as Pythagoras recommended; no longwinded sophist, such as Protagoras, with his μακρολογία. (The difficulties of brevity the σκαιός does not realize: σοφοῦ πρὸς ἀνδρὸς ὅστις ἐν βραχεῖ | πολλοὺς καλῶς οἷός τε συντέμνειν λόγους Eur. fr. 28.) ἁπλοῦς ὁ μῦθος τῆς ἀληθείας ἔφυ (Eur. Phoen. 469) is the creed of the ordinary person (φαῦλος). Subtilty or elaboration, the refinements (ἀκριβεια) of the philosopher or the smoothness of the rhetorician, he treats with equal suspicion—ταῦτ᾿ αὔθ᾿ ἕκαστα, μῆτερ, οὐχὶ περιπλοκὰς | λόγων ἀθροίσας εἶπον, ἀλλὰ καὶ σοφοῖς | καὶ τοῖσι φαύλοις ἔνδικα (ib. 494 ff.). Just what Mark Antony feigned to be, ‘ a plain blunt man’ who ’speaks right on,’ that Heracles really was: Eur. fr. 473 φαῦλον ἄκομψον, τὰ μέγιστ’ ἀγαθόν, | πᾶσαν ἐν ἔργῳ περιτεμνόμενον | σοφίαν, λέσχης ἀτρίβωνα. φαῦλος was a word of censure, which those at whom it was aimed somewhat contemptuously accepted: so it is applied by Cleon in Thuc. l.c., by Eur. Bacch. 431, Ion 834, and elsewhere. Hence φαυλότης is the condition of the ordinary person, ’the man in the street, ’ who has no technical skill: Eur. fr. 635 οἱ τὰς τέχνας δ’ ἔχοντες ἀθλιώτεροι | τῆς φαυλότητος, fr. 641 ἐν τῷ γὰρ ὄλβῳ φαυλότης ἔνεστί τις, | πενία δὲ σοφίαν ἔλαχε διὰ τὸ συγγενές.
