1 τοὺς πονοῦντας ὠφελεῖν, to aid the distressed, is the proper task not only of friends (Eur. Or. 665), but also of strangers: I. Α. 984 ἀλλ᾿ οὖν ἔχει τοι σχῆμα, κἄν ἄπωθεν ᾖ | ἀνὴρ ὁ χρηστός, δυστυχοῦντας ὠφελεῖν. Cf. ib. 1008, Or. 680, fr. 274.

2 Although Sophocles recognized that a generous deed rewards the doer (see Jebb on Ο. C. 309), yet such actions must be controlled by the supreme guidance of σωφροσύνη (φρόνησις ἁγαθή = εὖ φρονεῖν: cf. Eur. fr. 598, Chaerem. fr. 23), lest every reckless impulse should be blindly followed. — θεός: see n. on fr. 605. It should be observed that this tendency appears even in Aeschylus (Cho. 57 τὸ δ’ εὐτυχεῖν, | τόδ᾿ ἐν βροτοῖς θεός τε καὶ θεοῦ πλέον). Cf. Dicaeog. fr. 5 θεὸς μέγιστος τοῖς φρονοῦσιν οἱ γονῆς.

lg.l: ἀλλ᾿ οἱ κακῶς πράσσοντες οὐ κωφοὶ μόνον,

div.p: 923. 2 τἀμφανῆ A corr. m. sec.: τἀφανῆ MA
923 Stob. flor. 4. 1 (III p. 219, 14 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘ἀλλ᾿ οἱ...τἀμφανῆ.’

The stupefaction of the wretched is such that they are not only deaf (though they have ears), but having eyes they see not what is before them. The power of sensation depends on the mental balance, which is upset by misery: Epicharm. fr. 249 K. νοῦς ὁρῆι καὶ νοῦς ἀκούει· τἄλλα κωφὰ καὶ τυφλά. The result is distraction (παρακοπή) and loss of intelligence (ἄνοια); and these considerations explain why Stobaeus included the fr. in his chapter περὶ ἀφροσύνης. Cf. Philem. fr. 151, II 523 Κ. ἐπὰν ὁ νοῦς ᾖ μὴ καθεστηκώς τινι, | οὐκ ἔστ᾿ ἀκούειν οὐδὲν αὐτόν, οὐδ’ ὁρᾶν. Heraclit. fr. 34 D. ἀξύνετοι ἀκούσαντες κωφοῖσιν ἐοίκασι· φάτις αὐτοῖσιν μαρτυρεῖ παρεόντας ἀπεῖναι. Parmen. fr. 6, 5 D. ἀμηχανίη γὰρ ἐν αὐτῶν | στήθεσιν ἰθύνει πλακτὸν νόον· οἱ δὲ φοροῦνται | κωφοὶ ὁμῶς τυφλοί τε, τεθηπότες, ἄκριτα φῦλα κτἑ. But the best comment upon this passage is to be found in Plat. Tim. 86 B περιχαρὴς γὰρ ἄνθρωπος ὣν ἣ καὶ τἀναντία ὑπὸ λύπης πάσχων, σπεύδων τὸ μὲν ἑλεῖν ἀκαίρως τὸ δὲ φυγεῖν, οὔθ᾿ ὁρᾶν οὔτε ἀκούειν ὀρθὸν οὐδὲν δύναται, λυττᾷ δὲ καὶ λογισμοῦ μετασχεῖν ἥκιστα τότε δὴ δυνατός ἐστι.
The moral effect of misery, that it degrades as much as prosperity elevates the character, was pointed out by many of the early poets from Hom. σ 136 onwards. See also Adam on Plat. rep. 335 B.
1 Nauck would prefer ὡς οἱ κακῶς κτἑ.
924 δυσπάλαιστον Nauck: δυσπέλαστον codd. | ἐστιν add. Grotius | ἀμαθια A
924 Stob. flor. 4. 5 (III p. 220, 9 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘ὡς...κακόν.’

The reading of the MSS δυσπέλαστον would give the wrong sense, if retained. In Simon. fr. 29 ἀπέλαστον ἵππον ἤ κύνα the meaning is ‘unapproachable (in point of speed),’ and here δυσπέλαστον, which does not occur elsewhere, might mean ‘dangerous to approach.’ But that is not the reason why the enmity of the ἀμαθής is to be dreaded; it is not his active hostility, but his insensibility and brutality which make success impossible. ‘Against stupidity,’ as Schiller said (Jungfrau v. Orleans 3. 6. 28 mit der Dummheit kämpfen Götter selbst vergebens), ‘even the gods fight in vain.’ The danger of such an opponent owing to his lack of αἰδώς is pointed out by Euripides: Her. 299 φεύγειν σκαιὸν ἄνδρ' ἐχθρὸν χρεών, Hclid. 458 τοῖς σοφοῖς εὐκτὸν σοφῷ | ἔχθραν συνάπτειν μὴ ἀμαθεῖ φρονήματι, El. 294 ἔνεστι δ᾿ οἶκτος ἀμαθίᾳ μἐν οὐδαμοῦ, | σοφοῖσι δ’ ἀνδρῶν. The character of the man who neglects entirely μουσική and φιλοσοφία is thus described by Plato: rep. 411 D μισόλογος δή...ὁτοιοῦτος γίγνεται καὶ ἄμουσος...βίᾳ δὲ καὶ ἀγριότητι ὥσπερ θηρίον πρὸς πάντα διαπράττεται, καὶ ἐν ἀμαθίᾳ καὶ σκαιότητι μετὰ ἀρρυθμίας τε καὶ ἀχαριστίας ζῇ. Such a one is incurable from impervious self-satisfaction: symp. 204 A αὐτὸ γὰρ τοῦτό ἐστι χαλεπὸν ἀμαθία, τὸ μὴ ὄντα καλὸν κἀγαθὸν μηδὲ φρόνιμον δοκεῖν αὐτῷ εἶναι ἱκανόν.
925 Stob. flor. 4. 17 (III p. 223, 6 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘ἡ δὲ...ἔφυ.’ Cf. Prov. app. 3. 12 (Paroem. I 418).

It cannot be too strongly insisted that the Greeks drew no firm line between folly and wickedness. Intellectual dullness was a sign of moral depravity. To illustrate this adequately would require much space: see however Adam on Plat. Euthyphr. 2 C, rep. 382 A. Hence may be explained the Socratic identification of ἀρετή and ἐπιστήμη, and the paradox οὐδεὶς ἑκὼν πονηρός. Cf. Plat. Tim. 86 E κακὸς μὲν γὰρ ἑκὼν οὐδείς, διὰ δὲ πονηρὰν ἕξιν τινὰ τοῦ σώματος καὶ ἀπαίδευτον τροφὴν ὁ κακὸς γίγνεται κακός. soph. 228 D ψυχὴν ἀνόητον αἰσχρὰν καὶ ἄμετρον θετέον (with the context). Cleanth. fr. 106 τοὺς ἀπαιδεύτους (=σκαιούς, ἀμαθεῖς) τῇ μορφῇ τῶν θηρίων διαφέρειν. Το Socrates is attributed (Stob. flor. 4. 119): οὔτε τὰ τοῦ Ἀχιλλέως ὅπλα τῷ Θερσίτῃ, οὔτε τὰ τῆς ψυχῆς ἀγαθὰ τῷ ἄφρονι ἁρμόττει. See also on frs. 985, 1059.

οὐδεὶς ἑκὼν πονηρός. Cf. Plat. Tim. 86 E κακὸς μὲν γὰρ ἑκὼν οὐδείς, διὰ δὲ πονηρὰν ἕξιν τινὰ τοῦ σώματος καὶ ἀπαίδευτον τροφὴν ὁ κακὸς γίγνεται κακός. soph. 228 D ψυχὴν ἀνόητον αἰσχρὰν καὶ ἄμετρον θετέον (with the context). Cleanth. fr. 106 τοὺς ἀπαιδεύτους (= σκαιούς, ἀμαθεῖς) μόνῃ τῇ μορφῇ τῶν θηρίων διαφέρειν. To Socrates is attributed (Stob. flor. 4. 119): οὔτε τὰ τοῦ Ἀχιλλέως ὅπλα τῷ Θερσίτῃ, οὔτε τὰ τῆς ψυχῆς ἀγαθὰ τῷ ἄφρονι ἁρμόττει. See also on frs. 985, 1059.

lg.l: χαίρειν ἐπ᾿ αἰσχραῖς ἡδοναῖς οὐ χρή ποτε.

div.p: 926 Stob. flor. 5. 14 (III p. 256, 9 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ῾χαίρειν...ποτε.᾿ Cod. L adds ἐξ Αἴαντος from 13, which there follows. Cf. Menand. mon. 544 χαίρειν ἐπ’ αἰσχροῖς οὐδέποτε χρὴ πράγμασιν. Hense infers from the alphabetical order of the anthology that the line belonged to the Ἀχιλλέως ἐρασταί.

The philosophic view is that such pleasures are false : Plat. Phil. 40 C ψεύδεσιν ἄρα ἡδοναῖς τὰ πολλὰ οἱ πονηροὶ χαίρουσιν, followed by Arist. eth. N. 10. 5. 1176a 15. But we must be on our guard against a failure to appreciate the conventional Greek view. Although they would not have approved Tr. fr. adesp. 26 οὐδὲν ἦν πάντῃ καλὸν | οὐδ’ αἰσχρόν, ἀλλὰ ταὔτ᾿ ἐποίησεν λαβὼν | ὁ καιρὸς αἰσχρά κτέ., the chief characteristic of αἰσχρόν was personal disgrace, which was shunned for the same reasons as physical ugliness. Particularly significant in this respect are the lines of Eubulus fr. 67 (ΙΙ 187 K.).

lg.l: οὐ τοῖς ἀθύμοις ἡ τύχη ξυλλαμβάνει.

div.p: 927 Stob. flor. 8. 11 (III p. 342, 9 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ῾οὐ...ξυλλαμβάνει.᾿

‘Fortune favours the brave.’ Sophocles is followed by Menander fr. 572, ΙΙΙ 175 K. ὅταν τι πράττῃς ὅσιον, ἀγαθὴν ἐλπίδα πρόβαλλε σαυτῷ, τοῦτο γιγνώσκων ὅτι | τόλμῃ δικαίᾳ καὶ θεὸς συλλαμβάνει. Ter. Phorm. 203 fortis fortuna adiuvat, Verg. Aen. 10. 284. There is a close verbal resemblance to Eur. fr. 432 τῷ γὰρ πονοῦντι καὶ θεὸς συλλαμβάνει : see on fr. 407. Neil on Ar. Eq. 229 points out that the phrase was oracular. — For the position of the negative see Jebb on Phil. 1443: hence Naber's conj. τοῖς ὀξυθύμοις is unnecessary. Mekler thought that the next line was something like ἀλλ᾿ οἵ τι τολμῶσ᾿ ἐσθλὸν εὐκλείας χάριν.

lg.l: αἰδὼς γὰρ ἐν κακοῖσιν οὐδὲν ὠφελεῖ·

div.p: 928 Stob. flor. 13. 9 (III p. 458, 7 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘αἰδὼς . . . σύμμαχος.’

1 f. ‘Sophocles often thus uses γάρ in two successive clauses (Ai. 20 f., 215 f., 514 f., 1262 f.; Phil. 1158 f.; Ant. 1255 f.’ (Jebb on El. 180.) — τὠγκαλοῦντι is an almost certain correction of Cobet (V. L. p. 19): see cr. n. It is confirmed by Trach. 813 f. (to Deianira, after Hyllus's denunciation) τί σῖγ᾿ ἀφέρπεις; οὐ κάτοισθ᾿ ὁθούνεκα | ξυνηγορεῖς σιγῶσα τῷ κατηγόρῳ; λαλοῦντι, as J. remarks, could only mean ’one who prates (against us),’ and the essential point, — the mention of the adversary, — is omitted. It is curious that Soph. does not seem to use λαλεῖν, for λακεῖν is undoubtedly right in Phil. 110. — For the general sense cf. Eur. fr. 1037 ἀτὰρ σιωπᾶν τά γε δίκαι᾿ οὐ χρή ποτε, Ι.Α. 1142 αὐτὸ δὲ τὸ σιγᾶν ὁμολογοῦντός ἐστί σου. — The general statement of the first line is derived from the traditional maxim of popular wisdom that αἰδώς is not everywhere beneficial, and that false modesty is harmful to one who is visited with misfortune or is in the power of his enemies: see Hom. ρ 347 αἰδὼς δ’ οὐκ ἀγαθὴ κεχρημένῳ ἀνδρὶ παρεῖναι, Ω 45 αἰδώς, ἥτ’ ἄνδρας μέγα σίνεται ἠδ’ ὀνίνησιν, Hes. Op. 317 f. Hence Euripides speaks of two kinds of αἰδώς in Hipp. 385: cf. fr. 365 αἰδοῦς δὲ καὐτὸς δυσκρίτως ἔχω πέρι· | καὶ δεῖ γὰρ αὐτῆς κἄστιν αὖ κακὸν μέγα, fr. 285, 14. The closest parallel to our fr. is Tr. fr. adesp. 528 κακὸν γὰρ αἰδώς, ἔνθα τἀναιδὲς κρατεῖ.

lg.l: τί ταῦτ᾿ ἐπαινεῖς; πᾶς γὰρ οἰνωθεὶς ἀνὴρ
ἥσσων μὲν ὀργῆς ἐστι, τοῦ δὲ νοῦ κενός·
φιλεῖ δὲ πολλὴν γλῶσσαν ἐκχέας μάτην
ἄκων ἀκούειν οὓς ἑκὼν εἴπῃ λόγους.

div.p: ἧσσον S φιλεῖ A in rasura (quid prius fuerit incertum) | τε Clem. οὓς Plut. Stob.: ἅπερ Clem. | εἴπῃ λόγους Plut.: εἶπεν κακῶς Stob. Clem.

929 Stob. flor. 18. 1 (III p. 512, 14 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ῾τί . . . λόγους.᾿ Plut. de util. ex inim. percip. 5 p. 89 B quotes the words from γλῶσσαν . . . λόγους, introducing them thus: οὐδενὶ γὰρ οὕτως ἔοικε προστάττειν ὁ θεὸς ὡς τῷ μέλλοντι ψέγειν ἕτερον τὸ ῾γνῶθι σαυτόν,᾿ ἵνα μὴ λέγοντες ἃ θέλουσιν ἀκούωσιν ἃ μὴ θέλουσι. φιλεῖ γὰρ ὁ τοιοῦτος κατὰ τὸν Σοφοκλέα κτέ. Similarly Clem. Alex. Paedag. 2 p. 181 P. ῾πᾶς γὰρ οἰνωθεὶς ἀνήρ᾿ κατὰ τὴν τραγῳδίαν ῾ἥσσων . . . λόγους.᾿ Niceph. Greg. hist. Byz. 31. 28 (III p. 366) μάτην ἐκχέας κατὰ τὸν σοφὸν Σοφοκλέα τὴν ἄτοπον γλῶτταν. Cramer, anecd. Par. III p. 228, 15, quoting schol. on Hom. H 472 (Eustath. Il. p. 692, 12) οὐκ ἐπαινετὸν δὲ τὸ οἰνοῦσθαι . . . ὡς δηλοῖ καὶ παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ τὸ οἰνωθείς. This shows the trace of philosophic influence, introducing the distinction between οἰνοῦσθαι and μεθύειν, for which see J. P. xxx 219 ff.
2 ἥσσων, i. e. easily overcome by (anger): cf. Ant. 747 ἥσσω τῶν αἰσχρῶν.

3 The general sense recalls Hom. ξ 466 (οἶνος) καί τι ἔπος προέηκεν ὅπερ τ’ ἄρρητον ἄμεινον. Cf. Theogn. 479 ὃς δ’ ἂν ὑπερβάλλῃ πόσιος μέτρον, οὐκέτι κεῖνος | τῆς αὐτοῦ γλώσσης καρτερὸς οὐδὲ νόου, | μυθεῖται δ’ ἀπάλαμνα. — For γλῶσσαν in the sense of φωνήν J. refers to El. 596 ἢ πᾶσαν ἵης γλῶσσαν, Trach. 323 διήσει γλῶσσαν. — For ἐκχέας see Tucker on Aesch. Theb. 543 γλῶσσαν ῥέουσαν, and cf. Ο. C. 962 f. Blaydes quotes Plut. Caes. 54 εἰς ἀναίσθητον ἐκχέας ὀργὴν τοσαύτην, to which may
be added Pomp. 80 οἰμωγὴν ἐκχέαντες. Distinguish the use in Phil. 13, which is illustrated by Aristid. II p. 194 ἐξεχέοντο (’were wasted') ὑπὸ τοῦ δέους οἱ λόγοι.

4 echoes a very common Greek proverb popularly attributed to Chilon (Diels, Vorsokr. II³ 215, 22 μὴ κακολόγει τοὺς πλησίον· εἰ δὲ μή, ἀκούσῃ ἐφ᾿ οἷς λυπηθήσῃ), to the effect that when a man starts finding fault with another he must expect ’tit for tat.’ Cf. Hom. Υ 250 ὁπποῖόν κ' εἴπῃσθα ἔπος, τοῖόν κ' ἐπακούσαις, Hes. Op. 721 εἰ δὲ κακὸν εἴπῃς, τάχα κ᾿ αὐτὸς μεῖζον ἀκούσαις. Aesch. Ag. 1559 ὄνειδος ἥκει τόδ᾿ ἀντ' ὀνείδους, Cho. 308 ἀντὶ μὲν ἐχθρᾶς γλώσσης ἐχθρὰ | γλῶσσα τελείσθω, Eur. Alc. 704 f. εἰ δ᾿ ἡμᾶς κακῶς | ἐρεῖς, ἀκούσῃ πολλὰ κοὐ ψευδῆ κακά. The tag was adopted by the Latin playwrights: Caecil. 24 audibis male, si male dicis mihi. Plaut. Pseud. 1156 contumeliam si dicis, audies. Ter. Andr. 920 si mihi perget quae volt dicere, ea quae non volt audiet. The line of Terence resembles that of Soph. in its form, and both may ultimately be traced to Alcaeus fr. 83 αἴ κ' εἴπῃς τὰ θέλεις, <αὐτὸς> ἀκούσαις <κε> τά κ᾿ οὐ θέλοις. Valckenaer, diatr. p. 249, adds Aristid. ΙΙΙ p. 726 (=II p. 579 Dind.) ὁποῖ᾿ ἄττ᾿ ἂν εἴπῃ τοιαῦτ᾿ ἂν ἀκούσεσθαι χρὴ προσδοκᾶν. Job 11. 2 Should not the multitude of words be answered? And should a man full of talk be justified? J. cites El. 523 κακῶς δέ σε | λέγω, κακῶς κλύουσα πρὸς σέθεν θάμα, Ai. 1322 κλύοντι φλαῦρα συμβαλεῖν ἔπη κακά. See also his notes on Ant. 757, O.C. 189, and Eur. Hclid. 182 (n.). Tr.: ‘perforce must he listen to words that he freely spoke.’ — In place of οὓς (Plut. and Stob.) Clement has ἅπερ, while Clement and Stobaeus have εἶπεν κακῶς instead of εἴπῃ λόγους. The choice seems to lie between following Plutarch, and reading ἅπερ with κακά; and few will hesitate to accept the former alternative. Dindorf and Nauck prefer εἶπεν to εἴπῃ; but the use of the aor. subj., which in such cases as this takes the place of the logically more correct perfect (Goodw. §§ 90, 91), and the absence of ἄν are characteristic of Sophocles: see Phil. 1360, Ο.Τ. 1231, O.C. 395, Trach. 251, El. 771, ib. 1061, fr. 659. 4 (n.).

lg.l: κλέπτων δ᾿ ὅταν τις ἐμφανῶς ἐφευρεθῇ,
σιγᾶν ἀνάγκη, κἂν καλὸν φορῇ στόμα.

div.p: 930 Stob. flor. 24. 4 (III p. 602, 4 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ῾κλέπτων . . . στόμα.᾿ Maas assigned this fr. to the Ichneutae.
1 ἐμφανῶς should be taken with ἐφευρεθῇ, for the phrase is a substitute for ἐπ᾿ αὐτοφώρῳ ληφθῆναι.

2 κἄν καλὸν φορῇ στόμα, though he have an eloquent tongue. That φέρειν could mean, ‘to have in readiness for use,’ has been maintained from two passages in Aeschylus: Suppl. 1005 f. πᾶς δ’ ἐν μετοίκῳ γλῶσσαν εὔτυκον φέρει | κακήν, τό τ’ εἰπεῖν εὐπετὲς μύσαγμά πως, Cho. 579 ὑμῖν δ’ ἐπαινῶ γλῶσσαν εὔφημον φέρειν, | σιγᾶν θ᾿ ὅπου δεῖ καὶ λέγειν τὰ καίρια. In Ant. 1089 f. καὶ γνῷ τρέφειν τὴν γλῶσσαν ἡσυχωτέραν | τὸν νοῦν τ’ ἀμείνω τῶν φρενῶν ἢ νῦν φέρει, it is doubtful whether φέρει applies to γλῶσσαν as well as to νοῦν. Cobet, however, has shown (Coll. Crit. p. 205) that φέρειν and φορεῖν are constantly confused (L has φέρειν at O.C. 1357: cf. fr. 658, Jebb on Ο. T. 1320), and that φορεῖν is normal in speaking of parts of the body (γένειον φοροῦντα fr. 564) or of dress. Further, he contends that in both passages of Aeschylus, where the exercise rather than the faculty of speech is referred to, φορεῖν would be out of place. These considerations make a strong case for φορῇ here. The same point is illustrated with his accustomed learning by Lobeck, Phryn. p. 585 f., who quotes many exceptions to the rule. But it will be observed that nearly all of them come from late writers. νόημα (νοῦν) φέρειν must apparently be admitted: see Pind. Pyth. 6. 29, Ant. l.c. In illustration of καλὸν φορεῖν στόμα ‘to be eloquent, ’Cobet quotes Com. fr. adesp. 37 (III 405 K.) γλῶττάν τέ σοι | δίδωσιν ἐν δήμῳ φορεῖν | καλῶν λόγων ἀείνων | ᾗ πάντα κινήσεις λέγων, which he suspects of having been composed by Cratinus of Pericles. Blaydes conjectured λάλον for καλόν.

lg.l: ἢ δεινὸν ἆρ᾽ ἦν, ἡνίκ᾽ ἄν τις ἐσθλὸς ὢν

div.p: 931 Stob. flor. 24. 6 (III p. 602, 10 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘ἢ δεινὸν . . . συνείδῃ.’ The extract is omitted by MA.

1 f. δεινόν: a powerful aid. The temporal clause which follows is logically the subject, and its equivalent in English is the abstract notion ‘a good conscience.’ Hence we may the more readily compare El. 770 δεινὸν τὸ τίκτειν ἐστίν, Eur. Phoen. 355 δεινὸν γυναιξὶν αἱ δι’ ὠδίνων γοναί (n.). The general meaning is thus the same as that of Antiph. fr. 269 (II 123 K.) τὸ μὴ συνειδέναι γὰρ αὑτοῦ τῷ βίῳ | ἀδίκημα μηδὲν ἡδονὴν πολλὴν ἔχει.

ἆρ᾽ ἦν: the imperfect is used for the present, generally in the combination ἦν ἄρα, to express the ‘sudden appreciation of a real state of affairs’ (Gildersleeve, § 220). See also Goodwin, § 39. It is not easy to find an example of ἆρα (for ἄρα) in this idiom, since doubt has been thrown upon Ar. Nub. 1301 ἔμελλόν σ’ ἆρα κινήσειν ἐγώ, Ach. 347 ἐμέλλετ’ ἄρ’ ἅπαντες ἀνασείειν βοήν. But there is no more reason for suspecting its inferential use here than, e.g., its appearance in Eur. Hipp. 1012 μάταιος ἆρ’ ἦν, οὐδαμοῦ μὲν οὖν φρενῶν. See on fr. 5. Hermann in the Preface to his edition of the Oed. Col. (p. xvii) endeavoured to show that ἄρα is always either interrogative or exclamatory. Cobet prefers ἦν ἄρ’ ἡνίκ’ ἄν as being ‘multo usitatius.’ F. W. Schmidt proposed ἢ κλεινὸν εὕρημ’. Hense adopted ἀργεῖν for ἄρ’ ἦν from Buecheler; and Mekler, with still less probability, conjectured ἄρσην.

ἐσθλὸς ὤν. The supplementary participle after σύνοιδα, when it refers to the subject of the sentence, may be either in the nominative or in the dative, agreeing in the latter case with the reflexive pronoun following the verb: see Goodwin, § 908, Kuehner-Gerth, II 49. Cobet, holding that the passage is incomplete, would supply the words <μητρὸς ἢ πατρὸς κακά> from Eur. Hipp. 424 δουλοῖ γὰρ ἄνδρα κἂν θρασύσπλαγχνός τις ᾖ, | ὅταν ξυνειδῇ μητρὸς ἢ πατρὸς κακά. But his suspicion was quite uncalled for, and Hense rightly remarks that, if he were right, αὐτός rather than αὑτῷ would be required.

lg.l: ὅρκοισι γάρ τοι καὶ γυνὴ φεύγει πικρὰν
ὠδῖνα παίδων· ἀλλ’ ἐπὴν λήξῃ κακοῦ,

app.rdg: Hermann: ἐπ’ ἂν codd., ἐπεὶ Ellendt

div.p: 932 Stob. flor. 28. 1 (III p. 617, 7 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘ὅρκοισι . . . νικωμένη.’

1 f. ‘For, believe me, a woman may be eager to escape the pains of childbirth, aye, and even to swear to her resolution.’ ὅρκοισι: a strong instance of the instrumental dative, where we might expect a preposition (σὺν ὅρκῳ or δι’ ὅρκων). Somewhat similar is Eur. Her. 604 τῇ τ’ ἀσφαλείᾳ κερδανεῖς. — γάρ τοι: see Kuehner-Gerth II 153. — καί intensifies the following statement, ‘it is true . . .’ But τοι is merely ‘let me tell you.’ — φεύγει is a good example of the ‘dynamic’ (a better name than conative) present: see Wilamowitz on Eur. Her. 18. — ἐπήν: for the form see on fr. 1128, 5.

3 is an echo of Tr. fr. adesp. 300 ἐν τοῖς ἐμαυτοῦ δικτύοις ἁλώσομαι, a proverbial line recorded by Macar. 3. 85. Nauck (Index, p. xiv) conj. ἐν τοῖς ἔρωτος from Nicet. Eugen. de Dros. et Char. 4. 409 ἁλίσκεται γὰρ τοῖς Ἔρωτος δικτύοις. But the text is simpler and better; and,
if any change were required, it would be better to accept ἐν τοῖσιν αὑτῆς, as proposed by Papageorgius. Nothing can be inferred from Aesch. fr. 139, 4 τάδ’ οὐχ ὑπ’ ἄλλων, ἀλλὰ τοῖς αὑτῶν πτεροῖς | ἁλισκόμεσθα, which does not apply to the circumstances of the present fragment.

4 πρός with genit. of the agent is extremely common in Soph.: cf. fr. 84. — ἱμέρου: see on fr. 874. The word expresses the physical attraction of the beloved object. The line is repeated in the spurious Euripidean Danae (fr. 1132, 19).

lg.l: ὅρκος γὰρ οὐδεὶς ἀνδρὶ φηλήτῃ βαρύς.

app.rdg: B m. sec.: φιλήτηι vel φιλήτῃ (φιλητῇ, φϊλητη) rell.

div.p: 933 Stob. flor. 28. 5 (III p. 618, 1 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘ὅρκος . . . βαρύς.’

The value of an oath depends upon the character of the recipient: cf. Aesch. fr. 394 οὐκ ἀνδρὸς ὅρκοι πίστις, ἀλλ’ ὅρκων ἀνήρ. Democr. fr. 239 D. ὅρκους οὓς ποιέονται ἐν ἀνάγκηισιν ἐόντες οὐ τηρέουσιν οἱ φλαῦροι, ἐπὴν διαφύγωσιν. — φηλήτῃ, first in Hes. Op. 375 ὃς δὲ γυναικὶ πέποιθε, πέποιθ’ ὅ γε φηλήτῃσι, which recalls fr. 811, and in Hom. h. Herm. 66 οἷά τε φῶτες | φηληταὶ διέπουσι μελαίνης νυκτὸς ἐν ὥρῃ. For the ancient variant φιλήτης (φιλητής) see Sikes and Allen in loc., Tucker on Aesch. Cho. 999, and n. on fr. 314, 332. — ἀνδρί is used as in fr. 909 (n.). — Maas plausibly refers the fragment to the Ichneutae, thinking that Hermes’ oath of disclaimer is discredited by the Coryphaeus.

lg.l: οἴκοι μένειν δεῖ τὸν καλῶς εὐδαίμονα.

div.p: 934 Stob. flor. 39. 14 (III p. 724, 10 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘οἴκοι . . . εὐδαίμονα.’ (The extract is omitted by S.) Clement of Alexandria (strom. 6 p. 739 P.) attributes the line to Aeschylus with the addition καὶ τὸν κακῶς πράσσοντα καὶ τοῦτον μένειν (fr. 317). Nauck shows that it is several times quoted or parodied by the comic poets, as by Menander (fr. 145, III 42 K.) οἴκοι μένειν χρὴ καὶ μένειν ἐλεύθερον, | ἢ μηκέτ’ εἶναι τὸν καλῶς εὐδαίμονα. Cf. Theopomp. fr. 34, I 743 K. τἀλλότρια δειπνεῖν τὸν καλῶς εὐδαίμονα, Cratin. iun. fr. 4, II 290 K. πίνειν μένοντα τὸν καλῶς εὐδαίμονα, Menand. fr. 582 (III 177 K.) πατρῷ’ ἔχειν δεῖ τὸν καλῶς εὐδαίμονα. Diogen. 7. 35 quotes the line as a proverb without any gloss.

For the sentiment (‘There’s no place like home’) cf. Eur. fr. 30 ἀλλ’ ὅμως οἰκτρός τις αἰὼν πατρίδος ἐκλιπεῖν ὅρους, fr. 793 μακάριος ὅστις εὐτυχῶν οἴκοι μένει, with its ironic sequel, which Gomperz attributed to a comic poet, ἐν γῇ δ’ ὁ φόρτος καὶ πάλιν ναυτίλλεται. Hes. Op. 365 οἴκοι βέλτερον εἶναι, ἐπεὶ βλαβερὸν τὸ θύρηφι. Prov. app. 4. 14 (Paroem. I 438) οἴκοι γενοίμην. Sophocles conformed to the precept by his own practice, refusing to leave Athens, although often invited by foreign princes (vit. Soph. 5 p. LI Bl.). — καλῶς, ‘truly, thoroughly.’ So O.T. 1008 καλῶς εἶ δῆλος οὐκ εἰδὼς τί δρᾷς, Diod. 13. 108 ὅσα μὴ καλῶς ὑπὸ τοῦ πυρὸς ἐδόκει διεφθάρθαι. Hence τὸ καλόν in Theocr. 3. 3 τὸ καλὸν πεφιλαμένε, Herond. 1. 54 πλουτέων τὸ καλόν. Tucker interprets in this way βακχείας καλῆς in Aesch. Cho. 694.

lg.l: μή μοι κρυφαῖον μηδὲν ἐξείπῃς ἔπος·
κλῇθρον γὰρ οὐδὲν ὧδ’ ἂν εὐπαγὲς λάβοις

div.app: 935. 2 κλεῖθρον codd. | ὧδ’ M. Schmidt: ὡς δ’ codd. | εὐπαγὲς Cobet: εὐπετὲς SMA, εὐστεγὲς Hermann, etiam εὐερκὲς Cobet 3 οὗ Gomperz: οὐ codd.
div.p: 935 Stob. flor. 41. 3 (III p. 758, 1 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘μή μοι . . . διέρχεται.’

1 It has been generally felt that we require the addition ‘don’t tell to another.’ Hence F. W. Schmidt conjectured μὴ ἄλλοις, and Nauck was inclined to suggest μή τῳ (Blaydes, μηδενί). But, if the verse has been deliberately patched, as seems likely, the original is not easy to restore. I suspect that κρυφαῖον is an intruder, possibly in place of σύ γ’ ἑτέρῳ (Stadtmueller would substitute θυραῖον in v. 3).

2 f. The text of Stobaeus is corrupt. The passage, as restored above by M. Schmidt, Cobet and Gomperz, may be rendered, ‘You can find no lock for the tongue so secure, that no secret passes through it.’ The relative clause is thus consecutive, expressing result: see the examples given by Goodw. § 575, Kuehner-Gerth II 422, and especially Xen. Hell. 7. 5. 17 οὐδὲν γὰρ οὕτω βραχὺ ὅπλον ἑκάτεροι εἶχον, ᾧ οὐκ ἐξικνοῦντο ἀλλήλων. Apollodorus fr. 6 (K. III 283) καὶ κλείεθ’ ἡ θύρα μοχλοῖς, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ εἷς | τέκτων ὀχυρὰν οὕτως ἐποίησεν θύραν, | δι’ ἧς γαλῆ καὶ μοιχὸς οὐκ εἰσέρχεται was quoted by Cobet. The latter reads in v. 3 γλώσσης δι’ οὗ κρυφαῖον οὐ δ. Better would have been οὐδὲν ἔρχεται, as Blaydes conjectured, for, as J. remarks, κρυφαῖον without οὐδέν can hardly be right: but the remedy is, in either case, too violent. For the genitive with διέρχεται Gomperz cites Eur. fr. 901 πολλάκι μοι πραπίδων διῆλθε φροντίς: Trach. 717 is doubtful. The position of οὗ is an objection to Gomperz’s reading the importance of which will be variously estimated. It is avoided by Tucker’s οὗ δι’ οὐδὲν ἔρχεται, which however involves the rare anastrophe of διά. F. W. Schmidt observed that the singular of κλῇθρον occurs in tragedy only here and in Eur. fr. 362, but that seems scarcely an adequate reason for suspecting it. Anyhow his conjecture γλώσσης γὰρ οὐδαμῶς ἂν εὐπαγῆ λάβοις κλῇθρ’ ὧν κτέ. is impossible, if for no other reason, as giving to οὐδὲν οὐ διέρχεται the meaning of οὐδὲν διέρχεται (v. infra).

J. was inclined to read ὡς δ’ ἂν εὐπαγὲς λάβῃς, with a colon at οὐδέν in v. 2, interpreting: ‘Tell me no secret; for there is no way of securing it; and, however firm the guard one may place on the lips, every secret finds its way through them.’ In that case γλώσσης would be governed by διέρχεται. He admits that κλῇθρον γὰρ οὐδέν is somewhat harsh, as an unqualified assertion, but does not notice the comparative rarity of οὐδεὶς οὔ as the equivalent of nemo non (Kuehner-Gerth II 205). Campbell’s text (ὡς δ’ ἂν εὐλαβῇ λόγοις in v. 2, i.e., ‘however cautious you may be in discourse’) has the disadvantage of being still further removed from the traditional text. Buecheler conjectured: ὡς δ’ ἂν εὐπετὲς βάλοις | γλώσσης κρυφαῖον, οὐδὲν οὐ διέρχεται.

lg.l: ὅπου γὰρ οἱ φύσαντες ἡσσῶνται τέκνων,
οὐκ ἔστιν αὕτη σωφρόνων ἀνδρῶν πόλις.

div.p: 936 Stob. flor. 43. 11 (IV p. 4, 2 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘ὅπου... πόλις.’

‘Where parents must give way to their children,’ i.e. where the authority of the parent is not upheld. The expression is very similar to Tr. fr. adesp. 544 τοῦ γὰρ
πατρὸς κρατεῖν μὲν αἰσχύνην φέρει, | ἡσσημένῳ δὲ δόξα νικητήριος. Contrast Ant. 640 γνώμης πατρῴας πάντ᾿ ὄπισθεν ἑστάναι. τῶν γονέων μὴ λέγε δικαιότερα was an old saw attributed to Solon (Diels, Vorsokrat. II3 215, 13). The duties of children towards their parents were enforced at Athens by the γραφὴ γονέων κακώσεως, for which see Lipsius, Das attische Recht, p. 342 ff. Nevertheless, we are made familiar with complaints that the respect shown to parents had seriously diminished since the great days of the Μαραθωνομάχαι: see e.g. Ar. Nub. 994, Isocr. 7. 49.

937 Stob. flor. 43. 25 (IV p. 7, 9, Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘νόμοις ... καλόν.’ Cf. Menand. mon. 372 νόμοις ἕπεσθαι τοῖς ἐγχωρίοις καλόν. Bentley wrote τοῖς ἐπιχωρίοις, which Meineke (Com. IV 368 f.) and Blaydes approved, assigning the verse to Menander after Apostol. 12. 14 b. Cf. ib. 394 ξένος ὢν ἀκολούθει τοῖς ἐπιχωρίοις νόμοις.

The exhortation to ‘do at Rome as Rome does’ is connected by the paroemiographers with the figure of the polypus (πολύποδος πολυχρόου νόον ἴσχε), for which see on fr. 307. So Diogen. 1. 23 ἄλλοτε δ᾽ ἀλλοῖον τελέθειν καὶ χώρᾳ ἕπεσθαι, Zenob. 1. 24, Greg. Cypr. 1. 8. Prov. app. 1. 20 and Suid. s.v. preserve the hemistich ἀλλ᾽ ἕπου χώρας τρόποις (Tr. fr. adesp. 435). Ar. Plut. 47 ἀσκεῖν τὸν ὑὸν τὸν ἐπιχώριον τρόπον seems to be influenced by the proverb. For the variety of local custom and the respect which it seeks to impose upon strangers cf. O.C. 171, Plut. Them. 27 ὦ ξένε, νόμοι διαφέρουσιν ἀνθρώπων· ἄλλα δ' ἄλλοις καλά· καλὸν δὲ πᾶσι τὰ οἰκεῖα κοσμεῖν καὶ σῴζειν. Pind. fr. 215 ἄλλα δ' ἄλλοισιν νόμιμα. σφετέραν δ' αἰνεῖ δίκαν ἕκαστος. Eustath. Od. p. 1760, 2 refers to the proverb ἄλλα παρ᾿ ἄλλοις καλά. In O. C. 43 ἄλλα δ' ἀλλαχοῦ καλά the reference may be restricted to names. —For ἕπεσθαι νόμοις (νόμῳ), which is common enough, see the Lexx. Men. mon. 580 νόμοις ἕπεσθαι (νόμων ἔχεσθαι ib. 380) πάντα δεῖ τὸν σώφρονα.—Blaydes proposed τοῖσιν ἐγχώρων.

lg.l: πολλῶν καλῶν δεῖ τῷ καλόν τι μωμένῳ,
μικροῦ δ᾽ ἀγῶνος οὐ μέγ᾽ ἔρχεται κλέος.

div.p: 938 Stob. flor. 45. 11 (IV p. 186, 15 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘πολλῶν...κλέος.’

1 πολλῶν καλῶν. It has been generally assumed that the meaning is that which Euripides, —to take a particular instance, —expresses in fr. 236 σὺν μυρίοισι τὰ καλὰ γίγνεται πόνοις (cf. fr. 134). Hence many emendations: (1) πολλῶν πόνων, Nauck. (2) πόνων καλῶν Gomperz, quoting Ar. pol. 5 (8). 4. 1338b 30 οὐδὲ γὰρ λύκος οὐδὲ τῶν ἄλλων θηρίων ἀγωνίσαιτο ἂν οὐδένα καλὸν κίνδυνον. (3) πολλῶν παλῶν Bamberger, Kock, Wecklein, and Herwerden. (4) πολλῶν κάλων Bergk, or παντὸς κάλω Hense, with reference to πάντα κάλων ἐξιέναι. (5) Elter suggested that ἀνταγωνιστῶν had gone before. But the chapter in Stobaeus from which this extract is taken is entitled περὶ τῶν ἐν ταῖς πόλεσι δυνατῶν. That is to say, the subject is ‘the qualities which command success in politics,’ so that without πολλῶν καλῶν or its equivalent the quotation from Sophocles has so much the less relevance. The text is defended by Campbell, who renders ‘many favouring circumstances’; but J. rightly prefers ‘many noble qualities or gifts,’ i.e., the man who aims high must be well endowed. Cf. frs. 81 and 592 n. καλά is common in Pindar in this sense (e.g. Ol. 10. 18): see also Eur. fr. 15 τὴν ἀξίωσιν τῶν καλῶν τὸ σῶμ'
ἔχειν. —τι μωμένῳ : see cr. n. In spite of Hense's objection that τῷ καλῶς τιμωμένῳ is the point d'appui for the anthologist's title, Nauck's brilliant emendation appears certain: cf. Trach. 1136 χρηστὰ μωμένη. Campbell reads καλῶς τι μωμένῳ, but H. points out that probably καλόν was regarded as adverbial and glossed by καλῶς, as was μακρὰ δισκεύσαις in Pind. Isth. 2. 35 by μακρῶς, ἀνυμέναια by ἀνυμεναίως in Eur. Phoen. 347, and ἀπαρθένευτα by κακοπαρθενεύτως ibid. 1739. He traced the same corruption in Aesch. Cho. 642, where he restored παρεκβάντ᾽ ἐς οὐ θεμιστά for παρεκβάντες ἀθεμίστως, and ibid. 806, where Ahrens gave λαμπρόν for λαμπρῶς. See also Cobet, V. L. p. 153.—For the repetition of καλός Gomperz refers to fr. 839.—The dative after δεῖ in the combination δεῖ μοί τινος is normal: Jebb on El. 612.
2 ἔρχεται. Blaydes conj. αἴρεται, but cf. (e.g.) Ο. Τ. 307 ἔκλυσιν | μόνην ἂν ἐλθεῖν τοῦδε τοῦ νοσήματος. Observe that the line is explanatory of v. 1: ‘for (fr. 576, 4) he will be highly tried.’

lg.l: γνῶμαι πλέον κρατοῦσιν ἢ σθένος χερῶν.

div.p: 939 Stob. flor. 54. 3 (IV p. 348, 12 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘γνῶμαι...χερῶν.’

Nauck thought that the words ought to be corrected to γνῶμαι πλέον σθένουσιν ἢ κράτος χερῶν, objecting to πλέον κρατοῦσιν in the sense of ‘are stronger,’ as would appear from the fact that he wished also to introduce σθένει into Eur. fr. 736, 4 τὸ γὰρ ἔχειν πλέον κρατεῖ τῆς εὐσεβείας. But the passages support each other, and πλέον κρατεῖν is properly used for ‘to prevail more.’ Besides, κράτος χερῶν ought to mean ‘a victory won by force.’ —γνῶμαι is here equivalent to εὐβουλία (αι), ‘right judgements,’ as in Ai. 162 ἀλλ' οὐ δυνατὸν τοὺς ἀνοήτους | τούτων γνώμας προδιδάσκειν, where Campbell's rendering is to be preferred to Jebb's ‘maxims.’

The familiar saw, that wisdom is mightier than mere brute force, often recurs: see Eur. fr. 27 ἢ βραχύ τοι σθένος ἀνέρος· ἀλλὰ | ποικιλίᾳ πραπίδων | δεινὰ μὲν φῦλα πόντου...δάμναται, fr. 200 σοφὸν γὰρ ἓν βούλευμα τὰς πολλὰς χέρας | νικᾷ, fr. 290 ἀεὶ γὰρ ἄνδρα σκαιὸν ἰσχυρὸν φύσει | ἦσσον δέδοικα τἀσθενοῦς τε καὶ σοφοῦ. Agathon fr. 27 γνώμη δὲ κρεῖσσόν ἐστιν ἢ ῥώμη χερῶν. Tr. fr. adesp. 540 βουλαὶ τάδ᾽ ἐξέπραξαν, οὐ χερῶν σθένος.

lg.l: εἰ σῶμα δοῦλον, ἀλλ᾽ ὁ νοῦς ἐλεύθερος.

div.p: 940 Stob. flor. 62. 33 (IV p. 428, 2 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘εἰ... ἐλεύθερος.’

Nauck, comparing Greg. Naz. II p. 215 Α εἶναι γὰρ εἶναι τἀνδρός, ὡς ἀκούομεν, | τὸ σῶμα δοῦλον, τὸν τρόπον δ᾽ ἐλεύθερον, adds ‘τὸ σῶμα malim.’ But we could ill spare εἰ, answered in the apodosis by the idiomatic ἀλλά (‘at least’): cf. fr. 23, Sapph. fr. 1. 22 αἰ δὲ δῶρα μὴ δέκετ', ἀλλὰ δώσει, Ο. C. 241 ‘since (ἐπεί) ye have not borne my blind father,’ ἀλλ' ἐμὲ τὰν μελέαν, ἱκετεύομεν, | ὦ ξένοι, οἰκτίρατε, Hom. Α 81 εἴπερ γάρ τε χόλον γε καὶ αὐτῆμαρ καταπέψῃ, | ἀλλά τε καὶ μετόπισθεν ἔχει κότον. —ἐλεύθερος, = ἐλευθέριος : cf. Phil. 1006 ὦ μηδὲν ὑγιὲς μηδ' ἐλεύθερον φρονῶν, Trach. 62 ἥδε γὰρ γυνὴ δούλη μέν, εἴρηκεν δ᾽ ἐλεύθερον λόγον. The sentiment is such as we meet more frequently in Euripides, who in this as in other respects reflects the growing enlightenment of his age (Gomperz, Greek Thinkers, II p. 15): Hel. 729 ἐν τοῖσι γενναίοισιν ἠριθμημένος | δούλοισι, τοὔνομ᾿ οὐκ ἔχων ἐλεύθερον, | τὸν νοῦν δέ, Ion. 854 ἓν γάρ τι τοῖς δούλοισιν αἰσχύνην φέρει, | τοὔνομα· τὰ δ᾽ ἄλλα πάντα τῶν ἐλευθέρων | οὐδεὶς κακίων δοῦλος, ὅστις ἐσθλὸς ᾖ, fr. 511, fr. 831 πολλοῖσι δούλοις τοὔνομ' αἰσχρόν, ἡ δὲ φρὴν | τῶν οὐχὶ δούλων ἐστ᾽ ἐλευθερωτέρα. Mekler divided the line between two speakers: Α. εἶ σῶμα δοῦλον. Β. ἀλλ᾽ ὁ νοῦς ἐλεύθερος.

lg.l: ὦ παῖδες, ἥ τοι Κύπρις οὐ Κύπρις μόνον,
ἔστιν μὲν Ἅιδης, ἔστι δ᾿ ἄφθιτος βία,
ἔστιν δὲ λύσσα μανιάς, ἔστι δ᾿ ἵμερος
ἄκρατος, ἔστ᾿ οἰμωγμός. ἐν κείνῃ τὸ πᾶν
ψυχή· τίς οὐχὶ τῆσδε δεύτερος θεοῦ;
χέρσου δ᾿ ἔνεστιν ἐν τετρασκελεῖ γονῇ·
νωμᾷ δ᾿ ἐν οἰωνοῖσι τοὐκείνης πτερόν,
ἐν θηρσίν, ἐν βροτοῖσιν, ἐν θεοῖς ἄνω.
τίν’ οὐ παλαίουσ᾿ ἐς τρὶς ἐκβάλλει θεῶν;
εἴ μοι θέμις, θέμις δὲ τἀληθῆ λέγειν,
Κύπρις τὰ θνητῶν καὶ θεῶν βουλεύματα.

div.p: 941. 2 πολλῶν Plut.: πάντων Stob. 3 μία Α1 4 μανιάς Porson: μανίας Plut., μαινάς Stob. (nisi quod in S prius α ex αν correctum esse videtur)

941 Stob. flor. 63. 6 (iv p. 435, 12 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘ὦ παῖδες . . . βουλεύματα.᾿ The beginning of the passage is also quoted by Plut. amat. 13 p. 757 A as follows: ἀλλ᾿ ἀπὸ μιᾶς σκηνῆς ἀκούομεν ‘Ἕρως γὰρ ἀργὸν κἀπὶ τοιούτοις ἔφυ᾿ (Eur. fr. 322, 1) καὶ πάλιν αὖ ὧδε ‘οὐ Κύπρις μόνον . . . λύσσα μανιάς᾿ (vv. 1–4).

Nauck thinks that the fragment belongs to Euripides rather than to Sophocles, and refers to the opinions of Herwerden, Meineke and others to the same effect. So long as these views are put forward merely as records of individual impression they do not require criticism. Nauck, it is true, finds some corroboration in the words ἀπὸ μιᾶς σκηνῆς, as if they meant ‘from the same play,’ i.e. the Danae of Euripides. He admits that Clem. Alex. strom. 5 p. 717 Ρ. ὁ μὲν Σοφοκλῆς . . . ἐκβοᾷ, followed by Εὐριπίδης δὲ ἐπὶ τῆς αὐτῆς σκηνῆς τραγῳδῶν, is against him, but refuses to believe that Plutarch would have so expressed himself. It is difficult to appreciate the force of this reasoning, when Plutarch used, e. g. ἐκ τραγικῆς σκηνῆς (Demetr. 25) for ‘the tragic stage.’ — Dobree strangely thought that the fr. belonged to a satyr-play.
1 ἥ τοι Κύπρις. The particle τοι often is placed between the article and the noun, as e. g. at Phil. 637. A large number of examples is collected by Blaydes on Ar. Lys. 919.

2 πολλῶν ὀνομάτων ἐπώνυμος: cf. Aesch. Prom. 226 πολλῶν ὀνομάτων μορφὴ μία. ἐπώνυμος is usually combined with a genitive describing the (new) name attached to a person or thing: cf. fr. 323 ὄρνιθος ἦλθ᾿ ἐπώνυμος πέρδικος. The genitive here appears to be different in character only because we habitually translate ἐπώνυμος named after, as if it were the same as παρώνυμος. We should render, ‘bearing many names.’ Meineke's πολλῶν δυνάμεων and Herwerden's ἐπήβολος are unnecessary. For the general sense cf. Eur. Hipp. 1 πολλὴ μὲν ἐν βροτοῖσι κοὐκ ἀνώνυμος | θεὰ κέκλημαι Κύπρις, where this passage supports the view that πολλή = πολυώνυμος, Theocr. 15. 109 (Κύπρι Διωναία) πολυώνυμε καὶ πολύναε.

3 Ἅιδης. There is a certain amount of evidence, such as her title Ἐπιτυμβία at Delphi, pointing to the worship of Aphrodite as a goddess of death: see Gruppe, Gr. Myth. p. 1358, and in Bursians Jahresb. cxxxvii 400. She was addressed as ἀνδροφόνος at Pharsalus (Farnell, 11 665). But the poet was probably thinking less of the cult than of the effect of her power on her votaries, such as Phaedra and Procris. — ἄφθιτος βία, ‘imperishable might’: cf. Aristarch. fr. 2 (TGF p. 728) ἔρωτος ὅστις μὴ πεπείραται βροτῶν | οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ἀνάγκης θεσμόν. Jebb quotes W. G. Clark's lines: ‘Love almighty, love eternal | Laughs to scorn the might of Time.’ — Μ. Schmidt's αἰδώς and Bothe's βίος are instances of thoroughly bad conjectures, but the fact that they have been proposed shows that the verse cannot be passed over in silence.

4 f. λύσσα μανιάς: see cr. n. ‘Certainly μανιάς seems right. Cp. Eur. Or. 327 λύσσας μανιάδος. [ib. 270.] Soph. Ai. 59 μανιάσιν νόσοις (μαινὰς Βάκχη Eur. Bacch. 915 is the only instance of μαινάς as adjective).’ (J.) He seems to have overlooked Pind. Pyth. 4. 216, where μαινάδ᾿ ὅρνιν is applied to the ἴυγξ. For love as madness cf. Eur. fr. 161 ἤρων· τὸ μαίνεσθαι δ’ ἄρ᾿ ἦν ἔρως βροτοῖς. Prodicus fr. 7 (Vorsokr. 11 3 275, 20) ἐπιθυμίαν μὲν διπλασιασθεῖσαν ἔρωτα εἶναι, ἔρωτα δὲ διπλασιασθέντα μανίαν γίγνεσθαι. Plat. legg. 839 A λύττης δὲ ἐρωτικῆς καὶ μανίας . . . εἴργεσθαι ποιεῖ (ὁ νόμος). Every one will recall Shaksp. MND v. 1. 4 ff. —
6 ἡσύχαιον SM, ἡσύχιον A et primitus Μ 7 sq. suspecta | τίς] τῆς Α1 | οὐχὶ Grotius: οὔτι codd. | τῆσδε δεύτερος θεοῦ Nauck: τῆσδε τῆς θεοῦ βορός SM, τῆς (om. τῆσδε) θεοῦ βορός A

ἵμερος, yearning (fr. 149, 8), is sometimes half-personified as an objective loveliness, which is the source of passion: see on fr. 874. It is not easy to distinguish from πόθος; but the Stoics, who gave much attention to the definition of the emotions, and had much better sources of information than we have, regarded πόθος as a vague though passionate longing for an absent friend, whereas ἵμερος is the desire for his bodily presence (ἐπιθυμία φίλου ἀπόντος ὁμιλίας: see Stoic. Vet. Fr. III 395, 397 Arn.). — Why Bothe should have conjectured ἄκραντος for ἄκρατος, which Dindorf actually adopted, or Herwerden εὔκρατος, it is difficult to understand: ἄκρατος may be illustrated by Polyphemus' ἄκρατος ἡ χάρις (Eur. Cycl. 576), after swallowing the wine.

6 σπουδαῖον, active, zealous (Xen. mem. i. 3. 11 τί ἂν οἴει παθεῖν καλὸν φιλήσας; . . . σπουδάζειν δ’ ἀναγκασθῆναι, ἐφ᾿ οἷς οὐδ᾿ ἂν μαινόμενος σπουδάσειεν;), is contrasted with ἡσυχαῖον, which in its turn is opposed to ἐς βίαν ἄγον. Cf. Eur. Hipp. 444 ἣ (Κύπρις) τὸν μὲν εἴκονθ' ἡσυχῇ μετέρχεται with fr. 340 ἤν τ’ αὖ βιάζῃ, μᾶλλον ἐντείνειν φιλεῖ, | κἄπειτα τίκτει πόλεμον. Theophrastus (fr. 114 Wimmer) described Love as πάθος ψυχῆς σχολαζούσης.

7 f. ‘1. The only tenable version seems to be, "It sinks deep into all who have in them the breath of the lungs," i.e. the breath of life: ψυχὴ πλευμόνων = πνοὴ πλευμόνων (Plat. Tim. 84 D ὁ τῶν πνευμάτων τοῖς σώμασι ταμίας πλεύμων). Other explanations of the vulgate are as follows: 2. Ellendt: “It sinks into the lungs of all who have life in them." The gen. πλευμόνων with ἐντήκεται is "dictum exquisitius," he thinks, for the dative. He compares ἐμβαίνω, ἐμβατεύω, ἐντυγχάνω with the genitive. But ἐντήκομαί τινος would be very strange, and is not really like the other cases which he quotes. 3. Campbell says that πλευμόνων is a genitive of place, and quotes O. C. 729 f., where, however, ὀμμάτων and φόβον should be joined.

’The emendations which have been proposed are: 1. Meineke, ἀνθάπτεται. Cp. Trach. 778 σπαραγμὸς αὐτοῦ πλευμόνων ἀνθήψατο. Ar. Ran. 474 πλευμόνων τ᾿ ἀνθάψεται | ταρτησσία μύραινα. Meineke also conj. πνοή for ψυχή. [Blaydes, following Meineke, prefers ζόη.] 2. F. W. Schmidt, ἐντήκεται γὰρ τλημόνων, ὅσοις ἔνι, ψυχῇ (the latter after Hartung).’ (J.) J.'s rendering is the only possible one, but it is difficult to feel satisfied with πλευμόνων ψυχή. I believe that this passage has been imitated in a fr. of Plutarch's treatise de amore (ap. Stob. flor. 64. 32 [VII 134 Bern.]) ὁ ἔρως οὔτε τὴν γένεσιν ἐξαίφνης λαμβάνει καὶ ἀθρόαν ὡς ὁ θυμός, οὔτε παρέρχεται ταχέως καίπερ εἶναι πτηνὸς λεγόμενος· ἀλλ᾿ ἐξάπτεται μαλακῶς καὶ σχεδὸν οἷον ἐντήκων ἑαυτόν· ἁψάμενός τε τῆς ψυχῆς παραμένει πολὺν χρόνον. It is submitted that this quotation establishes ἐντήκεται and makes the dative ψυχῇ highly probable: cf. Alciphr. 1. 13 ἔρως ἐνέσκηψε καὶ ἐντακεὶς οὐκ ἀνίησιν, Lucian Peregr. 22 τοσοῦτος ἔρως τῆς δόξης ἐντέτηκεν αὐτῷ. Plut. Mar. 45 οὕτως δεινὸς αὐτῷ καὶ δυσπαραμύθητος . . . ἔρως ἐντετήκει. Soph. El. 1311. Com. fr. adesp. 431 (III 489 K.) οὕτως ἔρως ἰσχυρὸς ἐντέτηκέ μοι | τῆς πατρίδος. The last example makes against Jebb's view that the word tends to be used in a bad sense. The metaphor is from molten wax cleaving to the mould. In support of πλευμόνων, Blaydes refers to Phot. lex. p. 433, 17 πλευμονίαν· νόσον τὴν ἐρωτικήν. If we could assume that OCOICENI arose from ΕCΩΚΕΙΝΗ, the text might be due to a displacement in the order of words: κείνη γὰρ εἴσω πλευμόνων ἐντήκεται ψυχῇ.

τίς οὐχὶ κτἑ.: see cr. n. βορός is a vox nihili, although Campbell retains it, saying that it is a substantive here (βορός in Ar. Pac. 38 and Posidipp. ap. Athen. 414 D = gluttonous). Grotius corrected it to βορά, which Dindorf accepts; but this, as J. remarks, is untenable. I have adopted Nauck's δεύτερος, assuming that its compendium was misread as βορός and that the verse was subsequently patched for metrical reasons. J. proposed τίς οὐχὶ
9 πλωτῶν Arsen. 10 χέρσου δ' ἔνεστιν ἐν Nauck: ἔνεστι δ’ ἐν χέρσου codd. | γένει A 11 τοῦ κείνη M
τῆς θεοῦ ζυγηφόρος, coll. Aesch. fr. 326; but τῆσδε is wanted. Blaydes's substitutes πλέως and λάτρις have no probability. Hartung and F. W. Schmidt preferred πόρος.

9 εἰσέρχεται ’with dat.: O. C. 372 εἰσῆλθε τοῖν τρὶς ἀθλίοιν ἔρις κακή (n.). So in prose, with ref. to a feeling coming into the mind, Plat. Rep. 330 D εἰσέρχεται αὐτῷ δέος.’ (J.) The present instance is harsher than those quoted, since physical entrance is intended: Nauck thinks πλωτῶν γένη may be right (see cr. n.). — πλωτῷ, swimming: with verbal adj. in active sense, for which see on fr. 534, 4. J. quotes Arion fr. 4 περὶ δὲ σὲ πλωτοὶ θῆρες χορεύουσι κύκλῳ. For the general sense cf. fr. 684 ἔρως . . . κἀπὶ πόντον ἔρχεται. For Ant. 785 see Jebb's note.
10 See cr. n., and for a discussion of similar errors in the order of words Headlam in C. R. xvi 243.

11 νωμᾷ . . . τοὐκείνης πτερόν ‘Can mean only "her wing" (Cp. Ο. C. 97 πιστὸν ἐξ ὑμῶν πτερόν, “some faithful omen from you." This might be the sense here.) “is the guiding (or controlling) power among birds." For νωμᾷ could not be intransitive, nor could τοὐκείνης stand for τὸ ἑαυτῆς. But the absolute use οἱ νωμᾷ is somewhat harsh. We might read ἐν οἰωνοῖσί που κείνη, "she plies her wing among birds, I ween”.’ (J.) I doubt if που will be generally approved, and incline rather to the view that νωμᾷ is used for νωμᾶται = κινεῖται, i.e. ’ranges.’ In favour of this we have (1) the general analogy of verbs of motion, for which see on fr. 210, 8, and particularly that of δινεύω, a verb in many respects parallel (cf. Sappho fr. 1, 11); (2) the fact that ἐπινωμᾶν is intransitive in Phil. 168, and probably προσνωμᾶν ibid. 717. In Α. Ρ. 9. 339 ἔν ποτε παμφαίνοντι μελάντερον (so P: μελάντερος PI) αἰθέρι νωμῶν (κόραξ) Grotius adopted μελάμπτερος (prob. from Scaliger), but Brunck's μέλαν πτερόν is preferred by Stadtmueller. See further Lobeck on Ai. 604 and the notes on fr. 581. 4, 8. Bacchyl. 5. 26, being itself disputed, is of no help. There is no doubt that πτερόν is here used metaphorically to express ’influence’ or ‘inspiration,’ but the course of development is not so clear. J. makes ’omen’ the starting-point, but, unless O. C. 97 itself be such, there is no evidence of the extension: in Callim. Pall. Lav. 124 ποίων (sc. ὀρνίθων) οὐκ ἀγαθαὶ πτέρυγες the reference is solely to augury. The circumstances in the O. C. are different, and here the allusion to a sign seems out of place. I cannot find any trace of a winged Aphrodite, although we might think of her as identified for the nonce with her attendant doves, swans or sparrows. But any such special significance must surely be controlled by the metaphor which figures any violent transport of emotion in the guise of wings (cf. ἀναπτερῶ fr. 355, schol. Pind. Ol. 14. 35, and Starkie on Ar. Ach. 987). This applies to fear (Ap. Rhod. 4. 23 πτερόεις δέ οἱ ἐν φρεσὶ θυμὸς | ἰάνθη), to frenzy (Theogn. 1053 τῶν γὰρ μαινομένων πέτεται θυμός τε νόος τε, Eur. Bacch. 332), to poetic inspiration (El. 242 πτέρυγας ὀξυτόνων γόων, Pind. Isth. 1. 64 πτερύγεσσιν ἀερθέντ᾿ ἀγλααῖς Πιερίδων, Theogn. 237 f.), and in particular to love: see especially Plat. Phaedr. 246 D, 252 B, and the discussion of the allegory by Plut. Plat. qu. 6 p. 1004 C, which concludes with the words ἣν (τὴν διανοητικὴν δύναμιν) οὐκ ἀπὸ τρόπου πτερὸν προσηγόρευσεν ὡς τὴν ψυχὴν ἀπὸ τῶν ταπεινῶν καὶ θνητῶν ἀναφέρουσαν. Max. Tyr. 7. 5 Ἔρωτα . . . ὡσπερεὶ πτέρωμά τι κοῦφον καὶ μετάρσιον. I think the context is against an allusion to the arrow, which would be otherwise possible: Aphrodite is πότνια ὀξυτάτων βελέων in Pind. Pyth. 4. 213: see also on fr. 474. Herwerden proposed ποικίλοις, for τοὐκείνης; or, to avoid giving wings to the goddess, ναίει . . . ποικιλοπτέροις.
12 Herwerden rejected this v. and is so far justified in that it undoubtedly interrupts the orderly sequence of thought describing the power of Love in each
14 μοι] μα (ut videtur) Μ, μὴ A | λέγεις A

element. J. accepted Herwerden's view. But there is some compensation for the lack of symmetry in the link provided by ἐν θεοῖς ἄνω with the thought of v. 13, and the double significance of πτερόν, literal and figurative, enables a summary to be made of the preceding lines. φηρσίν (Meineke) is a bad conjecture. For the universal supremacy of Aphrodite cf. Hom. h. Aphr. 3 ff., 70 ff., Eur. Hipp. 447 f., 1268 ff., A. Ρ. 9. 221. — θηρσίν in the widest sense is not necessarily limited to wild beasts: cf. Ai. 366, with Jebb's n. —ἄνω: Wecklein substitutes κράτος, thus providing νωμᾷ with an object.

13 παλαίουσ᾿. Love is a wrestler (cf. fr. 618, 2 n.), just as he is a boxer in Anacreon fr. 62, Trach. 442 ff. — ἐς τρίς must be taken with ἐκβάλλει and not with παλαίουσ᾿ : the encounter in a wrestling-match did not consist merely of three bouts, within the course of which victory was adjudged to one or other of the adversaries, but lasted until one of them was forced to acknowledge defeat by having been thrice thrown. This appears clearly from Suid. τριαχθῆναι λέγουσιν οἱ παλαιστρικοὶ ἀντὶ τοῦ τρὶς πεσεῖν. Schol. Aesch. Eum. 592 (ἕν μὲν τόδ’ ἤδη τῶν τριῶν παλαισμάτων) ἀπὸ τῶν παλαιόντων, οἳ ἐπὶ τοῖς τρισὶ πτώμασιν ὁρίζουσι τὴν ἧτταν. Senec. de benef. 5. 3 luctator ter abiectus perdidit palmam. Α. Ρ. 11. 316 ἀνστὰς δ᾿ ἐν μέσσοισιν ἀνέκραγεν· οὐχὶ τρί᾿ ἐστίν· | ἓν κεῖμαι, λοιπὸν τἄλλα μέ τις βαλέτω. Cf. Aesch. Ag. 181 ὃς δ’ ἔπειτ᾿ ἔφυ, τριακτῆρος οἴχεται τυχών, Adam on Plat. rep. 583 B. —ἐκβάλλει seems to be a technical term of the arena for a decisive throw, but no parallel is quoted. We have, however, the analogy of the Latin abicere in Seneca (l. c.): cf. Cic. Tusc. 2. 36 (on the training of the Spartan youth) ergo his laboriosis exercitationibus et dolor intercurrit non nunquam, impelluntur, feriuntur, abiciuntur, cadunt. Verg. Aen. 10. 736 super abiectum posito pede nixus. Our ‘knock out’ is similar. It seems unnecessary to follow Herwerden in requiring the introduction of καταβάλλω (Plat. Euthyd. 277 D). — For Love as the most powerful of the gods cf. Eur. fr. 269 Ἔρωτα . . . τῶν ἁπάντων δαιμόνων ὑπέρτατον, Menand. fr. 235, ΙΙΙ 67 K. εἶτ᾿ οὐ μέγιστός ἐστι τῶν θεῶν ἔρως; fr. 449, III 129 K. Ἔρως δὲ τῶν θεῶν | ἰσχὺν ἔχων πλείστην, Eur. fr. 430 Ἔρωτα πάντων δυσμαχώτατον θεῶν. He rules the gods: Trach. 443 οὗτος γὰρ ἄρχει καὶ θεῶν ὅπως θέλει.
14 εἴ μοι θέμις, θέμις δέ κτἑ. Cf. Trach. 809 εἰ θέμις δ᾿ ἐπεύχομαι· θέμις δ᾿ , ἐπεί κτἑ, Phil. 661. Blaydes adds Eur. El. 300 λέγοιμ᾿ ἄν’, εἰ χρή· χρὴ δέ κτἑ. Pers. 1. 8 si fas dicere, sed fas.

15 ff. Διός: cf. fr. 684 καὶ τόνδ᾿ (sc. Ἔρωτα) ἀπείργειν οὐδ᾿ ὁ παγκρατὴς σθένει | Ζεύς, ἀλλ᾿ ὑπείκει καὶ θέλων ἐγκλίνεται, Menand. fr. 209, ΙΙΙ 60 K. δέσποιν’, Ἔρωτος οὐδὲν ἰσχύει πλέον, | οὐδ᾿ αὐτὸς ὁ κρατῶν τῶν ἐν οὐρανῷ θεῶν | Ζεύς, ἀλλ᾿ ἐκείνῳ πάντ᾿ ἀναγκασθεὶς ποιεῖ. Mosch. 2. 76 Κύπριδος, ἣ μούνη δύναται καὶ Ζῆνα δαμάσσαι. — ἄνευ δορός, ἄνευ σιδήρου form an oxymoron when combined with τυραννεῖ: Love is a tyrant with no body-guard, — for the essence of tyranny is its reliance upon force (Plat. rep. 566 B). This was observed by H., who quotes Hes. Op. 705 εὕει ἄτερ δαλοῦ (Eur. Or. 621 ὑφῆψε δῶμ᾿ ἀνηφαίστῳ πυρί), Aesch. Ag. 980 τὸν δ’ ἄνευ λύρας ὅμως ὑμνῳδεῖ θρῆνον Ἐρινύος, Eum. 196 ἄνευ βοτῆρος αἰπολούμεναι, Eur. Cycl. 245 θερμὴν ἔδοντος δαῖτ᾿ ἄτερ κρεανόμων (Dobree for τῷ κρεανομῳ), Plaut. Asin. 93 tu sine pennis vola. For the phrase ἄνευ δορός cf. fr. 493, and see n. on Eur. Hclid. 396. Grotius and Gaisford, who are followed by Dindorf, putting the colon after πλευμόνων, connect these words with what follows; but, apart from other considerations, the position of τοι, which goes with the whole clause, is decisive against this view. — συντέμνεται. This is one of the instances where the indirect middle is used ‘without any perceptible, or at any rate translatable, difference from the active’ (Gildersleeve, § 147), but I see no reason for suspecting the text: cf. fr. 878, 858 n. Herwerden,
however, followed by Nauck and Hense, altered Κύπρις to Κύπριδι with the object of making συντέμνεται passive. J. compared Plat. Phaedr. 266 A ὁ μὲν τὸ ἐπ᾿ ἀριστερὰ τεμνόμενος μέρος, πάλιν τοῦτο τέμνων οὐκ ἐπανῆκε, legg. 695 C διείλετο τὴν ἀρχὴν ἑπτὰ μέρη τεμόμενος (ὁ Δαρεῖος), polit. 262 D, 280 D, where ἀποτέμνομαι is used of separating or cutting so as to suit one's own view. συντέμνω here resembles the Lat. reseco in Hor. C. 1. 11. 7 et spatio brevi spem longam reseces.
The following is J.'s rendering (slightly modified):

‘My children, Love is not Love alone, but is called by many names; it is Death, it is immortal Might, it is raging Frenzy, it is vehement Desire, it is Lamentation: in Love is all activity, all peace, all that prompts to violence.

‘For Love sinks into the soul of all that breathe the breath of life; who must not yield to that deity? Love enters into the tribe of fish that swim the sea, and dwells in the four-footed creatures of the land; it is Love's pinion that is the guiding power [or "that moves”] among birds, among beasts, among men, among the gods above. Where is the god that Love, wrestling with him, cannot thrice overthrow? If it be lawful for me to say it — and lawful it is to speak the truth — Love rules like a tyrant over the heart of Zeus without the aid of spear or sword: even so Love cuts short all the plans of gods and men.’

lg.l: τίς δ᾿ οἶκος ἐν βροτοῖσιν ὠλβίσθη ποτὲ

div.p: 942 Stob. flor. 67. 5 (iv p. 495, 9 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘τίς δ’ . . . χλιδῇ.’ The extract is omitted by S.

’Where on earth could you find a home, however magnificent, that was blest with happiness, if lacking the presence of a good housewife?’ The wife was reckoned as herself the choicest ornament: Eur. fr. 137 τῶν γὰρ πλούτων ὅδ᾿ ἄριστος | γενναῖον λέχος εὑρεῖν, where Nauck should not have approved F. W. Schmidt's πότμων. fr. 164 ἄριστον ἀνδρὶ κτῆμα συμπαθὴς γυνή. Apollonides fr. 1 οὐ χρυσός . . . οὐ πλούτου χλιδὴ | τοσοῦτον εἶχε διαφόρους τὰς ἡδονὰς | ὡς ἀνδρὸς ἐσθλοῦ καὶ γυναικὸς εὐσεβοῦς | γνώμη δικαία. — ὀγκωθείς, of material luxury: cf. Eur. Suppl. 864 φεύγων τραπέζαις ὅστις ἐξογκοῖτ᾿ ἄγαν (i.e. a luxurious liver, awkwardly mistranslated by L. and S.). fr. 825 κρεῖσσον δὲ βαιὸς ὄλβος ἀβλαβὴς βροτοῖς | ἢ δῶμα πλούτῳ δυσσεβῶς ὠγκωμένον.

lg.l: κατ᾿ ὀρφανὸν γὰρ οἶκον ἀνδρόφρων γυνή

div.p: 943 Stob. flor. 73. 54 (IV p. 558, 8 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ῾κατ᾿ . . . γυνὴ.᾿ The extract is omitted by S.

This line occurs in the midst of a number of extracts filled with the strongest possible attacks upon women, so that it was scarcely intended to be complimentary to the sex. But that would be the effect of adopting Campbell's rendering, ‘A woman left to watch over an orphan home has the spirit and wisdom of a man.’ Either, then, the passage is incomplete, or we must throw the emphasis on ὀρφανόν: ’it is a desolate home where a woman takes the man's place.’ There is no better commentary on the position of women in Periclean Athens than Xen. oecon. 7 — 10, where the training of Ischomachus is represented as a remarkable education of the female intelligence, and it is difficult to avoid the suspicion of irony when Socrates says (10. 1): νὴ τὴν Ἥραν . . . ἀνδρικήν γε ἐπιδεικνύεις τὴν διάνοιαν τῆς γυναικός. Cf. Aesch. Ag. 11 γυναικὸς ἀνδρόβουλον κέαρ, of Clytaemnestra, the exception which proves the rule. Of course, Euripides writes in a different spirit: Or. 1204 (of Electra) ὦ τὰς φρένας μὲν ἄρσενας κεκτημένη | τὸ σῶμα δ᾿ ἐν γυναιξὶ θηλείαις πρέπον. For the formation ἀνδρόφρων cf. Eur. fr. 362, 34 γυναικόφρων, Tr. fr. adesp. 51 θηλύφρων.
944 συγκραθεῖσα Gesner: δυσκραθεῖσα SMA

944 Stob. flor. 96. 9 Διφίλου. ῾πενία . . . βίον.᾿ 96. 10 (iv p. 790, 6 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ῾ πενία δὲ τοῖς ἔχουσιν οὐ σμικρὰ νόσος· | πενίας γὰρ οὐδείς ἐστι μείζων πολέμιος.᾿ Brunck perceived that the lemmata had been interchanged, and he has been followed by all subsequent editors. Kock on Diphil. fr. 105 (ll 574) holds that Diphilus might have written these lines also, and Hense agrees.

Poverty forces a man into shameful courses, even when his natural impulses are good: Theogn. 651 αἰσχρὰ δέ μ’ οὐκ ἐθέλοντα βίῃ καὶ <δειλὰ> διδάσκεις, | ἐσθλὰ μετ’ ἀνθρώπων καὶ κάλ᾿ ἐπιστάμενον. 1062 τοὶ δ’ ἀρετὴν (sc. κατακρύψαντες ἔχουσιν) οὐλομένῃ πενίῃ. Timocles fr. 28, II 463 K. πολλοὺς γὰρ ἐνίοθ᾿ ἡ πενία βιάζεται | ἀνάξι᾿ αὑτῶν ἔργα παρὰ φύσιν ποιεῖν. Philemon fr. 157, II 524 K. ἡ γὰρ σπάνις πρόχειρος εἰς τὸ δρᾶν κακά. Eur. El. 375, Thuc. 3. 45. But the combination of poverty with an evil disposition led to βίος θηριώδης. Thus ordinary Greek morality would have repudiated Matth. ev. 19. 24 on the ground that ἀρετή requires a certain χορηγία.

1 πενία: Nauck would prefer σπάνις, but no change is needed. — συγκραθεῖσα: cf. Pind. Pyth. 5. 2 ἀρετᾷ κεκραμένον καθαρᾷ (sc. πλοῦτον). Blaydes quotes Menand. fr. 578, III 176 Κ. ἤθει δὲ χρηστῷ συγκεκραμένην ἔχειν (sc. τὴν τοῦ λόγου δύναμιν), fr. 785, III 217 K. ὡς ἡδὺ συνέσει χρηστότης κεκραμένη.

2 κατέστρεψεν: overturns. καταστρέφειν Βίον usually means ‘to bring one's career to a close’: see Jebb on Ο. C. 103. Hence Herwerden proposed μετέστρεψεν (as Meineke proposed μεταστροφαί in Aesch. Eum. 493): but the sense yielded (‘alters’) is unsuitable. He quoted Philem. fr. 111 (11 513 K.) ἅπαντα νικᾷ καὶ μεταστρέφει τύχη and Menand. fr. 5, ΙΙΙ 5 K. τἄνω κάτω | ἡμῶν ὁ βίος λήσει μεταστραφεὶς ὅλος. The fact that ἀνεῖλε precedes makes all the difference here.

lg.l: ὦ θνητὸν ἀνδρῶν καὶ ταλαίπωρον γένος,
ὡς οὐδέν ἐσμεν πλὴν σκιαῖς ἐοικότες,

div.p: 945. 1 ὦ θνητὸν Gesner: ὦ θνητῶν SMA, μοχθηρὸν F. W. Schmidt, ὦ τλῆμον H. Stadtmueller, ὦ λυπρὸν (vel τυφλὸν) Blaydes 2 σκιαῖς ἐοικότες SA (ἑοικότες Μ): σκιαῖσιν εἰκότες (εἰκότες iam Gesner) Pierson 3 ἀναστρωφώμενοι B et Gesner: ἀναστρεφόμενοι SMA

945 Stob. flor. 98. 1 (IV p. 824, 4 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ῾ ὦ . . . ἀναστρεφόμενοι.᾿ Nauck suggests that this passage is referred to by Philo de spec. leg. 8 11 p. 308 Μ. τὰ δὲ μηδαμῇ χρήσιμα τῷ βίῳ οὐδὲ ζῆν εἶναι λυσιτελές, περιττὸν ἄχθος ὄντα γῆς, ὡς εἶπέ τις. He also makes the ingenious conjecture that v. 2 is the line which is actually parodied in Ar. Lys. 139 (see on fr. 657); if that is so, the fragment belongs to the Tyro.
Tr.: ‘Alas! for the unhappy race of mortal men, that we are naught but the semblance of shadows, moving to and fro a useless burden to the earth.’

1 θνητόν has been suspected (see cr. n.); but the whole line is merely an echo of the δειλοὶ βροτοί of Homer and Hesiod (cf. Eur. fr. 196, fr. 1073, 5 θνητῶν δὲ θνητὸς ὄλβος), and θνητόν is much superior to the words which have been proposed as its substitutes. — For καί Blaydes conj. πᾶν. Better would be τῶν ταλαιπώρων.

2 οὐδέν ἐσμεν πλήν: cf. Eur. Her.
227 f. πρὸς δ’ ἔμ᾿ , ἀσθενῆ φίλον, | δεδόρκατ᾿ , οὐδὲν ὄντα πλὴν γλώσσης ψόφον, fr. 25 γέροντες οὐδέν ἐσμεν ἄλλο πλὴν ὄχλος. — For the comparison (σκιαῖς) see on fr. 13. — Cobet (Coll. Crit. p. 207) strongly advocated the adoption of σκιαῖσιν εἰκότες, without apparently being aware that the suggestion had been anticipated (see cr. n.), on the ground that εἰκέναι and εἰκώς are the only genuine Attic forms, and that ἐοικέναι and ἐοικώς were adopted by later writers under Homeric influence, and subsequently found their way into the texts of the Attic masters. So far as tragedy is concerned there is no instance of ἐοικέναι and no other of ἐοικώς. There are other isolated exceptions in comedy: Ar. Vesp. 1141 ἀτὰρ δοκεῖ γέ μοι | ἐοικέναι μάλιστα Μορύχου σάγματι, where Cobet reads προσεικέναι, fr. 646, I 552 K. οἶμαι γὰρ αὐτὸν κόλλοπι | ἐοικέναι. The instances in prose are more numerous: see Veitch s.v. There is some evidence of a tendency among copyists to introduce the longer form, but Cobet has not succeeded in persuading modern editors to banish it from their texts.

3 is a reminiscence of the well-known Homeric lines Σ 104 ἀλλ᾿ ἧμαι παρὰ νηυσὶν ἐτώσιον ἄχθος ἀρούρης, υ 378 οὐδέ τι ἔργων | ἔμπαιον οὐδὲ βίης, ἀλλ᾿ αὔτως ἄχθος ἀρούρης. Sophocles has given a general application to Homer's phrase, and in El. 1241 περισσὸν ἄχθος ἔνδον γυναικῶν ὂν ἀεί he uses it of the female sex. Cf. Plat. Theaet. 176 D οἴονται ἀκούειν ὄτι οὐ λῆροί εἰσι, γῆς ἄλλως ἄχθη, ἀλλ᾿ ἄνδρες οἵους δεῖ ἐν πόλει τοὺς σωθησομένους. H. quotes the Orphic Theogony on Man (from Malalas p. 75 περὶ δὲ τοῦ ταλαιπώρου γένους τῶν ἀνθρώπων . . . ) βροτῶν τ’ ἀλιτήρια φῦλα, ἄχθεα γῆς, εἴδωλα τετυγμένα.

lg.l: οὐ γὰρ θέμις ζῆν πλὴν θεοῖς ἄνευ κακῶν.

div.p: 946 Stob. flor. 98. 43 (IV p. 840, 7 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘οὐ γὰρ...κακῶν.’ The same line occurs in Menand. mon. 692 with the reading ἄνευ κακοῦ.

For the supreme good fortune of Zeus see on fr. 895. The unbroken happiness of the gods is an idea which perhaps goes back to Homer's θεοὶ ῥεῖα ζώοντες. Cf. Pind. Pyth. 10. 21 θεὸς εἴη ἀπήμων κέαρ. Aesch. Ag. 558 τίς δὲ πλὴν θεῶν | ἅπαντ' ἀπήμων τὸν δι' αἰῶνος χρόνον ; Eur. fr. 1075, 2 θεοῦ βίον ζῆν ἀξιοῖς ἄνθρωπος ὤν; Dionys. fr. 2 εἰ δ' ἀξιοῖς σοι μηδὲν ἀλγεινόν ποτε | μέλλειν ἔσεσθαι, μακαρίως ἔχεις φρενῶν· | θεῶν γὰρ ἄξειν βίοτον, οὐ θνητῶν δοκεῖς. The thought is echoed by the philosophers from Heraclitus (fr. 102 D. τῷ μὲν θεῷ καλὰ πάντα καὶ ἀγαθὰ καὶ δίκαια) to Aristotle (pol. 7. 1. 1323b 24, Newman 111 p. 316).

lg.l: στέργειν δὲ τἀκπεσόντα καὶ θέσθαι πρέπει
σοφὸν κυβευτήν, ἀλλὰ μὴ στένειν τύχην.

div.p: 947 Stob. flor. 108, 51 (IV p. 969, 8 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. 'στέργειν...τύχην.’ The second line is quoted by Hesych. II Ρ. 545 κυβευτήν. ‘σοφὸν κυβευτήν, ἀλλὰ μὴ στενὴν τυχεῖν.᾿ τὸν τοῖς κύβοις χρώμενον· ἐπιστήμην γάρ τινα ἐδόκουν τὸ δεξιῶς χρῆσθαι· ἐπιστημονικωτέραν τὴν πεττείαν τῆς κυβείας ἐνόμιζον.

1 f. For the game κυβεία, which, like our backgammon, involved a combination of luck and skill, and was therefore less scientific than πεττεία, see on fr. 429. The language is explained by Headlam on Aesch. Ag. 32 τὰ δεσποτῶν γὰρ εὖ πεσόντα θήσομαι | τρὶς ἓξ βαλούσης τῆσδέ μοι φρυκτωρίας: the skilful player should make the best of (στέργειν) his throws and dispose accordingly. Cf. Plat. rep. 604 C ὥσπερ ἐν πτώσει κύβων πρὸς τὰ πεπτωκότα τίθεσθαι τὰ αὑτοῦ πράγματα, Thuc. 1. 25 ἐν ἀπόρῳ εἴχοντο θέσθαι τὸ παρόν, Ter. Ad. 739 ita vitast hominum, quasi quom ludas tesseris, | si illud quod maxume opus est iactu non cadit, | illud quod cecidit forte, id arte ut corrigas.— ἐκπεσόντα corresponds to ἐκβολὰς ψήφων
in Aesch. Eum. 751: cf. Xen. symp. 5. 10 ἐπεὶ δὲ ἐξέπεσον αἱ ψῆφοι. —That θέσθαι could be used in this connexion as well alone as with εὖ or καλῶς (Ο.Τ. 633, fr. 350, and often in Eur.) is proved by the passages already quoted from Aeschylus and Thucydides. There is no need therefore for the conjecture of Hemsterhuis κεὖ (condemned by Porson on Eur. Phoen. 1422 on the ground that καί never makes crasis with εὖ except in compounds), or for Meineke's equally objectionable κἀνθέσθαι. It should be added that τἀμπεσόντα (for τἀκπεσόντα SMA) was a conjecture of Gesner, accepted by Brunck, against which Porson's fine taste protested in the note already referred to. Blaydes needlessly conjectured στέργειν τὰ προσπεσόντα (Eur. fr. 505). F. W. Schmidt, partly following a suggestion of Nauck, substituted καλῶς for πρέπει, which he removed to take the place of τύχην in v. 2. Hense suggests that πρέπει may have been introduced by the gnomologist.

lg.l: ἐλπὶς γὰρ ἡ βόσκουσα τοὺς πολλοὺς βροτῶν.

div.p: 948 Stob. flor. 110. 14 (IV p. 999, 20 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘ἐλπὶς... βροτῶν.' Schol. Eur. Phoen. 396, Prov. app. 1. 59, Menan. mon. 42 quote, without giving the author's name, a line very similar to this, αἱ δ' ἐλπίδες βόσκουσι τοὺς κενοὺς βροτῶν. (Blaydes thinks that Sophocles wrote κενούς.) Cf. Synes. de somn. 8 ἐλπίδες, αἳ τὸ ἀνθρώπων βόσκουσι γένος.

The combination 'hope feeds' or 'nourishes' was familiar: Eur. fr. 826 δι᾽ ἐλπίδος ζῆ καὶ δι᾽ ἐλπίδος τρέφου. Tr. fr. adesp. 252 παμβῶτὶς ἐλπίς. Ant. 1246 ἐλπίσιν δὲ βόσκομαι. Pind. fr. 214 γλυκεῖά οἱ καρδίαν | ἀτάλλοισα γηροτρόφος συναορεῖ | ἐλπίς. The phrase is more particularly applied to those who are empty of more solid nourishment, as in the proverb cited above and in Eur. Bacch. 617. Among those whom hope thus deludes is the exile (Aesch. Ag. 1668 οἶδ᾽ ἐγὼ φεύγοντας ἄνδρας ἐλπίδας σιτουμένους, Eur. Phoen. 396); but it is idle for Nauck to say that Euripides imitates Sophocles. See also Headlam in C. R. XV 102, and for βόσκειν n. on fr. 140.

lg.l: πάντ᾿ ἐμπέφυκε τῷ μακρῷ γήρᾳ κακά,
νοῦς φροῦδος, ἔργ᾿ ἀχρεῖα, φροντίδες κεναί.

div.p: 949 Stob. flor. 116. 29 (IV p. 1044, 1 Hense) ‘πάντ' ... κεναί.' The extract follows immediately after fr. 556 without a lemma, but is assigned to Sophocles by Clem. Alex. protr. p. 73 ἕπεται τοιγαροῦν ὑμῖν κατὰ τὸν Σοφοκλέα τὰ ἐπίχειρα τῆς ἐκλογῆς, ‘νοῦς φροῦδος... κεναί.'

1 τῷ μακρῷ γήρᾳ, of advanced old age, occurs also in O. T. 1112, as well as in Stob. flor. 101. 21, Polyaen. 8. 15, Lucian macrob. 23 (quoted by Nauck). Nauck unnecessarily objected to the phrase as unusual, and after proposing βαθεῖ for μακρῷ here and in Ο.Τ. l.c., finally (Addenda, p. XXIV) expressed a preference for τῷ μακρῷ βίῳ. Blaydes conjectured τ. μ. χρόνῳ.

2 The enumeration has very little in common with the famous description of old age in Arist. rhet. 2. 13, which reappears in Hor. A.P. 169 ff. But Arist.'s καὶ δειλοὶ καὶ πάντα προφοβητικοί illustrates φροντίδες κεναί. — ' A mind dislodged, acts that come to naught, and groundless anxieties': i.e. his sense of proportion goes, he is fussy and restless, and worries about trifles. νοῦς: there is an apparent discrepancy with fr. 261, but Soph. here is speaking of extreme old age. For φροῦδος cf. Ant. 564 οὐ...μένει | νοῦς τοῖς κακῶς πράσσουσιν ἀλλ᾽ ἐξίσταται (Jebb's
n.): hence νοῦ κενός Ο. C. 961, fr. 929. For the converse ἀπὸ νοῦ πεσών see Starkie on Ar. Vesp. 1370, Nub. 1273. Cf. Eur. fr. 25 (of old men) νοῦς δ᾽ οὐκ ἔνεστιν, οἰόμεσθα δ᾽ εὖ φρονεῖν. Hdt. 3. 134 φρένες γηράσκοντι συγγηράσκουσι καὶ ἐς τὰ πρήγματα πάντα ἀπαμβλύνονται. Lucr. 3. 446 pariterque senescere mentem ...(453) claudicat ingenium, delirat lingua, labat mens. — Clement's ὦτα (see cr. n. and cf. fr. 858) is a poor variant, destroying the correspondence of νοῦς, ἔργα and φροντίδες. Blaydes strangely prefers ὦτα for exactly the same reason. For the plur. φροντίδες of anxieties cf. Trach. 149, Eur. I.A. 646. — Nauck thought that Eur. Phoen. 528 ὦ τέκνον, οὐχ ἅπαντα τῷ γήρᾳ κακά, | Ἐτεόκλεες, πρόσεστιν κτέ. was an answer to this fragment.

lg.l: οὐκ ἔστι γῆρας τῶν σοφῶν, ἐν οἷς ὁ νοῦς

div.p: 950 Stob. flor. 117. 4 (IV p. 1055, 6 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ᾿ οὐκ ἔστι...μέγα.' The heading of the chapter in Stobaeus is ὅτι τὸ γῆρας ἀνεπαχθὲς καὶ πολλῆς αἰδοῦς ἄξιον ἡ σύνεσις ἀπεργάζεται, i.e. 'it is Intelligence which relieves old age of its burdens and makes it worthy of much reverence.'

1 f. ἐν οἷς ὁ νοῦς was altered to ὅσοις ὁ νοῦς by Blaydes, and to ὅσοισι νοῦς by Heimsoeth, on the ground that the dative is required by ξύνεστιν ; but the assumption is unnecessary, if the verb finds an object elsewhere. The words θείᾳ ἡμέρᾳ have been generally supposed corrupt, and have provoked a large number of conjectures: προμηθίᾳ ξύνεστιν εὖ τεθραμμένος Bergk, θείῳ ξύνεστιν ἱμέρῳ Meineke, θείῳ ξύνεστιν ἐν φάει Heimsoeth, ἤθει ξύνεστιν ἡμέρῳ or ἐσθλαῖσίν ἐστιν ἡδοναῖς Herwerden, μακρᾷ... ἡμέρᾳ or ἤθει... εὐσεβεῖ (with κεκραμένος) Blaydes, γραίᾳ ...ἡμέρᾳ Kock, πολιᾷ...ἡμέρᾳ Weil, σθένει (ἡβᾷ Enger, θάλλει Stadtmueller) ξυνούσαις ἡμέραις Holzner (with Stadtmueller), ὁσίᾳ ...εὐμαρῶς Nauck, who however pronounces the line to be 'graviter corruptus necdum sanatus.' J. says: ' θείᾳ ἡμέρᾳ. Corrupt. Ellendt (p. 308 b) “aetate a dis concessa augetur sapientia," i.e. with whom intelligence dwells, nurtured by the span of life which heaven grants: but θείᾳ ἡμέρᾳ could not mean that. Nor could it mean [what Campbell suggests] "propitious length of days." The context in Stobaeus shows that these verses are quoted by him to illustrate the fact that old age is alleviated and dignified by the wisdom which accompanies it. The corrupt words θείᾳ... ἡμέρᾳ must have referred to old age. I would read πλήθει...ἡμερῶν. When the letters πλη were lost, θει became θείᾳ, involving the change of ἡμερῶν to the dat. sing. The meaning is: "There is no old age for the wisdom in which the mind has been nurtured ere it reaches length of days." Wisdom which has grown with a man's years is still fresh in his old age. For πλήθει cp. Phil. 721 πλήθει πολλῶν μηνῶν: Thuc. 1. 1 διὰ χρόνου πλῆθος: Ar. Nub. 855 ὑπὸ πλήθους ἐτῶν. For the figurative sense of οὐκ ἔστι γῆρας cp. Aesch. Theb. 682 οὐκ ἔστι γῆρας τοῦδε τοῦ μιάσματος.' I cannot agree with J. that τῶν σοφῶν is neuter, or that the text of Stobaeus is appropriately illustrated by a statement that wisdom is ever young (ἀεὶ γὰρ ἡβᾷ τοῖς γέρουσιν εὐμαθεῖν Aesch. Ag. 589). H. briefly discussed the passage in J. P. XXXI 9. Although he also regarded τῶν σοφῶν as gen. of τὰ σοφά, he nevertheless treated ἐν οἷς as masc. (οὐ μέντοι τούτοις γηράσκει τὰ σοφά, ἐν οἷς κτέ.), and by his defence of θείᾳ ἡμέρᾳ he has, I believe, found the key to the true meaning. The following explanation is drawn in part from H.'s Ms notes, but he is only responsible for the details, so far as is expressly stated. Holding that there is no need for any of the somewhat desperate alterations which have been mentioned, but that the words θείᾳ ἡμέρᾳ are sound and only require explanation, he brings them into line with Ai. 622 ἦ που παλαιᾷ μὲν σύντροφος ἁμέρᾳ. Eur. Ion 720 νέαν δ ἁμέραν ἀπολιπὼν θάνοι. Herond. 4. 68 οὐχὶ ζόην βλέπουσιν ἡμέρην πάντες; Pind. Ol. 13. 39 ποδαρκὴς ἁμέρα. Further illustrations of
the same idiom will be found in my note on Eur. Phoen. 540: the underlying principle was long ago stated by Gronovius (ap. Blomfield gl. Aesch. Pers. 266) : 'ἦμαρ in hujusmodi locutionibus accipi pro conditione ac fortuna quam dies imponit.' Hence H. concludes that θεία ἡμέρα is equivalent to inspired vitality, quoting Aesch. Ag. 104 ff. κύριός εἰμι θροεῖν...ἔτι γὰρ θεόθεν καταπνεύει | πειθώ, μολπᾶν ἀλκάν, σύμφυτος αἰών. The thought that wisdom is inspired appears often in Pindar: see Ol. 11. 10 ἐκ θεοῦ δ᾽ ἀνὴρ σοφαῖς ἀνθεῖ πραπίδεσσιν ὁμοίως, ibid. 9. 28 ἀγαθοὶ δὲ καὶ σοφοὶ κατὰ δαίμον᾽ ἄνδρες | ἐγένοντ', and Headlam in J.P. XXX 304. The point is developed in my article on Possession in the Encycl. of Religion and Ethics. If this be so, the idea running through these lines is that wisdom is not something drawn from without, but a natural indwelling force which increases with length of time and depends for its permanence upon the co-operation of the human intelligence with the divine capacity which is inherited at birth. That is to say, the wise, whose mind has been reared in habitual converse with inspired vitality, never come to a useless old age; for their foresight is a great boon to their fellows. The sense thus gained is unexceptionable, and the only point in the language still requiring comment is that at first sight τεθραμμένος appears to be isolated. But in fact the preposition of ξύνεστιν extends its influence to the participle, although not repeated: the idiom was recognized by Kaibel (on El. 569), who quotes in illustration Trach. 89 οὐκ ἐῶ πατρὸς | ἡμᾶς προταρβεῖν οὐδὲ δειμαίνειν ἄγειν. This is the easier, since it has been pointed out by Jebb on O.T. 863 that ξύνειμι may be followed by a supplementary participle after the manner of διατελῶ. The subtilty of Sophoclean style finds a congenial field in the various applications of ξύνειμι, ξύνοικος, ξύντροφος and similar words: see for ξύνειμι Αί. 337, El. 611, O. C. 7, 946, 1244, Ant. 370. Whether σοφῶν is masc. or neut. is a subsidiary question, but the former alternative yields a simpler and more appropriate sense.

3 Bergk and Meineke think that this verse is disconnected with the two preceding; but the explanation given above shows that so far from this being the case its presence is essential in order to complete the sense. J. well compares Milton, Il Penseroso 173 'Till old experience do attain | to something like prophetic strain.' The proverbial character of προμηθία κέρδος has been shown on fr. 302.

lg.l: ὅστις δὲ θνητῶν θάνατον ὀρρωδεῖ λίαν
μῶρος πέφυκε· τῇ τύχῃ μέλει τάδε.
ὅταν δ᾽ ὁ καιρὸς τοῦ θανεῖν ἐλθὼν τύχῃ,
οὐδ᾽ ἂν πρὸς αὐλὰς Ζηνὸς ἐκφύγοι μολών.

div.p: 951. 3 δ' Grotius : γὰρ S 4 ἐκφύγοι Halm : ἐκφύγη S, ἐκφύγοις Dindorf
951 Stob. flor. 118. 12 (IV p. 1068, 5 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘ὅστις...μολών.’ The extract is omitted by MA.

1 f. A similar sentiment is quoted by Stobaeus (flor. 118. 16) from the Polyidus of Aristophanes (fr. 452, I 508 K.): τὸ γὰρ φοβεῖσθαι τὸν θάνατον λῆρος πολύς· | πᾶσιν γὰρ ἡμῖν τοῦτ᾽ ὀφείλεται παθεῖν. The reason there given is that death is inevitable, as here that it is uncertain. Heracles, recommending present enjoyment, combines both reasons in Eur. Alc. 782 βροτοῖς ἅπασι κατθανεῖν ὀφείλεται, | κοὐκ ἔστι θνητῶν ὅστις ἐξεπίσταται | τὴν αὔριον μέλλουσαν εἰ βιώσεται· | τὸ τῆς τύχης γὰρ ἀφανὲς οἷ προβήσεται κτέ.
3 δ' (see cr. n.) has been replaced by its gloss (ὁ δὲ ἀντὶ τοῦ γάρ), as in Ant. 672. See on fr. 873.

4 Flight to the upper air is often ironically mentioned as offering a means of escape from an inevitable evil. So Eur. Med. 1296 δεῖ γάρ νιν ἤτοι γῆς σφε κρυφθῆναι κάτω | ἢ πτηνὸν ἆραι σῶμ᾽ ἐς αἰθέρος βάθος, Phoen. 1216 ἣν μή γε φεύγων ἐκφύγῃς πρὸς αἰθέρα, Hec. 1099 ποῖ πορευθῶ; | ἀμπτάμενος οὐράνιον | ὑψιπετὲς ἐς μέλαθρον κτέ., Aesch. Suppl. 787
μέλας γενοίμαν καπνὸς | νέφεσσι γειτονῶν Διός. The earliest example of the hyperbole is said to be Anacreon fr. 24 ἀναπέτομαι δὴ πρὸς Ὄλυμπον πτερύγεσσι κούφαις | διὰ τὸν Ἔρωτ'· οὐ γὰρ ἐμοὶ παῖς ἐθέλει συνηβᾶν. — ἐκφύγοι: there is an ellipse of the subject (τις), an idiom found occasionally from Homer onwards. Cf. Hom. Χ 199 ὡς δ᾽ ἐν ὀνείρῳ οὐ δύναται φεύγοντα διώκειν, Aesch. Ag. 71 οὔθ' ὑποκαίων οὔτ᾽ ἐπιλείβων | ἀπύρων ἱερῶν | ὀργὰς ἀτενεῖς παραθέλξει, Soph. El. 696 ὅταν δέ τις θεῶν | βλάπτῃ, δύναιτ᾽ ἂν οὐδ᾽ ἂν ἰσχύων φυγεῖν, fr. 1120, 6. In subordinate, especially relative, clauses the usage is more frequent and varied: see Hom. e 400, ι 476, ν 400, h. 29. 6, h. Herm. 202, Hes. Op. 12, 290, Eur. Or. 707 ἔστη δ᾽ αὖθις ἣν χαλᾷ πόδα, Soph. Ai. 1081, Thompson on Plat. Men. 79 B, Arist. Ath. pol. 7. 4 ἐπειδὰν ἔρηται.

lg.l: ὅστις γὰρ ἐν κακοῖσιν ἱμείρει βίου,
ἢ δειλός ἐστιν ἢ δυσάλγητος φρένας.

div.p: 952 Stob. flor. 121. 21 (IV p. 1103, 16 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘ὅστις.. φρένας.’

This is the ordinary Greek view: a life which is separated entirely from τὸ καλόν is not worth living. Aesch. Prom. 776 κρεῖσσον γὰρ εἰσάπαξ θανεῖν, | ἢ τὰς ἁπάσας ἡμέρας πάσχειν κακῶς. fr. 177 τί γὰρ καλὸν ζῆν βίοτον ὃς λύπας φέρει; Soph. Ant. 463 ὅστις γὰρ ἐν πολλοῖσιν ὡς ἐγὼ κακοῖς | ζῇ, πῶς ὅδ᾽ οὐχὶ κατθανὼν κέρδος φέρει; El. 1485 τί γὰρ βροτῶν ἂν σὺν κακοῖς μεμειγμένων | θνῄσκειν ὁ μέλλων τοῦ χρόνου κέρδος φέροι; Αί. 473 αἰσχρὸν γὰρ ἄνδρα τοῦ μακροῦ χρήζειν βίου | κακοῖσιν ὅστις μηδὲν ἐξαλλάσσεται. Eur. Tro. 632 τοῦ ζῆν δὲ λυπρῶς κρεῖσσόν ἐστι κατθανεῖν. Isocr. 2. 36 αἱροῦ τεθνάναι καλῶς μᾶλλον ἢ ζῆν αἰσχρῶς. Eur. fr. 816, if ever I saw a blind man following his guide, ἀδημονοῦντα συμφοραῖς ἐλοιδόρουν, | ὡς δειλὸς εἴη θάνατον ἐκποδὼν ἔχων. See also on fr. 488. When the Stoics, treating life and death as things indifferent, laid down rules determining the conditions in which suicide was justifiable (εὔλογος ἐξαγωγή), and found it to be commensurate with external evils such as poverty, disease, or oppression (Sto. vet. fr. 111 768 Arn.), they were guiding the current sentiment to its logical conclusion. Aristotle, on the other hand, took the modern view of suicide, and declared the coward's part to consist in seeking death rather than in clinging to life (eth. N. 3. 7. 1116a 12).

δυσάλγητος is insensible, — here to what honour requires, — in O. T. 12 to the sufferings of others (σκληρός, δυσμετάκλαστος, ἀναλγής, ἀπαθής, ἀνηλεής, ἴσον τῷ ἀνάλγητος καὶ σκληρός schol.). ἀνάλγητος and its cognates are more often found in this sense. Cf. Plut. de vit. pud. 1 p. 528 D ἀναλγὴς μὲν γὰρ ὁ ἀναιδὴς πρὸς τὸ αἰσχρόν. Aristotle contrasts ἀναλγησία with δειλία, the excess of ἀφοβία with the excess of φόβος, both as extremes opposed to the mean ἀνδρεία (eth. Ν. 3. 7. 1115b 24). In Thuc. 3. 40 μὴ ἀναλγητότεροι φανῆναι is 'not to show yourselves less alive to danger.' Thus ἀναλγησία is a narrower form of ἀναισθησία.

lg.l: <Α. > θανόντι κείνῳ συνθανεῖν ἔρως μ᾽ ἔχει.

div.p: 953. 1 sq. personarum notas add. Dindorf | ἥξεις S : ἤρξης Μ, ἔρξεις Α | μόρσιμον μόνημον Μ
953 Stob. flor. 122. 11 (IV p. 1115, 7 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘θανόντι ... μόρσιμον.'
The Mss give no indication that the lines are part of a dialogue. Welcker assigns them to a play dealing with the story of Alcestis (see p. 60 [fr. 851]): but other inferences are equally possible.

1 θανόντι συνθανεῖν. Observe that the aor. part. is not necessarily coincident
in time with the inf. see on Eur. Hclid. 1025, and cf. Trach. 797 μὴ φύγῃς τοὐμὸν κακόν, | μηδ' εἴ σε χρὴ θανόντι συνθανεῖν ἐμοί. In other words, συνθνῄσκειν does not necessarily imply a simultaneous death, and the verse may mean: 'now that he is dead, I would gladly die too.' This is proved by Eur. Hel. 1401 f. The pres. is used in Eur. Suppl. 1006 ἅδιστος γάρ τοι θάνατος | συνθνῄσκειν θνήσκουσι φίλοις.—The inf. depends on the combined phrase ἔρως μ' ἔχει, as the equivalent of βούλομαι : logical grammar would require τοῦ συνθανεῖν. Cf. Eur. I.T. 1342 φόβῳ δ' ἃ μὴ χρῆν εἰσορᾶν καθήμεθα, Her. 710 ἀνάγκην προστίθης ἡμῖν θανεῖν.

2 τὸ μόρσιμον, here as the fixed goal towards which every man moves: Aesch. Cho. 102 τὸ μόρσιμον μένει. No one can escape from τὸ μόρσιμον (Pind. Pyth. 12. 30, Aesch. Theb. 268); hence παθεῖν τὸ μόρσιμον (Aesch. Theb. 249, Soph. Ant. 235). In Eur. Alc. 939 παρεὶς τὸ μόρσιμον is applied to the exceptional case of Admetus.
H. renders: 'A. I'm fain to share death with him. B. You will come— You need not hasten to the fated end.'

lg.l: χρόνος δ᾽ ἀμαυροῖ πάντα κἀς λήθην ἄγει.

div.p: 954 Stob. flor. 126. 8 (IV p. 1143, 9 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘χρόνος...ἄγει.’ The line is also quoted among the monosticha of Menander, 545.

Nauck refers to Aesch. Eum. 286 χρόνος καθαιρεῖ πάντα γηράσκων ὁμοῦ, which many editors reject as an interpolation. The language follows Simonid. fr. 4 ἐντάφιον δὲ τοιοῦτον οὔτ᾽ εὐρὼς | οὔθ' ὁ πανδαμάτωρ ἀμαυρώσει χρόνος: cf. Ai. 714 πάνθ᾽ ὁ μέγας χρόνος μαραίνει. Callim. aet. 429 (Ox. Pap. VII p. 53) ἀμαυρώσει χρόνος, Theodect. fr. 9, 3 ἀλλ' ὁ μυρίος χρόνος | τὰ πάντ᾽ ἀμαυροῖ χὑπὸ χεῖρα λαμβάνει. H. renders: 'Time makes all things faint | And brings them to oblivion.'
955 Stob. flor. IV p. 242, 8 Mein. (111 p. 430, 8 Hense) Σοφοκλέους. ‘τἀληθὲς ...λόγου.'

There is plainly some corruption here, although the general meaning is free from doubt. Nauck conj. ἰσχύειν λέγω, Conington ἰσχύει λόγῳ, F. W. Schmidt ἰσχύειν φιλεῖ. R. Prinz, as Mekler informed me, proposed δόλου for λόγου; but this would require us also to substitute πλεῖον (fr. 178n.) for πλεῖστον. Meineke in fact proposed πλεῖον, while in other respects adhering to the text, and Hense thinks that, so far as Stobaeus is concerned, he may have been right. H. in J.P. XX 306 suggested ἰσχύειν λόγος, inferring from 0.Τ. 356 τἀληθὲς γὰρ ἰσχῦον τρέφω that the saying was proverbial. To this he adds Dem. 19. 208 ὅτι τἀληθὲς ἰσχυρόν, Aeschin. 1. 84 ἀλλ' οὕτως ἰσχυρόν ἐστιν ἡ ἀλήθεια, ὥστε πάντων ἐπικρατεῖ τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων λογισμῶν, Dinarch. 1. 53, 54 ἴσχυσεν ἂν τὸ ψεῦδος τῆς ἀληθείας μᾶλλον ... ἰσχύσει μᾶλλον τῆς ἀληθείας ἡ ...διαβολή, Eur. fr. 343 θάρσει· τό τοι δίκαιον ἰσχύει μέγα, Philostr. vit. soph. 2. 1. 19 ἀλλ᾽ ὅμως τἀληθὲς ἴσχυεν. See also on frs. 78 and 588. Liban. epist. 1061.
Hense, arguing from the position of the extract in the Ms, is inclined to ascribe it to the Eriphyle.

lg.l: ὑπέρ τε πόντον πάντ᾽ ἐπ᾿ ἔσχατα χθονὸς
νυκτός τε πηγὰς οὐρανοῦ τ᾽ ἀναπτυχὰς

div.p: 956 Strabo 295 οὐδὲ γὰρ εἴ τινα Σοφοκλῆς τραγῳδεῖ περὶ τῆς Ὠρειθυίας λέγων ὡς ἀναρπαγεῖσα ὑπὸ Βορέου κομισθείη ‘ὑπέρ τε...κῆπον,᾽ οὐδὲν ἂν εἴη πρὸς τὰ νῦν.
For the question whether Sophocles wrote an Orithyia see on fr. 768. Wolff, who holds that he did not, assigns these lines to the Tympanistae (II p. 262).

1 ff. Translate: 'Far over the sea to the earth's confines, to the home of darkness, to the bright expanse of heaven, and to the old domain of Phoebus'. Blaydes unnecessarily suspects πάντ': it is strange that he did not recognize that his own conjectures πάντα τ' (or ἔς τε τἄσχατα) and ὅριά τ' would have been much more objectionable, if they had formed part of the tradition.—νυκτός τε πηγάς. In Aesch. Prom. 834 οἱ πρὸς ἡλίου | ναίουσι πηγαῖς the particular reference is to a fabulous lake in Libya. Here the words refer generally to the north (rather than the west, as assumed by Jebb on Ant. 803), always associated with darkness since the time of Homer's Cimmerians (λ 14 f.). — οὐρανοῦ τ᾿ ἀναπτυχάς, of the bright unclouded skies in the blessed land of the Hyperboreans. So Eur. Ion 1445 λαμπρᾶς αἰθέρος ἀμπτυχαί. Similarly I think that in Hipp. 601 ἡλίου τ' ἀναπτυχαί is not the 'unclouded orb of the sun,' but the open sky which the sun reveals. L. and S.'s view of this line cannot be supported.—Φοίβου τε κτέ. Hermann and others delete τε, in order that παλαιόν may be scanned as usual; and Wecklein conjectured τε λεῖον. But cf. Eur. El. 497 παλαιόν τε θησαύρισμα Διονύσου τόδε, Her. 446 ποσὶν ἕλκουσαν τέκνα καὶ γεραιόν (anap.), fr. 162; and in fact the copula is required by the sense. J. writes: 'κῆπον: the eastern sky is the "garden of Phoebus from of old," since he is a god of light. So Pindar (P. 5. 22) calls Cyrene γλυκύν ...κᾶπον Ἀφροδίτας, and Libya (P. 9. 53) Διὸς ἔξοχον...κᾶπον. Cp. fr. 24, 4 (Gomperz conj. σηκόν, comparing Tr. fr. adesp. 424 ἁγνὸν εἰς σηκὸν θεοῦ, but the notion of precinct or shrine seems less fitting here).' But the whole passage is descriptive of the northern region to which Boreas carried Orithyia. Now, according to a well-known story, the original home of Apollo from which he came to Delphi (Alcaeus fr. 2) was the land of the Hyperboreans: hence Pind. Ol. 3. 17 δᾶμον Ὑπερβορέων...Ἀπόλλωνος θεράποντα, Pyth. 10. 34 ὧν (sc. Ὑπερβορέων) θαλίαις ἔμπεδον | εὐφαμίαις τε μάλιστ' Ἀπόλλων | χαίρει. Further, I think it probable that Φοίβου κῆπος is to be identified with the garden of the Hesperides (fr. 320): see Apollod. 2. 113 ταῦτα δὲ ἦν, οὐχ ὥς τινες εἶπον ἐν Λιβύῃ, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπὶ τοῦ Ἄτλαντος ἐν Ὑπερβορέοις. Apollodorus in general followed the account of Pherecydes (FHG I 78); and in this particular is supported by Tzetz. Chil. 2. 357 ἐξ Ἑσπερίδων ἀγαγεῖν, ἐκ τῶν Ὑπερβορέων. This view has been anticipated by Wilamowitz (Eur. Her. II² p. 98). In Trach. 1100 Sophocles placed the garden ἐπ᾿ ἐσχάτοις τόποις.

lg.l: νὴ τὼ Λαπέρσα, νὴ τὸν Εὐρώταν τρίτον,
νὴ τοὺς ἐν Ἄργει καὶ κατὰ Σπάρτην θεούς.

div.p: 957 Strabo 364 τὴν δὲ Λᾶν οἱ Διόσκουροί ποτε ἐκ πολιορκίας ἑλεῖν ἱστοροῦνται, ἀφ᾽ οὗ δὴ Λαπέρσαι προσηγορεύθησαν· καὶ Σοφοκλῆς λέγει που ‘νὴ τὼ...θεούς.’

Meursius suggested that the lines came from the Lacaenae, and the same view was taken by Dindorf; it is a plausible guess, but nothing more. Nauck thought that the order of the verses should be inverted, and he was very likely right; as they stand, Strabo must be supposed to have started his quotation after a name
had been mentioned which would account for τρίτον. For the stress laid on the number three cf. Ai. 1174, O.C. 7, 331.

'Las was a mountain stronghold, on a spur of Taygetus, near the sea (vicus maritimus Liv. 38. 30, 31), on the west shore of the Laconian Gulf, about four miles south of Gytheion. It is mentioned in Il. 2. 585 οἵ τε Λάαν εἶχον. There was once a temple of Athena Asia there, said to have been built by the Dioscuri on their return from Colchis (Pausan. 3. 24. 7). The name Λᾶς is perhaps akin to λᾶας (stone): so Steph. Byz. p. 404, 8 κεῖται δὲ ἐπὶ πέτρας ὑψηλῆς, διὸ Λᾶ καλεῖται (Curtius, Peloponnesus, II p. 324). Preller (Myth. II p. 101) suggests that Lapersae may, like Lapithae, be connected with the same root, as="dwellers on rocky heights." The Dioscuri were evidently conceived as having dwelt at Las (Pausan. 3. 24. 7); cp. Hesych. III p. 13 Λαπέρσαι ...ἀπὸ Λαπέρσης πόλεως. The etymology from Λᾶς and πέρθω (Strabo) can hardly be right [Lobeck, Paralip. p. 78], though it may have been the popular one. Cp. Lycophron 511 τοῖς ἡμιθνήτοις διπτύχοις Λαπερσίοις, 1369 Ζηνὶ τῷ Λαπερσίῳ.' (J.) For the situation of Las see Frazer's Pausanias, III p. 392.

app.rdg: Herwerden: τετραορίστῳ vel τετρωρίστῳ vel τετραρίστῳ codd.

div.p: 958 Strabo 399 ἐνταῦθα δέ που (at Psaphis in the district of Oropus) καὶ τὸ Ἀμφιαράειόν ἐστι τετιμημένον ποτὲ μαντεῖον, ὅπου φυγόντα τὸν Ἀμφιάρεων, ὥς φησι Σοφοκλῆς, ‘ἐδέξατο...δίφρῳ.’

Welcker (p. 271) assigned this fragment to the Epigoni, which he identified with the Eriphyle; Brunck, after Meursius, to the satyric Amphiaraus.
