See I pp. 72, 129. —Three different localities are connected by tradition with the disappearance of Amphiaraus, after the defeat of the Argives before the walls of Thebes: (1) a sacred enclosure on the road from Potniae to Thebes (Pausan. 9. 8. 3); this was close to Thebes, and an oracle of Amphiaraus was established there. (2) Harma, on the main road from Thebes to Chalcis, and about half-way between the two (Pausan. 1. 34. 2, 9. 19. 4). The name of the place was supposed to have been suggested by the miracle. (3) The shrine of Amphiaraus in the neighbourhood of Oropus, actually about four miles to the SE. of the town (Strabo supr.). The dream-oracle at the Amphiareion near Oropus became very famous in later times, and it has been inferred that the cult was transferred thither from Thebes at some date between 431 and 414 B.C.: see Frazer's Pausanias, V p. 31. J. points out that Strabo's words do not necessarily mean that Sophocles indicated Oropus as the site of the disappearance; in fact, unless Θηβαία κόνις is unduly strained, the text is inconsistent with such a view.

1 ἐδέξατο ῥαγεῖσα: for the lengthening of the short syllable before ρ cf. Ant. 318 τί δὲ ῥυθμίζεις, ibid. 712 παρὰ ῥείθροισι, Ο. Τ. 847 εἰς ἐμὲ ῥέπον, Ο. C. 900 ἀπὸ ῥυτῆρος. Hilberg, who is dissatisfied (cf. fr. 498), would actually prefer ῥαγεῖσα Θηβαία κόνις ἐδέξατο.

2 αὐτοῖσιν ἵπποις. 'So Pind. Nem. 9. 24 κρύψεν ἄνδρ᾽ ἅμ' ἵπποις. Cp. note on El. 837 f.' (J.) Baton, the charioteer, shared his master's fate (Apollod. 3. 77, Pausan. 2. 23. 2). For the idiomatic αὐτοῖσιν cf. Ai. 26 αὐτοῖς ποιμνίων ἐπιστάταις.—τετραόρῳ: see cr. n. 'The corruption may have arisen from τετραόρῳ having been changed to the contracted form τετρώρῳ (Eur. Alc. 483 etc.), which was then expanded, for metre's sake, into τετρωρίστῳ. τετράορος is used in tragic iambics: Eur. Hel. 723 τετραόροις | ἵπποις, Suppl. 674 ὄχων | τετραόρων.' (J.) Wilamowitz on Eur. Her. 290 defended τετρώριστος as a formation similar to πελώριστος in Theocr. Id. 18.

lg.l: βροτοῖσι κλεινὴν Νῦσαν, ἣν ὁ βούκερως

app.rdg: CDFh, αὐτόμαιαν (potius αὐτομαῖαν Nauck) coni. Meineke

div.p: 959 Strabo 687 παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ δέ τις ἔστι τὴν Νῦσαν καθυμνῶν ὡς τὸ Διονύσῳ καθιερωμένον ὄρος· ‘ὅθεν...κλαγγάνει;’
Welcker (p. 307) assigned the fragment to the Triptolemus. Hartung printed it as belonging to the Διονυσίσκος.

1 ff. βεβακχιωμένην. This is generally connected with βροτοῖσι (so L. and S.); and Hartung renders, 'wo die Menschen selig schwärmen.' But, if Bruhn on Eur. Bacch. 109 is right in contending that βακχιόω is formed from Βάκχιος the god, not from βάκχος the worshipper, and means 'to fill with the divine presence,' the ordinary view cannot stand. Probably he unduly restricted the scope of the verb, which might either signify 'to fill with ecstatic frenzy,' or bear the narrower sense which he recommended. There is, however, another reason which makes strongly against the current interpretation; viz. that Nysa (for which see Jebb on Ant. 1131) is never represented as easy of access to the mortal followers of the god. It was, on the contrary, conceived as a mysterious and remote region, becoming ever farther away as the circle of geographical knowledge widened. Traditionally it was the home of the Nymphs who fostered the infant Dionysus: Hom. Ζ 133 Διωνύσοιο τιθήνας | σεῦε κατ᾿ ἠγάθεον Νυσήιον, Hom. h. Dion. 26. 3 ὃν τρέφον ἠύκομοι νύμφαι... Νύσης ἐν γυάλοις, Eur. Cycl. 68 οὐδ᾽ ἐν Νύσᾳ μετὰ Νυμφᾶν...μέλπω. Hence Kern (in Pauly-Wissowa V 1035) concludes: 'Nysa ist ein Land der Phantasie, ein glückliches Land, für keinen Sterblichen zum Aufenthalt bestimmt, sondern nur für den heiligen Zeussohn' etc. We must not therefore compare (with H.) Verg. Georg. 2. 487 virginibus bacchata Lacaenis Taygeta, but take βροτοῖσι with κλεινήν, as = 'of world-wide fame,' like ὁ πᾶσι κλεινὸς Οἰδίπους Ο.Τ. 8. — ὁ βούκερως Ἴακχος. 'The significance of the Ox-Dionysus is most clearly seen in the cultus of the Argives and Eleans. (1) The Argives called forth the βουγενής Dionysus from the lake of Lerna (Pollux 4. 86); by which he was said to have brought up his mother Semele from Hades (Paus. 2. 27. 3). Here he is evidently the generative and renewing force of nature. (2) The Eleans had a ὕμνος κλητικός (PLG III 656; Roscher I 1058) in which Dionysus is invoked to come ἐς ναὸν βοέῳ ποδὶ θύων. The refrain was ἄξιε ταῦρε, ἄξιε ταῦρε. Athen. 476 A says of D., ταῦρον καλεῖσθαι ὑπὸ πολλῶν ποιητῶν. ἐν δὲ Κυζίκῳ καὶ ταυρόμορφος ἵδρυται. Cp. (1) Nicander, Alexiph. 31 Σιληνοὶ κεραοῖο Διωνύσοιο τιθηνοί. (2) A.P. 9. 524, 20 ταυρωπόν, and ib. 23 χρυσόκερων. So also the Roman poets: Hor. C. 2. 19. 29; Tibull. 2. 1. 3; Prop. 3. 17. 19.' (J.) For the worship of Dionysus in bull-form see Frazer Golden Bough VII³ p. 16 f., and for possible explanations ibid. p. 288 ff.: Kern (l.c. 1041) treats the Elean bull-fetish as the original form of the cult. The worshippers are thought to have been called βουκόλοι: Starkie on Ar. Vesp. 10. This is the only passage from the Periclean age which expressly identifies Iacchus, the mystery-god at Athens and Eleusis, with Dionysus as otherwise worshipped; the other evidence pointing in the same direction is collected by Höfer in Roscher II 4 and Gruppe, Gr. Myth. p. 1435². Miss Harrison (Prolegomena, p. 544) attempts to minimize the significance of βούκερως as applied to Iacchus, but is not convincing. See also on fr. 668.—μαῖαν...νέμει, 'accounts his dear mother-land.' Cf. El. 598 καί σ' ἔγωγε δεσπότιν | ἢ μητέρ᾽ οὐκ ἔλασσον εἰς ἡμᾶς νέμω. For μαῖα see Aesch. Cho. 43 ἰὼ γαῖα μαῖα. The idea is paraphrased in Eur. Hclid. 826 τῇ τε βοσκούσῃ χθονὶ | καὶ τῇ τεκούσῃ. Cf. Eur. fr. 52 ἁ τεκοῦσα γᾶ, and the use of ἡ ἐνεγκοῦσα in Heliodorus (J. E. B. Mayor in J. P. XV 174).

4 τίς...οὐχί...; See Jebb on O.T.
1526 and cf. O. C. 1132 f., fr. 150. τίς οὐ = πᾶς is common in the orators: see e.g. Dem. 37. 14 ἀξιοῦντος δὲ τούτου καὶ πολλὰ δεηθέντος ἐμοῦ καὶ τί οὐ ποιήσαντος, Kuehner-Gerth II 522. Nysa resounds with the voices of all kinds of singing-birds. Miss Harrison, who translates (op. cit. p. 379) this passage as if Nysa were a silent land without the song of birds, evidently accepts Dindorf's and Meineke's view (O.C. p. VIII) that τις ὄρνις οὐχί = οὔτις ὄρνις.

lg.l: θαυμαστὰ γὰρ τὸ τόξον ὡς ὀλισθάνει.

div.p: 960 Suid. s.v. ὡς· λίαν... Σοφοκλῆς ‘θαυμαστὰ...ὀλισθάνει.’

For the gloss λίαν see on fr. 382. The construction follows the analogy of θαυμαστὸς ὅσος, θαυμασίως ὡς and the like. Kuehner-Gerth II 415 quotes as an example of the original subordinating idiom Hdt. 3. 113 ἀπόζει δὲ τῆς χώρης τῆς Ἀραβίης θεσπέσιον ὡς ἡδύ. So here it might be thought that θαυμαστά is the idiomatic nom. plural (Eur. Hclid. 507 n.): 'it is strange how the bow slips.' But analogy favours its interpretation as adverbial accusative (Jebb on O.T. 883 etc.), so that θαυμαστὰ ὡς was identical with θαυμασίως ὡς ('ever so strangely'). Thus the line is exactly parallel to Eur. I. A. 943 θαυμαστὰ δ᾿ ὡς ἀνάξι᾿ ἠτιμασμένη, where θαυμαστὰ ὡς qualifies ἀνάξια and the objection raised by some editors is seen to be unfounded.

lg.l: θεοῦ δὲ πληγὴν οὐκ ὑπερπηδᾷ βροτός.

div.p: 961 Theophilus ad Autol. 2. 8, p. 74 ὁ γοῦν Σοφοκλῆς ἀπρονοησίαν ἐν ἑτέρῳ λέγει ῾ θεοῦ . . . βροτός.᾿ The same line occurs without a lemma in Stob. ecl. 1. 3. 7 p. 53, 16 W. and in Men. mon. 251. Stobaeus and Theophilus (c. 175 A.D.) both drew from the same anthology, and there is a considerable foreign element in the collection known as the monosticha of Menander.

This line raises a question of some interest, since several critics have objected to the confusion of metaphors in the expression ‘to overleap a blow.’ Hence Heimsoeth conj. παγίδας, for which Nauck quoted Nicetas of Chonae (Nicetas Acominatus, a Byzantine historian who was born about the middle of the 12th century A.D.) p. 342, 14 μὴ ἐξεῖναί τινι τὰς πάγας ὑπεραλέσθαι ἢ τὸ ἀμφίβληστρον διεκδῦναι ὃ ἡ ἄνωθεν ἐξέτεινε πρόνοια, and Theophyl. (of Achrida, a Bulgarian archbishop and theologian of the 11th century A.D.) epist. 46 p. 82 πρὸς πᾶν ὁδηγοῖο καλόν, τὰς τοῦ πονηροῦ παγίδας ὑπερπηδῶν. The metaphor which Heimsoeth seeks to restore is several times employed by Aeschylus: Ag. 371 ὑπερτελέσαι μέγα δουλείας γάγγαμον, ib. 1374 πημονῆς ἀρκύστατ᾿ ἂν | φράξειεν ὕψος κρεῖσσον ἐκπηδήματος, Pers. 100 ἄρκυας ἄτας, τόθεν οὐκ ἔστιν ὑπὲρ θνατὸν ἀλύξαντα φυγεῖν, Eum. 112 ἐκ μέσων ἀρκυστάτων | ὤρουσεν. The force of this evidence cannot be ignored, but, if a change is necessary, Meineke's πηκτήν (Ar. Av. 528) would be easier. J. thinks that παγίδας is beneath the style of Attic tragedy; but the same might have been said of γάγγαμον, if an accident had not preserved it in Aeschylus. He accordingly prefers Herwerden's ὑπεκπηδᾷ: ‘no mortal can spring aside from the blow of a god.’

On the other hand, the text was defended by H., who thought confusion of metaphor characteristic of Sophocles (see C. R. xvi 442), and by Diels (Sitzungsb. d. preuss. Akad. 1901 p. 199). The latter argued that θεοῦ πληγή was so current and familiar a phrase that the catachresis is justified: he quotes Aesch. Ag. 379 Διὸς πλαγὰν ἔχουσιν, Ai. 137 πληγὴ Διός, ib. 278 δέδοικα μὴ ’κ θεοῦ πληγή τις ἥκῃ. (Hom. Il. 816 refers to an actual blow given by Apollo.) He also inferred from the silence of Euripides that the metaphor was worn out; and, though the phrase is now known to have
occurred in the Cretans (v. 29 [Berliner Klassikertexte, v 2 p. 73] κἀγὼ μὲν ἡ τεκοῦσα κοὐδὲν αἰτία | ἔκρυψα πληγὴν δαίμονος θεήλατον), the mode of its employment favours his general conclusion. For later Greek cf. Plut. de superst. 7 p. 168 B σώματος ἀρρωστία πᾶσα καὶ χρημάτων ἀποβολὴ καὶ τέκνων θάνατοι . . . πληγαὶ θεοῦ καὶ προσβολαὶ δαίμονος λέγονται. In view of these doubts, and still more in consequence of Aesch. Suppl. 885 Αἰγυπτίαν γὰρ βᾶριν οὐχ ὑπερθορῇ (οὐκ ἐκφύγοις schol.), where ὑπερθρῴσκω seems to mean merely ‘to escape,’ I have refrained from altering the text.

lg.l: εἰ δείν᾿ ἔδρασας, δεινὰ καὶ παθεῖν σε δεῖ.

div.p: 962 δείν᾿ ἔδρασας Stob.: δεινὰ ὀρέξας vel ὁ ῥέξας Theoph., δεινὰ δέδρακας schol. Dion. Thr. | σε δεῖ] εἶν ἔδει schol. Vat. C Dion. Thr., σ᾿ ἔδει coni. Usener

962 Theophil. ad Autol. 2. 37 p. 180 καὶ ὁ Σοφοκλῆς ῾ εἰ . . . δεῖ.᾿ The line is quoted without an author's name by schol. Vat. C Dionys. Thr. p. 288, 14 and schol. Marc. VN p. 439, 7 (ed. Hilgard) and without a lemma by Stob. ecl. 1. 3. 48a p. 61, 4 W. The curious error derived from Canter's edition by which the line was formerly assigned to the Αἴας Λοκρός is explained in Wachsmuth's note. Tr. fr. adesp. 500, which immediately follows in Stobaeus, was first recognized as a separate quotation by Seidler.
For the lex talionis cf. Aesch. Cho. 312 δράσαντι παθεῖν τριγέρων μῦθος τάδε φωνεῖ, with Tucker's note and n. on fr. 229.

lg.l: οἱ γὰρ γύνανδροι καὶ λέγειν ἠσκηκότες

div.p: 963 Tryph. περὶ τρόπων in Walz Rhet. Gr. VIII p. 741 ὅταν ἐπὶ συνθέτων ἐναλλάξῃ ὀνομάτων τις τὸ καθωμιλημένον, ὡς παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ ῾ οἱ γὰρ . . . ἠσκηκότες᾿ ἀντὶ τοῦ οἱ ἀνδρόγυνοι. To the same effect Polyb. Sardianus περὶ σχημάτων ib. p. 612.

This line might have come from the Clouds, so closely does it fit the pupils of the φροντιστήριον: 103 τοὺς ὠχριῶντας, τοὺς ἀνυποδήτους λέγεις, 931 καὶ μὴ λαλιὰν μόνον ἀσκῆσαι, 1058 (ἄδικος λόγος is speaking) τὴν γλῶσσαν, ἣν ὁδὶ μὲν | οὔ φησι χρῆναι τοὺς νέους ἀσκεῖν, ἐγὼ δὲ φημί. Effeminacy is, of course, commonly traced to σκιατροφία, as distinguished from a hardy outdoor life: see e.g. Eur. Bacch. 456. — For γύνανδροι cf. Phryn. praep. soph. p. 17, 13 ἀνδρόγυνον ἄθυρμα· εἰ θέλοις γύνιν (l. γύννιν) τινὰ σκῶψαι, χρήσαιο ἄν. — ἀσκεῖν is followed by an infin. also in El. 1024, Eur. fr. 1067 σωφρονεῖν τ᾿ ἠσκηκότα.

lg.l: θεοῦ τὸ δῶρον τοῦτο· χρὴ δ᾿ ὅσ᾿ ἂν θεοὶ
διδῶσι, φεύγειν μηδέν, ὦ τέκνον, ποτέ.

div.p: 964 [Plut.] vit. Hom. 158 (vii 426 Bernard.) πάλιν δὲ τὸ τοῦ Ὁμήρου (Γ 65) ῾ οὔτοι ἀπόβλητ᾿ ἐστὶ θεῶν ἐρικυδέα δῶρα’ Σοφοκλῆς παρέφρασεν εἰπών ῾ θεοῦ . . . ποτέ.᾿

As it is impossible to escape from the gifts of the gods, so men should make no attempt to shun them. Both points are fully illustrated by Headlam, On editing Aesch. pp. 88 — 90, and in J. P. xxiii 282. For the latter which is here inculcated cf. Hom. σ 142 τῷ μή τίς ποτε πάμπαν ἀνὴρ ἀθεμίστιος εἴη, | ἀλλ᾿ ὅ γε σιγῇ δῶρα θεῶν ἔχοι ὅττι διδοῖεν, Theogn. 444 ἀθανάτων δὲ δόσεις | παντοῖαι θνητοῖσιν
ἐπέρχοντ᾿ , ἀλλ᾿ ἐπιτολμᾶν | χρὴ δῶρ᾿ ἀθανάτων οἷα διδοῦσιν ἔχειν, Hom. h. Dem. 147 θεῶν μὲν δῶρα καὶ ἀχνύμενοί περ ἀνάγκῃ | τέτλαμεν ἄνθρωποι. There are many variations of the same theme, that man should submit to the inevitable decrees of heaven: see on frs. 196, 585, 680. H. used this passage to defend the integrity of Menander fr. 253, III 73 K. ἀλογίστου τρόπου | ἀτύχημα φεύγειν ἐστὶν οὐκ αὐθαίρετον, where the sense of φεύγειν (= ‘to shun’) had been missed, except by Enger.

2 In his 2nd edition Nauck printed μηδέν’, but in Index, p. xiv, he rightly gave the preference to μηδέν. The antecedent (τούτων) of ὅσα must be supplied. Welcker assigned this fragment to the Alcmaeon, on the ground that it corresponded to a line of Accius in the play so entitled: postremo amplexa fructum, quem di dant, cape (fr. VIII).

lg.l: ὀρθῶς δ᾿ Ὀδυσσεύς εἰμ᾿ ἐπώνυμος κακῶν·

div.p: 965. 1 κακῶν Blaydes: κακοῖς A vulg., κακός F, κακῶς CY Ricc. 2 δυσμενεῖς Nauck: δυσσεβεῖς codd.
965 Anon. vit. Soph. 12 (p. 131, 93 West.) παρετυμολογεῖ δὲ (sc. Σοφοκλῆς) καθ᾿ Ὅμηρον καὶ τοὔνομα τοῦ Ὀδυσσέως ῾ ὀρθῶς . . . ἐμοί.᾿

Brunck, followed by Dindorf, referred this fragment to the Νίπτρα, Welcker (p. 231) to the Phaeacians. — This derivation of the name Odysseus is taken from Hom. τ 407 ff., where Autolycus, the father of Anticlea (the mother of Odysseus), bids his daughter call her son ’the man of wrath,’ because he himself has come thither ‘as one that has been angered with many, — a man of many quarrels’ (Monro): πολλοῖσιν γὰρ ἔγωγε ὀδυσσάμενος τόδ᾿ ἱκάνω, | ἀνδράσιν ἠδὲ γυναιξὶν ἀνὰ χθόνα πουλυβότειραν· | τῷ δ᾿ Ὀδυσεὺς ὄνομ᾿ ἔστω ἐπώνυμον. L. and S. give ὀδυσσάμενος a passive sense, ’having given cause of offence,’ but for this there is no authority. The etymology is more than once elsewhere suggested in the Odyssey, as in α 62 τί νυ οἱ τόσον ὠδύσαο, Ζεῦ; ε 339 τίπτε τοι ὧδε Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων | ὠδύσατ᾿ ἐκπάγλως; τ 275 ὀδύσαντο γὰρ αὐτῷ | Ζεύς τε καὶ Ἠέλιος, where there is no possible doubt as to the sense of ὀδύσασθαι. But this does not prevent us from understanding Ὀδυσσεύς as the Angerer: Autolycus makes his grandson the scape-goat, as it were, of his own mischievous malice. H. points out that the case of Autolycus, in recording his own characteristics by the name given to his grandson, resembles those of Ajax in relation to Eurysaces, of Orestes to Tisamenus, of Perseus to Gorgophone (Pausan. 2. 21. 7), and of Achilles to Neoptolemus (Pausan. 10. 26. 4, with Frazer's n.).

1 ὀρθῶς is one of the adverbs that are prefixed to mark an etymological allusion: Aesch. Theb. 392 ὀρθῶς ἐνδίκως τ᾿ ἐπώνυμον, Eur. Tro. 990 καὶ τοὔνομ᾿ ὀρθῶς ἀφροσύνης ἄρχει θεᾶς. Ar. Thesm. 1215 (Blaydes's n.). So ἀληθῶς, ὄντως, εὐλόγως, σαφῶς (fr. 658), etc.: see Headlam, On editing Aesch. p. 140ff., Starkie on Ar. Vesp. 772. — κακῶν. I accept Blaydes's correction, for, although ἐπώνυμος occurs with the dative, it is mainly so employed in late Greek. It is more likely that κακῶν was corrupted by the later copyists than that Sophocles used the dative, contrary to the unvarying practice of the early poets. For the dat. cf. Plat. legg. 969 Α τὴν Μαγνήτων πόλιν, ἢ ᾧ (qu. ὧν) ἂν θεὸς ἐπώνυμον αὐτὴν ποιήσῃ, Polyb. 16. 25. 9 φυλὴν ἐπώνυμον ἐποίησαν Ἀττάλῳ, Dion. Hal. ant. Rom. 1. 9 Ῥωμύλου δὲ τὴν ἐπώνυμον αὐτῷ πόλιν οἰκίσαντος, Opp. hal. 2. 460 κέντροισιν ἐπώνυμοι ἀργαλέοισι.

2 δυσμενεῖς: see cr. n. Nauck's correction, if not absolutely necessary, is a great improvement. Some might feel inclined to read δυσσεβῶς, since adj. and adv. are so frequently confused; but it would be open to the same objection as δυσσεβεῖς, that the word is too strong for the context. The difficulties of Odysseus were not caused by the δυσσέβεια of his enemies. — Similar plays upon names often occur in tragedy: see the cases of Sidero (fr. 658), Ajax (Ai. 430 with J.'s n.), Prometheus (Aesch. Prom. 86), Thoas (Eur. I.T. 32), and others collected by Dobree, Adv. II p. 67.

lg.l: ὅταν τις ἄδῃ τὸν Βοιώτιον νόμον,
τὰ πρῶτα μὲν σχολαῖον, εἶτα δ᾽ ἔντονον.

div.p: 966. 2 εἶτα δ᾽ ἔντονον (εἶτα δ' εὔτονον Ο. Crusius) Blaydes: εὔτονος ἀεί cod.

966 Zenob. 2. 65 (Paroem. I 49) Βοιώτιος νόμος· ἐπὶ τῶν τὰς μὲν (μὲν om. S) ἀρχὰς ἠρεμούντων, ὕστερον δὲ τοῖς κακοῖς (τοῖς κακοῖς om. S) ἐπιτεινόντων, ὥς φησι (ὥς φησι om. S.) Σοφοκλῆς ‘ὅταν ...νόμον.’ The second line was first pub- lished by L. Cohn (Zu den Paroemiogr. in Breslauer philol. Abhandl. II 2, p. 70) from a Paris codex known as S (suppl. gr. 676).

1 f. J. writes: ‘Βοιώτιος νόμος occurs as a proverb (without the verses) in Greg. Cypr. 1. 92 (Paroem. 1 357), etc. The proverb was applied to things which are mild at the outset, but become severe or vehement as they go on. The character- istic of this νόμος was a crescendo with an acceleration of time. Cp. Ar. Ach. 14 Δεξίθεος εἰσῆλθ᾽ ἀσόμενος Βοιώτιον. The schol. there says that this Βοιώτιον μέλος was invented by Terpander, as well as the Φρύγιον.’ The most accessible account of the various kinds of nomes is to be found in Weir Smyth's Greek Melic Poets, pp. LVIII-LXVIII: for Terpander see ibid. p. 164 ff. It should be observed that Terpander's nomes were citharoedic, and that this was the case with the Βοιώτιος is expressly stated by Plut. de mus. 4 p. 1132 D: the schol. on Ar. Ach. l.c. rightly calls Dexitheus a κιθαρῳδός. This point requires emphasis, because Roberts's account (Ancient Boeotians, p. 34) might be taken to imply that it was auletic. Its characteristic feature is given also by Suidas s.v. Βοιωτία... ἐπὶ τῶν τὰς ἀρχὰς μὲν ἠρεμαίως (qu. -as) ἐχόντων, αὖθις δὲ σφοδρῶς ἐπιγινομένων (ἐπιτεινομένων Gais- ford rightly). Gomperz remarks that Sophocles may have used it to express the growth of a passion from gentle be- ginnings. —Βοιώτιον. ‘For οἴ, cp. El. 1058 (lyr.) οἴωνούς, Od. 7. 312 τοῖος ἐὼν οἷός ἐσσι.’ (J.)—ἔντονον see cr. n.: I have preferred ἔντονον to εὔτονον, — and the words are so constantly confused (e.g. in Polyb. 8. 7. 2) that the change is incon- siderable, — on the ground stated by Monk on Eur. Hipp. 117, that εὔτονος is robustus and ἔντονος violens. Thus ἔντονον provides a better antithesis to σχολαῖον, so far as we are able to judge in the absence of the context. Cf. fr. 842, Ar. Ach. 665 δεῦρο Μοῦσ᾽ ἐλθὲ φλεγυρὰ πυρὸς ἔχουσα μένος ἔντονος Ἀχαρνική. Its force is well marked in Plut. Tib. Gracch. 2 πρᾷος καὶ καταστηματικὸς ἦν ὁ Τιβέριος, ἔντονος δὲ καὶ σφοδρὸς ὁ Γάϊος (cf. σφοδρῶς ἐπιτεινομένων in Suid.). For τὰ πρῶτα adv. cf. fr. 149, 5.
967 Pollux 6. 39 ἄβρωτος δὲ ὁ νῆστις παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ, καὶ ἀβρωσία ἡ ἀσιτία.

Cobet (Coll. Crit. p. 208) very con- fidently emends to ἀβρώς, quoting the analogy of σαρκοβρώς, ὠμοβρώς, ἀνδροβρώς, τριχοβρώς, σιδηροβρώς, and χειροβρώς : not even Dionysius the elder, he thinks, would have ventured to use ἄβρωτος in the active sense. Although Nauck assents to this view, it is arbitrary to insist on so strict a uniformity. Chariton, it is true, is not an authority of much weight (6. 3 οἶδα γάρ σε ὑφ᾽ ἡδονῆς διημερεύοντα ἄβρωτον, ἄποτον) for the usage of the Periclean age, but we have already seen that the verbals in -Tos were employed with much less consistency than is gene- rally supposed: see on fr. 210, 8. Other examples from late Greek will be found in the Thesaurus.
968 Bekk. anecd. p. 336, 6 (Phryn. fr. 53 de B.) ἀγάζεις· ἀντὶ τοῦ θρασύνεις. Σοφοκλῆς.

H. brings this into connexion with Aesch. Suppl. 1071 f. τίνα καιρόν με διδάσκεις; τὰ θεῶν μηδὲν ἀγάζειν, = ‘to observe the rule μηδὲν ἄγαν in divine matters.’ (He compares Athen. 412 C μετριάζειν τὰ περὶ τὴν τροφήν, Ant. 1350 χρὴ δὲ τὰ γ᾽ εἰς θεοὺς μηδὲν ἀσεπτεῖν : and for the association with καιρός Theogn. 401 μηδὲν ἄγαν σπεύδειν, καιρὸς δ᾽ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἄριστος, epigr. ap. schol. Eur. Hipp. 263 [PLG III 434] μηδὲν ἄγαν· καιρῷ πάντα πρόσεστι καλά.) The gloss is then justified in the sense of ‘to exalt over-much,’ to fill with θράσος—the rash, confident sense of security which goes before a fall: Thuc. 2. 40 ὁ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἀμαθία μὲν θράσος, λογισμὸς δὲ ὄκνον φέρει. So μεγαλύνω, μεγαλίζεσθαι, πυργοῦν (Eur. Or. 1568 πεπύργωσαι θράσει), ὑψοῦσθαι et sim.
969 Phot. ed Reitz. p. 13, 3 ἀγαί· ἠμόνες. οὕτω κέχρηται Σοφοκλῆς. Cf. Etym. M. p. 8, 49 ἀγαί· ἠιόνες. Hesych. 1 p. 12 ἀγαί· αἰγιαλός Ἴωνες.
This word was conjectured by H. L. Ahrens in Aesch. Ag. 975. For further information see Bury on Pind. Isth. 2. 42 and Jacobs, Anth. Pal. XII p. 96.

970 Phot. p. 13, 6 Reitz. (Phryn. fr. 54 de B.)=Bekk. anecd. p. 336, 7 ἀγάμετος (ἀγάμητος de Borries) ἀντὶ τοῦ ἄγαμος. Σοφοκλῆς. Hesych. I p. 13 has ἀγάμητος· ἄγαμος, ἄζυξ, where Salmasius corrected ἄζυξ, and M. Schmidt con- jectured <Σοφοκλῆς> Ἀμύκῳ. Brunck gave ἀγάμητος, but whether as his own conjecture or as the reading of the Ms, does not appear. He is followed by Lobeck (Phryn. p. 514) and Nauck, who however subsequently (p. XXIV) thought that the attribution of the word to So- phocles was an error. The new text of Photius confirms Bekker's codex, and there is nothing to show that Hesychius was quoting Sophocles (see Pollux 3. 49). It is arbitrary therefore to prefer ἀγάμητος, since ἀγάμετος (cf. γαμετή) may just as well have occurred beside ἄγαμος and ἀγάμητος, ὡς ἀμάχετος (fr. 813, Aesch. Theb. 85) beside ἄμαχος and ἀμάχητος, and ἀκόρετος beside ἄκορος and ἀκόρητος. Add ἀπεύχετος (Aesch. Cho. 155, 623), ἀνάρχετος (Aesch. Eum. 529, according to Wieseler's conj.), πανάρκετος (Aesch. Cho. 68), ἀλάμπετος (Α. Ρ. 9. 540). All these formations are secondary (deno- minative): see on fr. 1014. The earliest example is the Homeric ἀριδείκετος.

971 Phot. p. 13, 28 Reitz. = Bekk. anecd. p. 325, 22 and Suid. ἀγάσματα· σεβάσματα, ἃ ἄν τις ἀγάσαιτο. Σοφοκλῆς κέχρηται. Cf. Hesych. I p. 14 ἀγάσματα· σεβάσματα. Eustath. Il. p. 971, 16 ἀγῶ τὸ σέβομαι, ἀφ᾽ οὗ ἀγάσματα τὰ σεβάσματα.
Nauck conjectured that Sophocles wrote ἀγαστά; but there is no objection to ἄγασμα, except its rarity, and the evidence of its existence seems sufficient.
There is nothing in the enumeration of Pollux 2. 14 to suggest that the reference here is really intended for Ant. 608. ἀγήρατος occurs also in Eur. I. A. 567.
972 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 16, 25 ἀγήρατον· ἀρρενικῶς εἶπε Σοφοκλῆς, θηλυκῶς δὲ Ξενοφῶν (Cyr. 8. 7. 22). καὶ ἀγήρων Πλάτων κτέ.
973 Phot. p. 26, 23 Reitz. = Bekk. anecd. p. 340, 22 (Phryn. fr. 68 de B.) ἄγχαζε· ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀναχώρει. οὕτω (οὕτως Phot.) Σοφοκλῆς. Cf. Hesych. I p. 35 ἄγχαζε· ἀναχώρει.

ἀναχάζω is generally found in the middle (= to retreat), and ἀνέχασσαν in Pind. Nem. 10. 69 = drove back. But Xen. anab. 4. 1. 16 ἐπιδιώκοντες καὶ πάλιν ἀναχάζοντες is parallel to this fragment; and for the tendency of verbs expressing movement to become intransitive see on fr. 210, 9. — For the apocope see on fr. 422.

974 Phot. lex. p. 6, 19 (p. 27, 20 Reitz.) = Bekk. anecd. p. 340, 26 ἀγωγεύς· ὁ ἱμὰς τῶν κυνηγετικῶν κυνῶν. οὕτω (οὕτως Phot.) Σοφοκλῆς. Cf. Hesych. I p. 38 ἀγωγεύς· ὁ ἱμάς, which Reitzenstein refers to Phryn. (Bekk. anecd.) p. 22, 20 [praep. soph. p. 37, 14] ἀγωγεύς· ὁ ἱμὰς τῶν κυνηγετικῶν κυνῶν, ᾧ ἐπάγονται ὑπὸ τῶν κυνηγετῶν. Στράττις (fr. 52, I 726 K.) δὲ τὸν ἵππου ἱμάντα, ᾧ ἐφέλκεται καὶ ἐπάγεται, ἀγωγέα λέγει. The latter sense appears in the gloss Phot. lex. p. 6, 17 (p. 27, 19 Reitz.) ἀγωγεῖ· τῷ ἱμάντι, ᾧ ἄγεται ὁ ἵππος. ὃ καὶ ῥυτὴρ καλεῖται, which was probably taken from Xen. eq. 6. 5 (cf. ibid. 8. 3).
975 Pollux 3. 141 Σοφοκλῆς δὲ τὴν ἀγωνοθεσίαν ἀγωνοθήκην μοχθηρῶς ἐκάλεσεν.

A similar formation is quoted from Timon Sill. fr. 9, 4 D. ἐκ παθέων δόξης τε καὶ εἰκαίης νομοθήκης. The criticism which Pollux records is made from the Atticist point of view: whether Sophocles made an experiment in language, or whether a precedent existed for the use of θήκη as a nomen actionis, there is no evidence to determine. All the other compounds follow the pattern of ἀρτοθήκη, βελοθήκη, σκευοθήκη etc.: see Lobeck, Paralip. p. 374.

976 Phot. lex. p. 9, 22 (p. 30, 11 Reitz.) ἀδηφάγοι· ἀγωνισταὶ ἵπποι οὕτως ἐκαλοῦντο ὡς Ἀριστοφάνης (fr. 736, I 569 K.) καὶ Φερεκράτης (fr. 197, I 202 Κ.). ἔφη δὲ καὶ ἀδηφαγοῦσα Σοφοκλῆς καὶ ἀδηφαγεῖν Ἕρμιππος (fr. 84, I 251 K.). ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀδηφάγον εἶπε Λυσίας (fr. 103 Sch.) τὴν τέλειον μισθὸν λαμβάνουσαν τριήρη κτέ.

Naber, Nauck, Dindorf and Blaydes agree in thinking that ἀδηφαγοῦσα is a corruption of ἀδηφάγον νόσον, and that the reference is to Phil. 313. I am unable to assent to this view, which appears to me to be highly improbable, if the whole scope of the article in Photius is considered and compared with the parallel extracts in Hesych. I p. 45, Suid. s.v. ἀδηφαγία, and Harpocr. p. 5, 12 ἀδηφάγους τριήρεις. All of these go back ultimately to a common source, the objects of which were to show that the κυριολογία of ἀδηφάγος was its application to race-horses, and to illustrate its metaphorical use. In each case the quotation from Lysias is the first of the metaphorical examples; but, if we accept ἀδηφάγον νόσον, we must also assume that the subject of ἀδηφαγεῖν has dropped out, since it is incredible that a return to the κύριον would have been so awkwardly placed, however much the extract may have been abbreviated. Dindorf's remark that, if Sophocles had used the verb, Photius would have written καὶ ἀδηφαγεῖν Σοφοκλῆς καὶ Ἕρμιππος falls to the ground, if the grammarian was quoting the actual words. Although mares were employed in racing (Jebb on El. 705), since ἀδηφάγος was a technical equivalent of τέλειος ἵππος )( πῶλος (Hesych., etc.), Sophocles cannot have written ἀδηφαγοῦσα πῶλος. But ἀδηφαγοῦσα ξυνωρίς would be a possible expression after the pattern of ἵππων ζεύγει ἀδηφάγῳ in C.I.A. II 965.
977 Bekk. anecd. p. 343, 11 ἀδικότροπος ἐρεῖς καὶ ἀδικοχρήματος, ὡς Κράτης (fr. 42, I 142 K.), καὶ ἀδικόχειρας, ὡς Σοφοκλῆς.
For the formation cf. καρτερόχειρ, θρασύχειρ, ὀξύχειρ.
978 Hesych. I p. 48 ἀδρέπανον· ἄδρεπτον· θεοῖς ἀνακείμενον. Σοφοκλῆς.

The reference is to a sacred meadow, which is under a taboo forbidding the operation of the scythe: cf. Trach. 200 ὦ Ζεῦ, τὸν Οἴτης ἄτομον ὃς λειμῶν' ἔχεις (Jebb). So the Megarians were charged, before the Peloponnesian war, as ἀποτεμνομένους τὴν ὀργάδα (Dem. 13. 32, Plut. Per. 30). There might also be a prohibition on grazing, as in the famous passage Eur. Hipp. 75 ff. Such we may suppose to have been the character of the meadow of Artemis at Aulis (Eur. Ι. Α. 1464), and of Hera on Mt Cithaeron (Phoen. 24). Nauck brackets ἄδρεπτον, and suggests either that ἀδρέπανον, with λειμῶν' ἔχων, was the original reading in Trach. 200, to which this gloss refers, or that ἀδρέπανον has displaced the original ἄτομον in Hesychius, which it once explained (i. e. ἄτομον· ἀδρέπανον). I see no reason for this scepticism, which sufficiently refutes itself.

979 Phot. p. 34, 9 Reitz. = Bekk. anecd. p. 345, 13 ἁδρῦναι· ἁδρὸν ποιῆσαι καὶ μέγα (κ. μ. π. cod. Bekk.). Σοφοκλῆς. Cf. Phryn. (Bekk. anecd.) p. 21, 2 [praep. soph. p. 34, 6] ἁδρῦναι· ἁδρὸν ποιῆσαι καὶ μέγαν (l. μέγα).

Neither ἁδρός, for which see Blaydes on Ar. Ran. 1099, nor ἁδρύνω occurs elsewhere in tragedy. It might, therefore, be conjectured that the verb was used by Sophocles in a satyr-play: see however on fr. 210, 47.

980 Phot. p. 38, 4 Reitz. ἄζειν· τὸ διὰ τοῦ στόματος ἀθρόως ἐκπνεῖν Ἀττικοί, μιμούμενοι τὸν ἦχον τοῦ πνεύματος. οὕτως Νικοχάρης (fr. 19, I 774 K.). καὶ τὸ στένειν Σοφοκλῆς. The same occurs in Bekk. anecd. p. 348, 17 in two glosses, and with reversed order. Cf. Hesych. I p. 58 ἄζειν· στενάζειν ἢ ἐκπνεῖν διὰ στόματος. Etym. M. p. 22, 52 τὸ στόμα (qu. τῷ στόματι) ἀθρόως προσπνεῖν.

As used by Sophocles, ἄζειν was formed like ὤζειν, φεύζειν, μύζειν etc. Nauck conjectured πάρα γὰρ στενάχειν, πάρα δ᾿ ἄζειν in Eur. Phoen. 1551. For the other application cf. Arist. probl. 34. 7 ὁ δὲ ἀάζων ἀθρόον ἐκπνεῖ· διὸ θερμόν.

981 Phot. p. 38, 14 Reitz. = Bekk. anecd. p. 348, 26 Ἀζησία· οὕτως ἡ Δημήτηρ παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ καλεῖται. οἱ δὲ τὴν εὐτραφῆ. Cf. Hesych. I p. 59 Ἀζησία· ἡ Δημήτηρ, ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀζαίνειν τοὺς καρπούς, whence it appears that in Photius the explanation οἱ μὲν ἀπὸ τ. ἀζ. τ. κ. has dropped out.

According to other authorities Azesia was the ἐπίκλησις of Persephone: Suid. s.v., Zenob. 4. 20 (Paroem. I 89) ἱστορεῖ Δίδυμος, ὅτι Ἀμαία μὲν ἡ Δημήτηρ παρὰ Τροιζηνίοις προσαγορεύεται, Ἀζησία δὲ ἡ Κόρη. C. O. Mueller (Aeginet. p. 171) and others have taken the view that these names are merely variants for or erroneous perversions of Δαμία and Αὐξησία, for whom see Hdt. 5. 82 ff., Pausan. 2. 32. 2. But the Epidaurian inscription (Collitz, G.D.I. III 3337 θεῶν Ἀζεσίων Δαμίας Αὐξησίας) in which Damia and Auxesia are called Azesian shows that such is not the case. The derivation given by Hesychius seems satisfactory for a name given to the corn-goddess, as expressing the power of the summer heat (Usener, Götternamen, p. 243), and is confirmed by the proverb ἡ Ἀμαία τὴν Ἀζησίαν μετῆλθεν. It is possible however, as Jebb (on O.C. 1600) seemed to think, that the title expressed the evil, i.e. parching drought, which the goddess was required to avert. Another view (Cook in C. R. XVII 177) analyses the name as ἀΖησία, i.e. the Zeus-maiden. Danielsson connected the word with αἰζηός, as if Ἀζησία = κόρη : see Gruppe, Gr. Myth. p. 1930. The corresponding Ἀμαία is generally explained as 'reaper' (ἀμάω), which seems better than Lobeck's view that Ἀμμαία = 'mother' should be written (Aglaoph. p. 822).
982 Bekk. anecd. p. 353, 4 ἀθαυμάστως Σοφοκλῆς εἶπεν.
ἀθαύμαστος is otherwise unknown in tragedy.
983 Steph. Byz. p. 37, 13 Αἰανῖτις, Ναβαταίων χώρα. Οὐράνιος Ἀραβικῶν β΄. τὸ ἐθνικὸν Αἰανῖται· προκατελήφθη γὰρ ἐν πρωτοτύπῳ. διὰ διφθόγγου. Σοφοκλῆς δὲ Αἰαντία γράφει δίχα τοῦ ν.

This is a very obscure matter, and I agree with Dindorf in thinking it not unlikely that the reference was meant for Sophocles, the commentator on Apollonius Rhodius, who is cited by Stephanus elsewhere. In the last sentence Westermann corrected Αἰαντίς γράφει δίχα τοῦ ῖ, after Salmasius and Gronovius, the latter of whom thought that Ἀανῖτιν was the word cited.

984 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 44, 17 αἰγίζει· ἀντὶ τοῦ καταιγίζει. οὕτως Σοφοκλῆς. Cf. Hesych. I p. 69 αἰγίζει· καταιγίζει. διασπᾷ. The second interpretation reappears in the following gloss, which is also in Suid. s.v.: αἰγίζειν· διασπᾶν. ἐκ μεταφορᾶς. παρ' ὃ καὶ τὸ αἰγίζεσθαι, ἀπὸ τῶν καταιγίδων. Αἰσχύλος (fr. 407). The introduction of διασπᾶν (cf. Bekk. anecd. p. 357, 29) is no doubt to be explained by the medical use of αἰγίζω and καταιγίζω (cf. χειμάζω, fr. 314. 267). The latter is well attested for Hippocrates: Blomfield, gl. Aesch. Theb. 63, Erotian p. 106, 17.
985 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 47, 20 ἀϊδροδίκης· Σοφοκλῆς ἔφη.

Cf. Pind. Nem. 1. 63 θῆρας ἀϊδροδίκας, where Dissen quotes Hom. ι 215 (ἄνδρα) ἄγριον, οὔτε δίκας ἐὺ εἰδότα οὔτε θέμιστας. So ib. 189 ἀθεμίστια ᾔδη. Ameis-Hentze give a long list of similar examples from Homer, which illustrate the Greek tendency to ascribe the absence of moral feeling to a lack of intelligence. See on fr. 925, and the article by the present writer on Greek Ethics and Morality in Hastings's Encyclopaedia of Religion and Ethics, V p. 490.
986 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 49, 18 αἰέλουρος· τετρασυλλάβως Ἀριστοφάνης (Ach. 879 σκάλοπας, ἐχίνως, αἰελώρως, πικτίδας) καὶ Σοφοκλῆς.

Etym. M. p. 31, 44, quoting from Herodian περὶ παθῶν, says that the form αἰέλουρος is not due to πλεονασμός but to P. III. ἀντίθεσις (used very vaguely: see Rutherford, Annotation, p. 327), as being derived from αἰόλος and οὐρά. Moeris calls it the Attic form: p. 189, 11 αἰέλουρος Ἀττικοί, αἴλουρος Ἕλληνες. The reference may be to the Ichneutae (fr. 314. 296).
987 Bekk. anecd. p. 360, 18 αἱματῶσαι· ἀντὶ τοῦ φονεῦσαι. Σοφοκλῆς.

The same gloss occurs in Hesych. I p. 79 αἱματῶσαι· φονεῦσαι. ἢ φοινίξαι, and in Etym. Μ. p. 35, 8 αἱματῶσαι· φονεῦσαι. 'To shed the blood' of another will often amount to slaying him, as e.g. in Eur. Phoen. 1288 πότερος ἄρα πότερον αἱμάξει.
988 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 58, 9 <ἀ>κάμπιον· ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀκαμπές. Σοφοκλῆς. Cf. Bekk. anecd. p. 370, 31 ἀκάμπιον· ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀκαμπές.

This rare word appears also in Etym. Μ. p. 45, 3 ἀκάμπιος· ὁ ἐπ᾿ εὐθείας περιπατῶν· παρὰ τὸ καμπὴν μὴ ἔχειν. Μεθόδιος. καὶ ἀκάμπιοι δρόμοι οἱ εὐθεῖς καὶ ἁπλοῖ. Similarly Suid. s.v. ἀκαμπίας and Bekk. anecd. p. 363, 21 (Ael. Dion. fr. 26 Schw.). ἀκάμπιον, of a race-course, appears in an inscription of the 3rd cent. B.C. (I. G. II 966 A 43).
989 Phot. p. 61, 2 Reitz. = Bekk. anecd. p. 367, 15 ἀκληρία· [ἀντὶ τοῦ cod. Bekk.] ἀτυχία. [οὕτω cod. Bekk.] Σοφοκλῆς.

It is strange that Nauck should have been persuaded by F. W. Schmidt to alter this to ἀκαιρία. Similar glosses are found elsewhere: see especially Antiatt. (Bekk. anecd.) p. 77, 24 ἄκληρος· ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀτυχής. ἀκληρίαν· Ἀντιφάνης Ἀδώνιδι (fr. 14, 11 15 K.). ὁ αὐτὸς εὐκλήρωμα ἀντὶ τοῦ κατόρθωμα. Suid. s.vv. ἀκληρήμασι, ἀκληρίας, ἀκληρούντων, giving in illustration excerpts from Polybius. It is not difficult to see how the general sense of misfortune arose from that of poverty (Hom. λ 490 ἀνδρὶ παρ' ἀκλήρῳ, ᾧ μὴ βίοτος πολὺς εἴη), and it is probably accidental that the evidence of such usage in the classical age is so meagre. Cf. Teles ap. Stob. flor. 40. 8 οὔκουν ἀκλήρημά τι καὶ ὄνειδος ἐμόν, εἰ μετὰ πονηρῶν οἰκήσω; id. ap. Stob. flor. 108. 83 σὺ δὲ, ὅτι μὲν ἀπογέγονεν (sc. ὁ φίλος), ἀκληρεῖν οἴει· ὅτι δὲ ἐγένετο, οὐκ εὐκληρεῖν. Polybius, who has several examples of ἀκληρία (e.g. 22. 11. 9) and its cognates, draws the following distinction (38. 5. 7): ἀκληρεῖν μὲν γὰρ ἅπαντας ἡγητέον καὶ κοινῇ καὶ κατ᾿ ἰδίαν τοὺς παραλόγοις συμφοραῖς περιπίπτοντας, ἀτυχεῖν δὲ μόνους τούτους οἷς διὰ τὴν ἰδίαν ἀβουλίαν ὄνειδος αἱ πράξεις ἐπιφέρουσι. Diodorus has ἄκληρος (3. 29), ἀκληρία (17. 69), and ἀκληρεῖν (3. 12, 13). Add M. Ant. 10. 33 τούτων δὲ τῶν καλουμένων ἀκληρημάτων οὐδὲν βλάπτει νόμον. Heliod. 10. 16 ὀλίγον μὲν τῆς ἀκληρίας λόγον ποιουμένῳ.
990 Phot. p. 62, 27 Reitz. = Bekk. anecd. p. 367, 32 ἀκολουθία· ἡ ἀκολούθησις. Σοφοκλῆς.

ἀκόλουθος occurs in O. C. 719, but neither it nor its cognates elsewhere in tragedy. ἀκόλουθος etc. are mainly prose words, but the adjective is used by Bacchyl. 14. 55. For Wilamowitz's suggestion that the lemma belongs to the Ichneutae see on fr. 314. 15.

991 Phot. p. 64, 2 Reitz. = Bekk. anecd. p. 369, 13 ἀκουσείων ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀκουσόμενος. Σοφοκλῆς. There is also a mysterious entry Phot. p. 65, 3 Reitz. = Bekk. anecd. p. 372, 14 ἀκουσέτην Σοφοκλῆς (ἔφη add. Bekk. anecd.), ἀκούσεσθαι δὲ Ἀριστοφάνης. Most critics have inclined favourably to Dobree's ἀκουσείειν, but Reitzenstein leaves ἀκουσέτην, suggesting ἀκούσεσθε for ἀκούσεσθαι. It is difficult to believe in an entirely anomalous ἀκουσέτην, which not only implies an early ἀκούσω, but has an unexampled dual ending. Kenyon defends τὰς τῶν ἀκουσόντων ψυχάς in Hyperid. 6. 34 against Cobet and Blass, but all the certain instances of ἀκούσω are much later. L. Sternbach (Wiener Stud. VIII 231) proposed to follow up Dobree's correction by reading ἀκουσείεσθαι for ἀκούσεσθαι, but this would be a very strange passive, and it should be observed that ἀκουσείων )( ἀκουσόμενος corresponds to ἀκουσείειν )( ἀκούσεσθαι. In Hesych. I p. 103 Fix conjectured ἀκουσείων for ἀκουστιῶν· ἀκουστικῶς ἔχων, but see Curtius, Greek Verb, p. 536 E. tr.

For the derivation of these desideratives (ὀψείων = ὄψει ἰών) see Brugmann, IV 446. The only other examples in tragedy are δρασείω (Ai. 326, 585, Phil. 1245, Eur. Med. 93, Phoen. 1208), ἐργασείω (Trach. 1232, Phil. 1001) and φευξείω (Eur. Her. 628).

992 Phot. p. 68, 27 Reitz. = Bekk. anecd. p. 373, 15 ἀκροφύσιον· τὸ τῇ χώνῃ προστιθέμενον. Σοφοκλῆς. Cf. Hesych. I p. 107 ἀκροφύσια· τὰ ἄκρα τῶν ἀσκῶν, ἐν οἷς οἱ χαλκεῖς τὸ πῦρ ἐκφυσῶσι. [The text is hardly sound. Bloomfield (on Thuc. 4. 100) deleted ἐν, but it may be that τὰ τοῖς χοάνοις προστιθέμενα or some such words have fallen out after ἀσκῶν.] Etym. M. p. 53, 20 ἀκροφύσια· τὰ ἀκροστόμια τῶν ἀσκῶν. Eustath. Il. p. 1153, 33 ἰστέον δὲ ὅτι τὰ μέρη τῶν φυσῶν τὰ τοῖς χοάνοις ἐνιέμενα ἀκροφύσια ἐλέγοντο καὶ ἀκροστόμια, οἷς φυσῶσιν οἱ χαλκεῖς.

ἀκροφύσιον was the nozzle or blowpipe attached to the end of the skins of which the bellows were made. See Dict. Ant. 1870a. The gloss of Photius recalls Hom. Σ 470 φῦσαι δ᾽ ἐν χοάνοισιν ἐείκοσι πᾶσαι ἐφύσων. Perhaps Sophocles was describing the workshop of Daedalus in the play called by his name.
993 Bekk. anecd. p. 383, 4 ἀλεύσω· ἀντὶ τοῦ φυλάξω. Σοφοκλῆς. The gloss appears in Phot. p. 73, 20 Reitz., but without the reference to Sophocles.

The explanation φυλάξω is not altogether clear, and Blaydes suggests φυλάξομαι. But this would rather have been attached to the middle: thus in Ai. 656 L has ἐξαλεύσωμαι with φυλάξωμαι, ἐκκλίνω written above, and the schol. on Aesch. Prom. 589 explained Ἀλευάδα (written as one word) by ὃν δεῖ φυλάξασθαι (καὶ ἐκκλῖναι recc.). On the other hand Suid. has ἄλευε· Ἴωνες τὸ φύλαξαι οὕτως λέγουσι· καὶ παροιμία· ἄλευ᾿ ἀπὸ μείζονος ἀνδρός. This is interesting as showing that the imperative at any rate could be used not merely = averte, as in Aesch. Theb. 87 ὀρόμενον κακὸν ἀλεύσατε (cf. ib. 128, Suppl. 537), but also intransitively ('look out'). See also Zonar. p. 135 ἀλεύειν τὸ φυλάττειν. οἱ Ἴωνες οὕτω λέγουσι, continuing as Suid., and there is the same inconsistency in Hesych. I p. 115 ἄλεε· φύλασσε, and p. 118 ἄλευε· φύλαξαι. The upshot is that φυλάσσειν was used in these glosses in a sense not much different from that of φυλάσσεσθαι, i.e. to keep an eye on another, where the middle voice emphasizes the notion of one's own protection. This, of course, is common enough in classical Greek also: a good instance is Eur. I. A. 538.

994 Hesych. I p. 132 Ἀλύβας· ὄρος. παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ. ἢ πόλις. οἱ δὲ λίμνη ἐν Ἰταλίᾳ καὶ ἐν Τροίᾳ. Cf. Etym. M. p. 70, 41 Ἀλύβας· ὄρος οἳ δὲ λίμνην. εἶναι δὲ καὶ πόλιν Ἀλύβην. Hesych. I p. 121 ἀλίβας· νεκρός, ἢ βροῦχος (βρῦτος conj. M. Schmidt), ἢ ποταμός, ἢ ὄρος. Suid. s.v. ἀλίβας. ὁ νεκρός. ἢ ποταμὸς ἐν Ἅιδου κτέ. So Bekk. anecd. p. 376, 21, Eustath. Od. p. 1679, 32.

It is by no means clear that this fr. ought to be separated from fr. 790, or that we have anything more than a confused tradition that Alybas or Alibas was a place-name in Sophocles. Few will credit that Sophocles mentioned the obscure Alybas as a mountain in one passage, and spoke of 'descending into Alibas' in another. There does not seem to be much advantage in following M. Schmidt in correcting ἢ πόλις ἐν Ἰταλίᾳ· οἱ δὲ λίμνη. But the tradition is probably mutilated. (1) The statement about ὄρος is due to a confusion with Abila, the name given to the spurs of the Atlas range in Mauretania. (2) λίμνη ἐν Ἰταλίᾳ appears to cover a reference to Alybas-Metapontum (Steph. Byz. p. 79, 3: see also on fr. 790), as well as to the ποταμὸς ἐν Ἅιδου recognized as a congener of the Ἀχερουσία λίμνη (fr. 523). Is it possible that λίμνην Ποντικήν in Steph. Byz. p. 79, 12 is an error for Μεταποντικήν? (3) The words καὶ ἐν Τροίᾳ are treated by Schmidt as an error. They may be an anticipation of the gloss next following which calls the Ἀλυβή of Hom. B 857 πόλις Τρωϊκή wrongly. Or, if Soph. (or another poet) mentioned Ἀλίβας in connexion with a Trojan incident, they may represent a geographical note controverting the localization of it in Italy.
995 Phot. p. 75, 1 Reitz. = Bekk. anecd. p. 383, 11 ἀλίνουσιν· [ἀντὶ τοῦ cod. Bekk.] λεπτύνουσι. Σοφοκλῆς.

In agreement with this gloss ('to pound fine') is Hesych. I p. 116 ἀλεινόν· ἀσθενές, λεπτόν, and perhaps ib. p. 122 ἀλινόν· ἀμυδρόν. Κρῆτες. On the other hand, there is evidence of ἀλίνω 'to anoint': Hesych. I p. 116 ἀλεῖναι· τὶ ἐπαλεῖψαι. τοίχῳ. ib. p. 122 ἀλῖναι· ἐπαλεῖψαι and ἀλίνειν· ἀλείφειν. The two words, identical in form, appear to be of distinct origin. The verb in the text is akin to ἀλέω: for ἀλίνω 'ἀλείφω' cf. Lat. lino, and see Brugmann, Comp. Gr. IV 150 E. tr.
996 Phot. p. 76, 13 Reitz. = Bekk. anecd. p. 383, 31 (Phryn. fr. 155 de B.) ἀλκάθω καὶ ἀλκάθειν· Σοφοκλῆς καὶ Αἰσχύλος (fr. 411). σημαίνει δὲ τὸ βοηθεῖν.

Since Elmsley's note on Eur. Med. 187 his conclusion has been generally accepted that ἀλκάθω, ἀμυνάθω, εἰργάθω, εἰκάθω, διωκάθω, σχέθω as present indicatives are figments of the grammarians (e.g. Etym. M. p. 8, 18), and that the infinitives and other forms are always aoristic and should be accented accordingly. His strongest points were (1) that there is no certain instance in literature of the pres. ind.; (2) that Phot. lex. p. 70, 14 explained ἠμύναθον by the aor. ἤμυνα; and (3) that the usage is aoristic. Cobet (N. L. p. 495) quoted appositely from Julian 'memor antiqui moris,' p. 237 Α μὴ ὑπεικάθῃς. The Mss, however, invariably give ἀλκάθειν etc. (not ἀλκαθεῖν), and there has been a tendency in
recent discussions to revert to the traditional accentuation (see Kuehner-Blass II 178 anm.), and to admit the existence of a present stem: Tucker on Aesch. Theb. 75, Neil on Ar. Eq. 320, Starkie on Ar. Nub. 1323, Brugmann, Comp. Gr. IV p. 223 E. tr. There is still no decisive evidence of ἀλκάθω etc. as indicatives; and usage, though not constant, often favours Elmsley's view, as Jebb on O. T. 651 remarked.
997 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 78, 11 = Bekk. anecd. p. 376, 31 ἀλλάχθητε· ἀντὶ τοῦ διαλλάχθητε. Σοφοκλῆς. The same in Suid. s.v., Zonar. lex. p. 134.
No other evidence of this usage is quoted.
998 Steph. Byz. p. 78, 6 Ἄλος, πόλις Ἀχαΐας καὶ Φθιώτιδος ὑπὸ τῷ πέρατι τῆς Ὄθρυος. τὸ ἐθνικὸν Ἀλεύς, Σοφοκλῆς δὲ Ἀλουσίους, τινὲς δὲ τῶν γλωσσογράφων Ἀλίους. The same in Etym. Voss. p. 189 E Gaisf.

The town Halus (or Alus) in Phthiotis was said to have been founded by Athamas (Strabo 433), and, according to the statement of Stephanus, was named after the maid-servant who informed Athamas of the trick played by Ino of roasting the corn-seeds. See also Ov. Fast. 6. 551 ff. Plut. qu. Rom. 16 gives the servant's name as Antiphera. Nauck infers with reason that the Alusii were mentioned in the Athamas.
999 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 88, 6 ἁμαρτωλή· Φρύνιχος καὶ Σοφοκλῆς ἁμαρτάς. Cf. p. 88, 7, where ἁμαρτάδας is attributed to Aeschylus: hence perhaps Hesych. I p. 139, Suid. s.v.
ἁμαρτάς is an Ionism with the sense of ἁμαρτία, used by Herodotus (e.g. 1.91) and Hippocrates. It was not previously known as tragic also.

1000 Phot. ed Reitz. p. 89, 14 ἄμβλωσις καὶ ἀμβλωθέντες· Λυσίας (fr. 24 S.). καὶ ἀμβλουχία Σοφοκλῆς καὶ ἄμβλωμα Ἀντιφῶν (fr. 148 Β1.2). Lysias and Antiphon are also cited by Pollux 2. 7, but the word ἀμβλουχία attributed to Sophocles is new. It implies a stem-variation ἀμβλο, and was presumably a synonym of ἄμβλωσις.

1001 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 89, 16 ἀμβλωπός· Εὐριπίδης Ἀνδρομέδᾳ ‘ἀμβλωπὸς ὄψις.’ καὶ ἐν Θησεῖ· ‘καὐτῷ δ᾽ ἔπεισι νυκτὸς ἀμβλωπὸν σέλας.’ καὶ ἀμβλῶπας ὁ αὐτὸς ἐν Θυέστῃ· ‘ἀμβλῶπας αὐγὰς ὀμμάτων ἔχεις σέθεν.’ καὶ Ἴων καὶ Σοφοκλῆς καὶ Πλάτων (i.e. the comic poet).

ἀμβλῶπες αὐγαί occurs in Rhes. 737, and ἀμβλωπός in Aesch. Eum. 955. Pollux (2. 51) also attributes to Euripides (fr. 1096) the form ἀμβλυωπός, which he calls ποιητικώτερον as compared with the more correct ἀμβλυώττων. Nauck was inclined to think that ἀμβλυωπός was a mistake for ἀμβλῶπες (or ἀμβλωπός?), and the additional evidence would probably have strengthened his opinion.
1002 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 95, 25, quoted on fr. 402.
1003 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 96, 15 ἀμυντρόν καὶ ἀμυνάνδρως· Αἰσχύλος· ἀμύνανδρον δὲ Σοφοκλῆς. Cf. Hesych. I p. 154 ἀμύνανδρος· δυνάμενος ἄνδρας ἀμύνεσθαι.

There seems to be no other evidence for this isolated word, but Amynandros, who is quite unknown, was the mythical founder of the γένος Ἀμυνανδρίδαι (Hesych. l. c.), ἐξ οὗ ἱερεῖς Ἀθήνησιν. See Pauly- Wissowa I 2003. The coincidence recalls ἀλλ᾽ ὁ θυμὸς εὐθὺς ἦν ἀμυνίας in Ar. Eq. 570.
1004 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 96, 17 = Suid. s.v. ἀμύνασθαι· Θουκυδίδης (I. 42) μὲν ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀμείβεσθαι, Σιμωνίδης (fr. 229) δὲ ἀντὶ τοῦ χάριτας ἀποδιδόναι, Σοφοκλῆς δὲ ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀπαλεξῆσαι.

Nauck thinks that the reference may be to O. C. 873 ἔργοις πεπονθὼς ῥήμασίν σ' ἀμύνομαι, but that is improbable, since the line is a stock example for the meaning τὸ κακῶς παθόντα ἀντιδιατιθέναι: see Suid. s.v. ἀμυνόμενοι, and Eustath. Il. p. 546, 28. On the other hand the active ἀμῦναι is glossed by ἀπαλεξῆσαι in Hesych. I p. 154, and by ἀλεξῆσαι in Etym. M. p. 88, 22. It appears then that Sophocles, like Homer, used the middle practically as equivalent to the active: so Aesch. Ag. 1380, Eur. Hclid. 302.

1005 Phot. p. 97, 18 Reitz. ἀμυχρόν· τὸ μὴ μυσαρόν, ἀλλ᾽ ἁγνὸν καὶ καθαρόν. οὕτως Σοφοκλῆς. Suid. has exactly the same gloss attached to the lemma ἀμυχνόν, adding the words γράφεται δὲ καὶ ἀμυχρόν, and also to the lemma ἀμυγνόν, but without the addition. He also records ἀμύσκαρον· τὸ ἁγνόν.

ἀμυσχρός is generally considered the best-attested form of this obscure word, and should probably be attributed to Sophocles: see Hesych. 1 p. 155 ἀμυσχρόν· καθαρόν, ἁγνόν, ὁλόχροον (= Phot. p. 97, 16 Reitz., where however ἀλλόχροον has by an error been substituted for ὁλόχροον). Etym. Μ. p. 87, 26 ἀμυσχρός· ὁ καθαρός, ὁ μὴ μύσει χρανθείς, ὁ ἀμίαντος κτέ. Cf. Parthenius ap. Hephaest. p. 4, 7 ἀμυσχρὸν οὔνομ᾽ ἔσσετ᾽ Ἀρχελαΐδος. Meineke (Anal. Alex. p. 261), while pointing out that analogy favoured ἀμυχρόν, acquiesced in ἀμυσχρόν, as supported by better authority.

1006 Eustath. Od. p. 1405, 30 (Pausan. fr. 307 Schw.) καὶ ἀμφώβολα, φασί, παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ αἱ διὰ σπλάγχνων μαντεῖαι. Cf. Hesych. I p. 166 ἀμφώβολα (ἀμφόβολα cod., against the alphabetical order) ἡ διὰ τῶν σπλάγχνων μαντεία. Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 105, 11 ἀμφώβολα· τὴν διὰ σπλάγχνων μαντείαν. Σοφοκλῆς.

Nauck thinks that the statement of these grammarians is incredible; and Wecklein mentions with approval a suggestion that ἀμφώβολα was an error for ἀμφίβολα, and referred to the dark saying of Tiresias in O.T. 328 f. I do not share this scepticism. It has been pointed out by Stengel (griech. Sakralalt. 2 § 40 p. 56) that ἱεροσκοπία was only employed in the case of victims whose flesh was edible, and that this limitation is implied in Pausan. 6. 2. 2, where the dog is mentioned as being useless for the purpose. The sacrificial animal (ἱερεῖον) was consumed entirely, being eaten by the worshippers or burnt in honour of the gods, with the exception of the tongue and the stomach (Plut. Phoc. 1). In the latter term (κοιλία) the σπλάγχνα, as contrasted with the ἔντερα, were certainly not included. Thus, although it is true that the inspection of the exta preceded the sacrificial feast (Eur. El. 826 ff.), it is evident that they were subsequently roasted. It is impossible to justify the gloss by guessing at the context, but such a phrase as ἀμφώβολα σπλάγχνων σημεῖα would be quite intelligible. That ἀμφώβολα is appropriate to the circumstances appears from Hom. h. Herm. 121 ὤπτα δ᾽ ἀμφ' ὀβελοῖσι πεπαρμένα δουρατέοισι, | σάρκας ὁμοῦ καὶ νῶτα γεράσμια καὶ μέλαν αἷμα | ἐργμένον ἐν χολάδεσσι. According to the explanation of the Homeric phrase given by Ameis-Hentze and Leaf (on γ 462, Α 465), ἀμφί denotes the projection of the spit on either side.

1007 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 113, 14 (Phryn. fr. 181 de B.) ἀνακαλπάζει· τινὲς μὲν ὡς οὐ δόκιμον ἐφυλάξαντο τὴν φωνήν, Αἰσχύλος δὲ ἐχρήσατο Μυσοῖς ὡς δόκιμον· λέγει γάρ· ‘εἶδον καλπάζοντας ἐν αἰχμαῖς.᾽ ὁμοίως Σοφοκλῆς, Ἀριστοφάνης, καὶ Πλάτων καὶ ἕτεροι.

It is not clear whether Sophocles used καλπάζειν or ἀνακαλπάζειν, and further information as to the meaning would have been welcome. καλπάζειν is specifically used of a horse's paces: for a description of the κάλπη, or trotting-match, at Olympia, see Pausan. 5. 9. 1. But Suid. s.v. has καλπάζειν· τὸ ἁβρῶς βαδίζειν, and in Plut. Alex. 6 παρακαλπάσας seems to mean ‘running beside (the horse).’ Reitzenstein concludes from the use of φωνή that the extract came from Phrynichus.
1008 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 113, 21 ἀνάκλητος· ὁ μετακληθείς. Σοφοκλῆς.
The gloss belongs to Phrynichus (praep. soph. p. 48, 9), as appears from Bekk. anecd. p. 27, 22 ἀνάκλητος καὶ μετάκλητος· ὁ μετακληθεὶς καὶ μεταπεμφθείς, ὥσπερ καὶ μετάπεμπτος.
1009 Steph. Byz. p. 92, 16 Ἀνακτόριον (Ἀνακτόρειον cod. R). Ἀκαρνανίας πόλις...ἀρσενικῶς παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ.

See on fr. 916. ἀρσενικῶς can only mean that the adjective was of two terminations: for the variation we might compare Pergamus and Pergamum, Pedasus and Pedasum (Strabo 611). Sophocles probably used the form Ἀνακτόρειος.

1010 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 117, 7 Ἀναξιδώρα· ἡ ἀνάγουσα καὶ ἀνιεῖσα τοὺς καρποὺς ἐκ γῆς Δημήτηρ. Σοφοκλῆς δὲ καὶ ἀναγαγεῖν ἀμπελῶνάς φησιν. The first part of the gloss up to the word Δημήτηρ occurs also in Hesych. I p. 178.

Ἀναξιδώρα is a parallel form to Ἀνησιδώρα (Pausan. 1. 31. 4, Hesych. I p. 203). As a general rule the attributes of Demeter (ξηρὰ τροφή) and of Dionysus (ὑγρὰ τροφή) are kept distinct; but for their natural affinity Gruppe (p. 116711) quotes Callim. hymn. 6. 71 f. καὶ γὰρ τᾷ Δάματρι συνωργίσθη Διόνυσος· | τόσσα Διώνυσον γὰρ ἃ καὶ Δάματρα χαλέπτει. Moreover the vine was sacred to the Great Mother (Ap. Rhod. 1. 1117 ff.), who was often identified with Demeter (fr. 290 n.).
1011 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 126, 1 ἀνδραποδοκλόπος· Σοφοκλῆς, ἀνδραποδοκλέπτης δὲ Μένανδρος.

The word probably occurred in a satyr-play. It is a synonym of the ordinary ἀνδραποδιστής, which is defined as οὐ μόνον ὁ τοὺς ἐλευθέρους δουλούμενος, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ τῶν δεσποτῶν τοὺς δούλους ἀποσπῶν εἰς ἑαυτόν (schol. Ar. Plut. 521, Bekk. anecd. p. 394, 11).
1012 Hesych. I p. 184 ἀναστρέφων· ἀρνούμενος. Σοφοκλῆς.

ἀναστρέφειν is to invert and in its application to language may be compared with our phrase ‘to turn inside out.’ Similarly Aesch. Suppl. 631 δημηγόρους δ᾿ ἤκουσεν εὐπιθεῖς στροφάς. ἀναστροφή became a grammarian's term to express an inversion of the order of words (Rutherford, Annotation, p. 251). But ἀνατρέπειν is to upset and so to refute (Ar. Nub. 901).
1013 Hesych. I p. 186 ἀναψύχουσα· ξηραίνουσα, ῥιπίζουσα. Σοφοκλῆς.

The verb means ‘to revive,’ especially by ‘fanning’ or exposing to the fresh air. For the particular application to drying cf. Plut. Them. 30 τὰς αὐλαίας διαβρόχους γενομένας ἐκπετάσαντες ἀνέψυχον, Sull. 29 διαλιπὼν δ’ ὅσον ἀναψῦξαι τὸν ἱδρῶτα τῶν ἵππων. As the physical sense is secondary, there is nothing strange in the word being also used of wetting the feet to cool them (Eur. I. A. 421).
1014 Pollux 3. 147 τὸν δὲ ἄνοσον καὶ ἀνόσητον Σοφοκλῆς.

So Sophocles has ἀλύπητος : ἄλυπος, ἀπόνητος: ἄπονος, ἀφώνητος : ἄφωνος, ἀφόβητος : ἄφοβος, ἀψόφητος : ἄψοφος, ἀμούσωτος : ἄμουσος. These forms are not verbals, although editors often so describe them. Rather the suffix has become secondary, as explained by Brugmann, Comp. Gr. II p. 229 E. tr. See also on frs. 249, 819, 825, 970, Eur. Phoen. 2, Kaibel on El. 1065.
1015 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 144, 10 <ἄ>νους· Πλάτων νόμων ιβ΄ (962 C), ἀνούστερος δὲ καὶ ἀνουστέρα Σοφοκλῆς, ἀνούστατος δὲ Φερεκράτης.
If ἀνουστέρως is right in fr. 589, the reference cannot be to that passage.
1016 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 151, 16 ἄνυμφον· κακόνυμφον, ἢ τὴν οὐχ οἷαν τε νυμφευθῆναι. Σοφοκλῆς.

If the reference is to El. 1183 φεῦ τῆς ἀνύμφου δυσμόρου τε σῆς τροφῆς, as has been suggested, it is difficult to understand why the lemma is in the accusative. The schol. on El. 492 explains ἄνυμφα by κακόνυμφα, and the alternative renderings given here perhaps point to an exceptional situation, such as that of Auge or Tyro.
1017 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 153, 16 ἀολλεῖς· παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ τὰς συνηγμένας.
The Homeric ἀολλής is not found either in Aeschylus or in Euripides. The reference here cannot be to Trach. 513 or Phil. 1469, where alone the word occurs in the extant plays of Sophocles.

1018 Hesych. I p. 224 ἀπαιόλημα· ἀποκάθαρμα ἢ ἀπάτημα (ἀποπάτημα cod. : but see Suid. s.vv. ἀπαιόλημα, παιόλημα) ἢ ἀποπλάνημα. Σοφοκλῆς. Cf. Bekk. anecd. p. 419, 13 ἀπαιόλημα· ἀποπλάνημα, ἀποκάθαρμα, ἢ θεόν τινα ἀπατητικόν. Eustath. Il. p. 352, 36 ἀπαιόλημα τὸ ἀποπλάνημα καὶ ἀποκάθαρμα.

The commentators on Aesch. Cho. 1000 (schol. ἀπάτημα) are not agreed whether the word is there applied to a person or not: see also on fr. 913. Cf. Ar. Nub. 728 ἐξευρετέος γὰρ νοῦς ἀποστερητικός, | κἀπαιόλημα. There is no ground for Ellendt's view that the word is comic, and therefore probably occurred in a satyr-play. No doubt it is derived from αἰόλος in the sense of cunning. The explanation θεόν τινα ἀπατητικόν in Bekker's codex is curious: does it refer to Strepsiades' invocation of παμβασίλει' Ἀπαιόλη (Ar. Nub. 1150)?
1019 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 155, 22 ἁπαλά· οἷον ἐξηλλαγμένα καὶ καινά. Εὐριπίδης καὶ Σοφοκλῆς.

It is not easy to understand the explanation, unless it refers to the contrast of recent or imported luxury with the simplicity of former times. Cf. Com. fr. adesp. 56, III 410 Κ. θερμολουσίαις ἁπαλοί, μαλθακευνίαις ἁβροί, with the gloss ἐπὶ τῶν ὑπὸ τρυφῆς καὶ ἁβρότητος διαρρεόντων.
1020 ἀπάνος cod.: corr. Musurus

1020 Hesych. I p. 226 ἀπάνθρωπος· σκληρός, ἀνόητος, ἄφρων, ἀνελεήμων. Σοφοκλῆς ἀπανί.... The last word has been supposed by some to conceal the name of the play, but without much probability, as Nauck remarks. M. Schmidt suggested that it was the remnant of the gloss ἀπανθρωπία· σκληρότης preserved in Cyrill. Dresd. Or it may be due to the immediately succeeding ἀπαντίζορα (ἀπαντίξοα or ἀντίξοα Voss).

The gloss itself has this much of interest, that it vindicates for the fifth century B.C. the sense 'inhuman,' which would otherwise have been known only as post-classical. It is common in Plutarch: poet. aud. 8 p. 27 Β τῆς Πηνελόπης τοῖς μνηστήρσι προσδιαλεγομένης οὐκ ἀπανθρώπως, Sull. 30 ταῖς μεγάλαις ἐξουσίαις...τὰ ἤθη... ἔμπληκτα καὶ χαῦνα καὶ ἀπάνθρωπα ποιούσαις, Alc. 8 αὕτη μὲν οὖν οὐ παντελῶς ἔδοξεν ἡ βία παράνομος οὐδ᾽ ἀπάνθρωπος εἶναι. The fact that Hesychius associates ἀνόητος and ἄφρων with σκληρός and ἀνελεήμων illustrates the absence in the Greek mind of the sharp distinction which we draw between moral and intellectual qualities (σκαιός, ἀμαθής, κακῶς φρονεῖν : fr. 925 n.): cf. Plut. Pericl. 24 ταῦτα μὲν ἐπελθόντα τῇ μνήμῃ κατὰ τὴν γραφὴν ἀπώσασθαι καὶ παρελθεῖν ἴσως ἀπάνθρωπον ἦν, of unreasonable fastidiousness.
Pollux 7. 44 ἀποδῦσαι καὶ ἀπολωπίσαι, ὡς Σοφοκλῆς, καὶ περιλωπίσαι.

ἀπολωπίζειν (cf. λωποδυτεῖν) does not occur elsewhere, and Nauck suggests with some probability that ἀπολωπίσαι is an error for ἐκλωπίσαι, which is used in Trach. 925 ἐκ δ' ἐλώπισεν | πλευρὰν ἅπασαν ὠλένην τ' εὐώνυμον. The mistake might either be due to a slip of memory or to the influence of the neighbouring ἀποδῦσαι.
Bekk. anecd. p. 432, 6 ἀπόμορφα· ξένα, οὐκ ἐοικότα τοῖς ἤθεσιν. οὕτω Σοφοκλῆς.
For ἀπόμορφος : ἄμορφος see on fr. 558. Blaydes, missing the meaning, strangely suggests ἠθάσιν.
Bekk. anecd. p. 439, 10 ἀποφανῶσαι· εἰς τὸ φανερὸν καταστῆσαι. οὕτω Σοφοκλής.

Dindorf remarked that ἀποφανερῶσαι might have been expected, since φανόω is an unknown word. But the restoration ἀποφανῶ σε...καταστήσω has since been made by Contus, and was accepted by Nauck. For the word cf. fr. 74.

Etym. Gud. p. 185, 19 de St. Ἀργειφόντης· ὁ Ἑρμῆς παρ' Ὁμήρῳ καὶ παρὰ πολλοῖς· παρὰ δὲ Σοφοκλεῖ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ Ἀπόλλωνος, καὶ παρὰ Παρθενίῳ (fr. 35 Mein.) καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ Τηλέφου. This account is fuller and more correct than Cramer, anecd. Par. iv p. 60, 21 Ἀργειφόντης· ὁ Ἑρμῆς παρ' Ὁμήρῳ καὶ παρὰ Σοφοκλεί, ἐπεὶ δὲ Ἀπόλλωνος καὶ Παρθενίῳ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ Τηλέφου, and Etym. Sorb. ap. Gaisford on schol. Hes. Op. 84.

Apollo received this title as the slayer of the Pythian dragon, and Meineke concludes that there must have been a similar legend concerning Telephus. Cf. Eustath. Il. p. 183, 13 (Pausan. fr. 65 Schw.) ἀργειφόντης· ὁ ὀφιοκτόνος. ἄργην γάρ, φησίν, ἔνιοι τὸν ὄφιν καλοῦσιν. Hesych. I p. 273 Ἀργῆν ἔπεφνεν (printed by Nauck as Tr. fr. adesp. 199)· ὄφιν. ἔστι δὲ ἐπίθετον δράκοντος. For ἀργᾶς = ὄφις the fullest explanation is given by Harpocr. p. 32, 15, partly reproduced by Bekk. anecd. p. 442, 29, Suid. s.v., and elsewhere.
The points of contact in the worship of Apollo and Hermes have been collected by O. Seeck, Unterg. d. antik. Welt, II p. 573.
Bekk. anecd. p. 447, 5 ἄρταμος· κρεουργός, μάγειρος. τάττει αὐτὸ Σοφοκλῆς ἐπὶ τοῦ φονέως.

Gaisford conjectured that Tr. fr. adesp. 148 ἦ γὰρ βέβηκε χεῖρας ἀρτάμων φυγών; was the passage indicated. But that line is quoted to illustrate ἄρταμος, ὁ μάγειρος (Etym. M. p. 149, 55), and might well refer to the escape of a sacrificial victim. It is probable that the meaning ‘slayer’ was not unfamiliar in tragedy, and it has been introduced by several critics in Aesch. Ag. 1076. Cf. Lycophr. 236 στυγνὸς ἄρταμος τέκνων, 797 κέλωρ δὲ πατρὸς ἄρταμος κληθήσεται. Shakespeare's use of butcher and shambles will occur to everyone. Tzetz. Lycophr. 797 explains ἄρταμος by σφαγεύς, and derives it from ἄορ and τέμνειν.

1026 Bekk. anecd. p. 459, 31 ἀτιμαγέλης· ὁ ἀποστάτης τῆς ἀγέλης ταῦρος. οὕτω Σοφοκλῆς. Cf. Hesych. I p. 314 ἀτιμαγέλας· ὁ ἀτιμάζων (Nauck conj. μονάζων, which is unnecessary) καὶ τῇ ἀγέλῃ μὴ συνυποταττόμενος.

Aristotle explains the matter thus (hist. an. 6. 18. 572b 17): ὁ δὲ ταῦρος, ὅταν ὥρα τῆς ὀχείας ᾖ, τότε γίγνεται σύννομος, καὶ μάχεται τοῖς ἄλλοις, τὸν δὲ πρότερον χρόνον μετ᾿ ἀλλήλων εἰσίν· ὃ καλεῖται ἀτιμαγελεῖν· πολλάκις γὰρ οἵ γε ἐν τῇ Ἠπείρῳ οὐ φαίνονται τριῶν μηνῶν. This is evidently the source of Vergil's well-known description of the defeated bull in Georg. 3. 225 ff., followed by Stat. Theb. 2. 323 ff. and Lucan 2. 601 ff. The solitary wanderings of the bull, without the particular explanation, are mentioned by Sophocles himself in O.T. 476 φοιτᾷ γὰρ ὑπ᾽ ἀγρίαν | ὕλαν ἀνά τ᾽ ἄντρα καὶ | πέτρας ἰσόταυρος κτέ. Cf. Theocr. 14. 43 αἰνός θην λέγεταί τις, ἔβα καὶ ταῦρος ἀν᾿ ὕλαν. Schol. Theocr. 9. 5 μηδὲν ἀτιμαγελεῦντες]...τοὺς γὰρ καταλιπόντας τὸ κοινὸν τῆς ἀγέλης, καὶ καθ' ἑαυτοὺς νεμομένους, οὕτω καλοῦσιν. Philostr. iun. imag. 2 (of Neoptolemus in Scyros) ἀπαυχενίζων τοὺς ἀτιμάζοντας τὴν ἀγέλην ταύρους.

1027 Hesych. I p. 323 αὐλῶπιν· αὐλοὺς ἔχουσαν. Σοφοκλῆς δὲ τὴν λόγχην τὴν μακρὰν αὐλῶπιν εἶπεν. The words Σοφοκλῆς...εἶπεν appear in the codex as part of the gloss to αὐλῶνες, and were transferred to their right place by Heinsius.

Sophocles described a spear as αὐλῶπις, in reference to the hollowness of the shaft, or rather of the pipe of the spear-head into which the shaft was fixed. His usage therefore might be adduced in support of the interpretation of the Homeric αὐλῶπις τρυφάλεια which is given e.g. by schol. AD on Λ 353 αὐλοὺς ἔχουσα εἰς οὓς οἱ λόφοι κατακλείονται. Although the word is not so used in Homer, his spears were evidently so constructed: cf. ι 156 αἰγανέας δολιχαύλους (schol. T αὐλὸς δὲ τὸ κοῖλον τῆς ἐπιδορατίδος, εἰς ὃ ἐντίθεται τοῦ ξύλου τὸ ἄκρον). And this is perhaps the meaning of αὐλόν in P 297, where see Leaf.
1028 Bekk. anecd. p. 467, 28 (Phryn. fr. 280 de B.) αὑτόν· Σοφοκλῆς ἀντὶ τοῦ ἐμαυτόν, καὶ Λυσίας ἐν τῷ κατ' Ἰφικράτους (fr. 133 Tur.) καὶ πολλοὶ ἄλλοι.

It is possible, but not very likely, that the reference is to O.C. 966 ἐπεὶ καθ' αὑτόν γ᾽ οὐκ ἂν ἐξεύροις ἐμοὶ | ἁμαρτίας ὄνειδος, as Meineke thought. For αὑτοῦ = ἐμαυτοῦ see Jebb on O. T. 138, Ai. 1132.
1029 Bekk. anecd. p. 467, 15 αὐτόπαιδα· αὐτὸν τρόπῳ τινὶ παῖδα ὄντα. οὕτω Σοφοκλῆς. The same in Hesych. I p. 328 without the reference to Sophocles.

Nauck in his first edition was inclined to assign the reference to Trach. 826 τῷ Διὸς αὐτόπαιδι, but subsequently preferred the Phaedra for a reason given in the note on fr. 691. Neither the lemma nor the explanation suits the passage in the Trachiniae, and it seems that Sopocles used the word for 'a mere child, an absolute child.' For this use of αὐτός in composition see on fr. 130.
1030 Phryn. praep. soph. p. 50, 14 (Bekk. anecd. p. 28, 27) ἀχανές· τὸ μὴ ἔχον στέγην ἢ ὄροφον. ἐπὶ τοῦ λαβυρίνθου. Σοφοκλῆς.

The earliest example of ἀχανής is Parmen. fr. 1, 18 D. ταὶ δὲ θυρέτρων | χάσμ᾽ ἀχανὲς ποίησαν ἀναπτάμεναι, i.e. 'a yawning void': cf. A.P. 9. 423 ἐς βυθὸν ἐξ ἀχανοῦς χάσματος ἠρίπετε, of Bura and Helice destroyed by an earthquake. It is a favourite word of Plutarch, particularly in the combination ἀχανὲς πέλαγος, mare vastum, for which see Wyttenbach, Plut. mor. VI p. 559 (on 76 c). The interpretation given by Phrynichus is probably an attempt to define an intentionally vague description. 'Vast' would do well enough for the labyrinth; but the Egyptian labyrinth, which Daedalus is said to have copied (Diod. 1. 61), certainly had a roof (Hdt. 2. 148). Apollod. 3. 11 defines it as οἴκημα καμπαῖς πολυπλόκοις πλανῶν τὴν ἔξοδον, in which Nauck recognized a tragic fragment (fr. adesp. 34). The word probably occurred in the Camici or the Daedalus.
1031 Pollux 7. 70 ἡ δὲ βαίτη ἔστι μὲν προμήκης χιτών, οὕτω δὲ Σοφοκλῆς καὶ τὰς σκηνὰς τὰς βαρβαρικὰς καλεῖ. Cf. Hesych. I p. 353 βαίτη· ... ἔνιοι δὲ σκηνὴν δερματίνην.

The Homeric κλισίαι were probably wooden huts, but the tents of the ancients were generally made of skins. There is a parallel to the double meaning of βαίτη in the case of διφθέρα, which is used both of a skin-coat (Ar. Nub. 72) and of a tent (Xen. anab. 1. 5. 10 διφθέρας ἃς εἶχον στεγάσματα).
1032 Athen. 690 C μνημονεύει τῆς βακκάριδος καὶ Σοφοκλῆς.

βάκκαρις was an oriental unguent extracted from the root of the plant which bears the same name (Plin. n. h. 21. 29). Athenaeus (690 A—D) collects a number of quotations illustrating its use by the Greeks. According to some authorities, it was especially in vogue with the Lydians: see schol. Aesch. Pers. 42 καὶ τὴν βάκκαριν δὲ ἔνιοι Λυδῶν μύρον ἔφασαν.

1033 Harpocr. p. 43, 11 βάσανος· λίθος ἐστὶν ἡ τὸ χρυσίον παρατριβόμενον δοκιμάζουσα. οὕτως Ἀντιφῶν (fr. 157 Β.) καὶ Πίνδαρος (Pyth. 10. 67) καὶ Σοφοκλῆς. This is the reading of cod. Palat. (Bekker's E), with which Suid. s.v. βάσανος agrees: Pindar and Sophocles are not mentioned in the vulgate text. The definition is given in the same words by Etym. M. p. 189, 1 with the addition οὕτω πάντες κέχρηνται οἱ ἀξιόλογοι. Observe that παρατριβόμενον is ‘when rubbed beside’ or ‘in comparison with’ (something else), and cf. Theogn. 417 ἐς βάσανον δ’ ἐλθὼν παρατρίβομαι ὥστε μολίβδῳ | χρυσός, Hdt. 7. 10.
The touchstone was usually called Λυδία λίθος: see on fr. 800.
1034 Hesych. I p. 362 βάσκανος· φθονερός... Σοφοκλῆς δὲ ἰδίως τὸ βάσκανον (βάσκανος conj. Nauck) ἐπὶ τοῦ (ἔπειτα cod.) ἀχάριστος.

The word βάσκανος does not occur elsewhere in tragedy, except in the doubtful Eur. fr. 933. The exceptional (see for ἰδίως Rutherford, Annotation, p. 21023) usage attributed to Sophocles is nothing very remarkable: malignity might show itself specifically as ingratitude. Thus in Dem. 18. 119 Aeschines is characterised as βάσκανος ὄντως on this ground: τὸ λαβεῖν οὖν τὰ διδόμενα ὁμολογῶν ἔννομον εἶναι, τὸ χάριν τούτων ἀποδοῦναι παρανόμων γράφῃ.
1035 Hesych. I p. 408 βωλόναι· οἱ μὲν κολώνας, οἱ δὲ τὸ Κίλλαιον ἀκούουσι, διὰ τὸ ἀνακεχῶσθαι, παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ.

βωλόναι seems to mean tumuli, mounds formed with clods, a derivative from βῶλος. The alternative glosses are: (1) barrows, or (2) the Cillaeum, because it is raised in the form of a mound. The distinction is not clear, but the second alternative can be elucidated from Strabo 612 f. Cilla was a place in the south of the Troad on the gulf of Adramyttium, with a temple of Apollo Cillaeus, which is referred to in Hom. A 38, 450. But Strabo goes on to say (613) that there is a tomb of Cillus (or Cillas) close to the temple of Cillaean Apollo, ‘a great mound’ (χῶμα μέγα), and that this Cillus was the charioteer of Pelops. We should infer that τὸ Κίλλαιον in Hesych. denotes this grave rather than the temple of Apollo, which was not a χῶμα. According to Theopompus (FHG
I 331 from schol. Hom. A 38) Cillus died in Lesbos, and appeared after death to Pelops asking for funeral honours; consequently, Pelops raised a magnificent tomb in his honour, and built over against it a temple of Cillaean Apollo. Cillus seems to have been a tribal hero of the Aeolians, and τὸ Κίλλαιον was in consequence located in several Aeolean settlements. Strabo states (612) on the authority of Daes of Colonae that the temple of Cillaean Apollo was founded in Colonae first of all by the Aeolians who sailed from Hellas. The coincidence of the name suggests that Hesychius’ κολώνας should be read as a proper noun, and that the Sophoclean βωλόναι was identified with a site on the coast of the Troad, i.e. either with Colonae or the barrow of Cillus at Cilla. In that case the quotation is made from one of the Trojan plays, — perhaps the Ποιμένες, seeing that Colonae was the home of Cycnus. For Apollo Κιλλαῖος see the article of de Witte in Rev. Num. xi (1864) pp. 16—33, who derives the epithet from κίλλος an ass, and quotes Pind. Pyth. 10. 36.
1036 Steph. Byz. p. 202, 14 Γενήτης, λιμὴν καὶ ποταμός (Καππαδοκίας add. Meineke). Ἀπολλώνιος ἄκραν Γενηταίαν φησί (2. 378, 1009). Σοφοκλῆς ποταμὸν Γένητα φησίν.

Strabo 548 places the river Genetes between the Iasonian promontory and Cotyora on the Pontic coast. See Ruge in Pauly-Wissowa VII 1132. It has been supposed that Sophocles, the commentator on Apollonius Rhodius, is meant; but the form of the citation does not favour this view. See also on fr. 1096.

1037 Hesych. I p. 434 γλοίας· ἡ κακοήθης ἵππος καὶ πολυδίκ (so the cod. according to Nauck: M. Schmidt reports its reading as πολυδίκη) παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ· καὶ γλοίης τὸ αὐτό. Meineke proposed to heal the corruption by reading πολὺ δεικνύουσα τὸ θάρσος, but this is hardly appropriate; and Blaydes's πολύδικος (a thrower) has no probability. I should prefer πολυδάκνης (φιλοδακής Ellendt): cf. Theocr. 15. 40 μορμώ, δάκνει ἵππος. See also Herodian II 680, 26 γλοίης, γλοίητος (σημαίνει δὲ τὸν κακοήθη).

On the strength of Ar. Nub. 449 μάσθλης, εἴρων, γλοιός, ἀλαζών Brunck interpreted γλοιάς as 'likely to fall.' γλοιός is 'slippery,' being connected with γλία 'glue.' But Brunck's view takes no account of κακοήθης, although this is the connecting link with γλοιός and γλοιάζειν 'to leer.' For the latter cf. Etym. M. p. 234, 44 (partly in Bekk. anecd. p. 233, 7) γλοίης ὁ νωθρός· καὶ γλοίητα τὸν λιπαρὸν καὶ μοχθηρὸν τῷ ἤθει· καὶ γλοιάζειν, τὸ τοῖς ὄμμασιν ἐπιμύοντα μυκτηρίζειν καὶ κακοηθεύεσθαι. οἳ δὲ διαγελᾶν. In judging the points of a horse, the shifty look of the eye was considered indicative of temper: so at least we may infer from Aesch. fr. 243 νέας γυναικὸς οὔ με μὴ λάθῃ φλέγων | ὀφθαλμός...ἔχων δὲ τούτων θυμὸν ἱππογνώμονα, and from the evidence of the writers on Physiognomy adduced by Headlam in his notes on Aesch. Ag. 283, 784. I understand that the ἱππογνώμονες of to-day attach much importance to the size and brightness of the eye, and that if the whites are shown and the ears laid back at the same time, the horse is considered to be of uncertain temper.

1038 Hesych. I p. 438 γνώμων· συνετός. Σοφοκλῆς. Cf. Etym. M. p. 236, 53 ἐγὼ δὲ εὗρον ἐν τοῖς ῥητορικοῖς τὴν λέξιν σημαίνειν οὕτως· γνώμων· ὁ συνετός, where the presence of the article should be observed, i.e. the expert or connoisseur. There is no evidence for γνώμων as an adj. = 'intelligent.' Nauck, adopting Naber's reading γνώμων in Phil. 910, observed that that passage was not referred to here. But, if the original gloss was ὁ συνετός, the remark does not apply.
1039 Schol. Apoll. Rhod. 3. 281 ὀξέα δενδίλλων]... Σοφοκλῆς δὲ ἐπὶ τοῦ περιβλέπειν τέθεικε τὴν λέξιν.

Sophocles and Apollonius followed Hom. I 180 δενδίλλων ἐς ἕκαστον Ὀδυσσῆι δὲ μάλιστα, where the scholl. interpret διανεύων τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς ἢ περιβλέπων. Apollon. lex. p. 57, 15 δενδίλλων· περιβλεπόμενος. The word was very rare, but the gloss in Hesych. I p. 473 δενδίλλει· σκαρδαμύττει. διανεύει. σημαίνει. ἀτιμάζει. σκώπτει does not seem to refer to Sophocles.
1040 Pollux 3. 73 δέσποινα δεσπόζουσα...οὐ γὰρ προσίεμαι τὴν Σοφοκλέους δεσπότειραν ἢ τὴν Εὐριπίδου (Med. 17 etc., but also used by Soph. El. 597, Trach. 407) δεσπότιν.

δεσπότειρα assumes the existence of δεσποτήρ: for similar examples see Brugmann, Comp. Gr. II pp. 336, 379 E. tr., and the note on θηλάστρια (fr. 98). Dindorf quoted δυνάστειρα from an Alexandrian inscription published by Lenormant in Rh. Mus. IX 371.
1041 Pollux 9. 158 ὁ ἀνὴρ φυγάς, ἐξόριστος...τραγικὸς (τραγικὸν conj. Nauck) γὰρ ὁ παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ διωκτός.

διωκτός is simply 'a man driven into exile' (not 'to be pursued,' as L. and S.), in accordance with the original force of the verbal adjective: see Brugmann, II pp. 218—220. For the corresponding use of the verb itself cf. Hdt. 5. 92. 5 πολλοὺς μὲν Κορινθίων ἐδίωξε, πολλοὺς δὲ χρημάτων ἀπεστέρησε, and for the verbal noun Eur. I.T. 1175 πάσης διωγμοῖς ἠλάθησαν Ἑλλάδος.

1042 Hesych. II p. 9 ἐγκουράδες... εἰ μὴ ἄρα ἰσοδυναμεῖ ὡς κότῳ καὶ ἐνεκότουν παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ. The reading is uncertain, and most critics follow Musurus in restoring τῷ for ὡς, and suppose that the words εἰ... Σοφοκλεῖ belong to a lost lemma ἔγκοτος, or that they have been disconnected from ἐγκότημα. M. Schmidt, however, would keep ὡς and read κοτῶ.
Blomfield (on Theb. 804) remarked that Aeschylus affected the compounds of κότος, and ἐγκοτεῖν is found in Cho. 41.
1043 Etym. M. p. 333, 40 ἔλυτρον· κάλυμμα, ἐκπέτασμα, ἐνείλημα. ὁμοίως καὶ ἡ θήκη τοῦ τόξου. καὶ πληθυντικῶς Σοφοκλῆς ἔλυτρα.

ἔλυτρον was a cover generally, and might be used specifically for a bow-case, the proper name for which was γωρυτός (Hom. φ 54). Ellendt should not have identified it with φαρέτρα, although the bow-case frequently held the arrows as well as the bow: see Dict. Ant. I 171a. It is not quite clear that Sophocles is quoted for the meaning 'bow-case,' as the intention may be only to take notice of his use of the plural (Kuehner-Gerth I 18) in place of the singular.
1044 ἐνόλμιος Etym. M.: ἔνολμος Zenob., ἔνολμις (?) Etym. Flor.

1044 Etym. M. p. 344, 40 ἐνολμίς· ἦν τι γένος μάντεων οὕτω καλούμενον...ὁ δὲ Σοφοκλῆς ἐνόλμιος. In Etym. Flor. (Miller, Mélanges) p. 114 the last words appear as ὁ δὲ Σοφοκλῆς ἔνολμιν τὸν Ἀπόλλωνα λέγει. Zenob. 3. 63 καὶ Ἀπόλλων ὑπὸ Σοφοκλέους ἔνολμος.

From the last-quoted authorities it becomes clear that Sophocles employed ἐνόλμιος (or ἔνολμος) as a title of Apollo, i.e. μαντικός. The current explanation was given by Aristophanes of Byzantium ap. Zenob. l.c.: καὶ Ἀριστοφάνης ὁ γραμματικός φησιν, ὡς οἱ ἐν ὅλμῳ κοιμηθέντες μαντικοί· καὶ τοὺς τρίποδας τοῦ Ἀπόλλωνος ὅλμους καλεῖσθαι (cf. schol. Ar. Vesp. 238). Hence the proverb ἐν ὅλμῳ εὐνάσω. Eustath. Il. p. 836, 42 περὶ τοῦ τοιούτου λόγος ἦν ὡς οἱ κοιμώμενοι ἐν αὐτῷ μαντικοὶ ἐγένοντο. Παυσανίας (fr. 167 Schw.) γοῦν φησι παροιμιακῶς ‘ἐν ὅλμῳ ἐκοιμήσω’ ἤγουν μαντικὸς ἐγένου. The alternative explanation that Ὅλμος was a prophet (Zenob., Hesych. ΙΙ p. 105) may be disregarded. A more precise assertion defines ὅλμος as the lid (ἐπίθημα) of the tripod, on which the Pythia sat: schol. Ar. Plut. 9, Pollux 10. 81.
1045 ἑξπηχυστί (ἕξπηχυς V) codd.: corr. Dindorf
1045 Etym. M. p. 346, 16 Ἀττικῶς μὲν ἕξπουν καὶ ἕξκλινον λέγεται ὥσπερ καὶ παρὰ τῷ Σοφοκλεῖ ἑξπηχυστί καὶ παρὰ Πλάτωνι τῷ κωμικῷ (fr. 242, I 664 K.) ἕξπουν.

It is difficult to credit Sophocles with
the form ἑξπηχυστί, and Dindorf suggested ἕξπηχυ in order to bring the word into line with the other neuters. The statements of the Atticists, that ἑξάπους and the like are later than the classical period, are confirmed by the evidence of inscriptions: Meisterhans³, p. 159. But both ἕξπους and ἕκπους are found on the stone records: ibid. pp. 109, 158. Hence it was unnecessary for Porson to introduce ἑκμέδιμνον for ἑξμέδιμνον in Ar. Pac. 631. In O.T. 1137, however, the same critic rightly gave ἑκμήνους for ἐμμήνους of the best MSS. Cf. Phryn. p. 412 ἑξάπηχυ καὶ ἑξαέτης· καὶ ἐντεῦθεν ἀφαιρήσεις τὸ ᾱ, ἕξπηχυ καὶ ἑξέτης καὶ ἕκπλευρον, where Lobeck has a full discussion of the literary evidence. See also Jebb on Ant. 1275 λακπάτητον.

1046 Eustath. Od. p. 1562, 38 (Ael. Dion. fr. 57 Schw.) καὶ ἔπηλις ἡ ἐπὶ τοῦ προσώπου μελανία, καὶ τὸ πῶμα τῆς λάρνακος, ὡς φασὶν οἱ παλαιοὶ κατὰ τὸν Σοφοκλῆν. ἡ δ᾽ αὐτὴ καὶ ἔφηλις κοινῶς ὡς ἀπὸ τοῦ ἥλου (al. ἡλίου). Cf. Hesych. II p. 146 ἔπηλις· τὸ πῶμα τῆς λάρνακος.

Eustathius quotes ἔπηλις as an example of ψίλωσις in Ionic, comparing it with λεύκιππος, ἀντήλιος, and ἀπηλιώτης. Το the same effect Bekk. anecd. p. 424, 25 (Suid. s.v. ἀπηλιώτης) καὶ πάντα τὰ ὅμοια ψιλῶς. καὶ ἡ ἔπηλίς ἐστι παρὰ Ποσειδίππῳ (fr. 41, III 347 K.). The last example has been considered as an illustration of the meaning μελανία, but without reason, since Eustathius, deriving from the same source, connects ἔπηλις with ἀντήλιος etc. in exactly the same way. Schwabe brackets the clause ἡ δ' αὐτὴ...ἡλίου (sic) as not belonging to Aelius: anyhow, no one will now believe that ἔπηλις was derived from ἥλιος in the one sense and from ἦλος in the other. Ionic ψίλωσις is illustrated by Smyth (Ionic Dialect, p. 322 f.). No importance should be attached to the appearance of the form ἔφηλις in Hippocrates. So far as the meaning goes, it would be easy to treat the sense eruption as secondary (cf. the medical use of patch), but the history of the word is obscure.
1047 Pollux 3. 145 τοὺς δὲ βραβευτὰς καὶ ἐπιστάτας ὠνόμαζον, ὅθεν καὶ τὸ βραβεύειν ἐπιστατεῖν Σοφοκλῆς.

For the judges at the pan-Hellenic games see Jebb on El. 690, and for the use of ἐπιστατεῖν cf. Plat. legg. 949 A γυμνικῶν τε καὶ ἱππικῶν ἄθλων ἐπιστάτας, Xen. rep. Lac. 8. 4 οἱ ἐν τοῖς γυμνικοῖς ἀγῶσιν ἐπιστάται.

1048 Eustath. Od. p. 1856, 11 ἐπιβόητος ὁ μοχθηρὰν ἔχων φήμην, καθ᾽ οὗ δηλαδὴ βοαὶ γίνονται, ὃν ἐπίβωτον Ἀνακρέων (fr. 60) φησίν· οὗ ἑτεροῖος ὁ διαβόητος ὡς ἐπ᾿ ἀρετῇ ἐγνωσμένος. ὁμοία δὲ ἐναντιότης ('hostility') τῷ ἐπιβοήτῳ καὶ ἐν τῷ ἐπίφατος, ὁ κεῖται παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ. There is an extract from the same original (Herennius Philo) in Etym. Gud. p. 142, 46, where in place of the reference to Sophocles by name we find τοῦτον (sc. τὸν ἐπιβόητον) δὲ ἔνιοι τῶν ποιητικῶν (l. ποιητῶν) ἐπισφατον (l. ἐπίφατον) καλοῦσι; and also ib. p. 199, 5 τοῦτον δὲ ἔνιοι τῶν ποιητῶν ἐπιοφαττὸν (l. ἐπίφατον) καλοῦσι.

I do not know why the citation of Eustathius has been ignored, seeing no reason to discredit the statement that Sophocles employed ἐπίφατος in the sense of ἐπιβόητος and ἐπίρρητος. It is obvious,
as Hermann pointed out, that the grammarian was not referring to ἐπίφαντον in Ant. 841, whether the usual interpretation of that word is correct or not. Further, there is no connexion between this word and ἐπίσφατος (?)—ὁ ὀλέθριος παρὰ τὸ πεφάσθαι—quoted in Eustath. Od. p. 1728, 14. In Hesych. II p. 174 ἐπίφατος is probably an error for ἐπίφαντος.
1049 Phot. lex. p. 37, 9 εὐορνιθίαν. Σοφοκλῆς ἐπὶ οἰωνῶν. Eustath. Od. p. 1439, 34 καὶ εὐορνιθία κατὰ τοὺς παλαιοὺς παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ τὸ ἀγαθὸν οἰώνισμα.
Eustathius compares the word with εὐερμία, a particular piece of good luck. Blaydes adds εὐοδία, = 'bon voyage,' in Ar. Ran. 1528.
1050 Etym. Μ. p. 462, 24 εὐτυχία· εὕρηται καὶ εὐτύχεια παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ.

Sophocles employs forms in ειο, which are often metrically convenient, in place of the normal ιο as follows: Ἐφέσειος (fr. 97), Βοσπόρειος (fr. 707), Ἀνακτόρειον (fr. 916), ἐπινύμφειος (Ant. 814), ἐπινίκειος (Ο. C. 1088), ἐναίθρειος (Ant. 358). See also on fr. 398, 3 παγκάρπεια. The converse case is illustrated by εὐσεβίαν for εὐσέβειαν in Ant. 943, where see Jebb. εὐτύχεια might be a legitimate and regular formation from εὐτυχεσ, but, since εὐτυχία was well established, it is more probable that it was the product of a new analogy.
1051 Pollux 6. 161 ἐκ δὲ τοῦ ημι τάδε τὰ ὀνόματα. ἡμιμανής...καὶ ἡμίκακον δὲ Εὐκλείδης λέγει καὶ Σοφοκλῆς. Ἀριστοφάνης δὲ καὶ ἡμικάκως (Thesm. 449).

Phrynichus, p. 336 Lob., condemned the word: ἡμίκακον, οὐχ οὕτως ἀλλ᾽ ἡμιμόχθηρον (Plat. rep. 352 C) φάθι. It is difficult to understand why he took this line: possibly he thought it less suited to an elevated prose style than ἡμιμόχθηρος, and Sophocles may have used ἡμίκακον in a satyr-play. The Antiatticist (Bekk. anecd. p. 98, 13) quotes ἡμίκακον from Ἄλεξις Αἰχμαλωτῷ (fr. 10, II 300 K.).

app.rdg: θάμος vel θάμιος codd.: corr. Sylburg

div.p: 1052 Etym. Μ. p. 441, 24 θαλαμίδιοι κῶπαι· αἱ ἠρέμα ἐλαύνουσαι. ὁ κατώτατος ἐρέτης θάμος (θάμιος cod. M, θαλάμιος Sylburg) λέγεται, ὁ δὲ μέσος ζύγιος, ὁ δὲ ἀνώτατος θρανίτης. Σοφοκλῆς is added after λέγεται by the codd. DPM.

The rowers on the lowest bench of the trireme used the shortest oars, and received the least pay: schol. Ar. Ran. 1074. They were also known as θαλάμακες and θαλαμῖται. Cf. the contemptuous reference in Aesch. Ag. 1617 σὺ ταῦτα φωνεῖς νερτέρᾳ προσήμενος | κώπῃ. The accentuation θαλαμιός follows the authority of Arcad. p. 40, 13, but the Mss generally give θαλάμιος: Chandler, § 245. Blaydes thinks that Sophocles the grammarian was meant: see on fr. 983.

1053 Etym. M. p. 450, 50 θήλεια... παρὰ τὸ θάλλειν καὶ γεννᾶν· ὅθεν καὶ ἡ ὕπομβρος νὺξ παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ θήλεια καλεῖται. To the same effect Etym. Gud. p. 261, 25, with νῦν for νύξ and the addition of διὰ τὸ θάλλειν ἐν αὐτῷ τοὺς καρπούς.

Possibly Sophocles wrote θήλεια νὺξ | ὕπομβρος. The adjective follows the Homeric θήλυς ἐέρση ε 467 (schol. ἡ τρόφιμος δρόσος), where the context shows that the epithet is conventional. So Hes. Sc. 395 (τέττιξ) ᾧτε πόσις καὶ βρῶσις θήλυς ἐέρση. Callim. fr. 296 θηλύτατον πέδιον, which Schneider refers to the plain of Eleusis as the scene of the story of Triptolemus. The passages quoted by L. and S. from Theophrastus are beside the mark, and the usage in question was entirely literary. Contrast ἄρσενας χοάς, fr. 523 (n.).

1054 Choerob. in Theod. p. 123 [= p. 221, 6 Hilgard] (Bekk. anecd. p. 1381) τὸ γὰρ θήλυδος παρὰ τῷ Σοφοκλεῖ κλιθὲν διὰ τοῦ δος ἡμάρτηται. H. refers to p. 232 [= p. 231, 6 H.] (Bekk. anecd. p. 1408) πάλμυς πάλμυος· τὸ γὰρ πάλμυδος διὰ τοῦ δος κλιθὲν παρ' Αἰσχίνῃ (al. Αἰσχύλῳ) ἡμάρτηται· ἔστι δὲ ὄνομα κύριον βασιλέως, where he conjectures παρ' Αἰσχρίωνι, on the ground that the word πάλμυς was used by Hipponax, Callimachus, and Lycophron, and may well have belonged to Aeschrion also.

It is at first sight remarkable enough to find θήλυς passing over to the υδ stems in a writer like Sophocles, though we are not surprised when Lobeck quotes τοῦ θήλυος from Josephus (Phryn. p. 246). The introduction of δ (cf. χλαμύς, ἔπηλυς) is similar to its appearance in ι stems (ἔριδος beside ἔριν, μήνιδος later than μήνιος). It should not be forgotten that θήλυς served originally as a feminine (Brugmann, Comp. Gr. II p. 335 Eng. tr.), and is actually so found eight times in Homer (Ameis-Hentze on ε 467, Leaf on E 269). This may have contributed to its association with a nominal stem.
1055 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 43, 4 = Bekk. anecd. p. 352, 16 ἄθρακτος· ἀτάραχος· καὶ τὸ συνεχύθη ἐθράχθη Σοφοκλῆς λέγει (ὡς Σοφοκλῆς Phot.). Cf. Hesych. I p. 65 ἄθρακτοι· ἀτάρακτοι.

θράσσω occurs in fr. 177, as well as in Aesch. Prom. 655, Eur. fr. 600 and Rhes. 863. Cf. Pind. Isth. 6. 39. θράσσω: τραχύς and τέτρηχα shows that in the adjective the aspirates have been dissimilated. Cf. θρίξ: τριχός, θρέξομαι: τρέχω, and other examples given by King and Cookson, p. 200. ταράσσω follows ταραχή. ταράσσω became universal later, as is shown by Moeris' mistaken θράττει Ἀττικοί, ταράσσει Ἕλληνες (p. 199, 3).

1056 Etym. Μ. p. 42, 41 ἁμάρτημα τὸ παρὰ τῇ Σαπφοῖ (fr. 166) πολυΐδριδι, καὶ παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ ἴδριδα (πολυΐδριδα of Etym. Flor. ap. Miller, Mélanges, p. 16 is an error) καὶ παρὰ Φρυνίχῳ (fr. 22) ἴδριδες. Schol. A Hom. Γ 219 ὁ γὰρ Σοφοκλῆς ἴδριδα ἔφη τὴν αἰτιατικὴν ὅ τε Φρύνιχος τὴν εὐθεῖαν ἴδριδες. Eustath. Il. p. 407, 38 οὐ γάρ ἐστιν οὐδὲ τὸ ἄϊδρις παρώνυμον μακροπαράληκτον, ἵνα διὰ τοῦ δ κλίνηται· ὥστε...ἁμαρτάνει Σαπφὼ καὶ Σοφοκλῆς καὶ Φρύνιχος διὰ τοῦ δ κλίνοντες.

ἴδριν is accepted by modern editors in O. C. 525. The passing of ι stems wholly or partially into the ιδ class (ἔριν, ἔριδα : γλαυκώπιν, γλαυκώπιδα) is well known: see Monro, H.
