G.2 § 97; Giles, Manual, § 348; Brugmann, II 408. By a strange error de Borries includes this gloss in his edition of Phryn. praep. soph. p. 136.
1057 Pollux 7. 185 ἱπποφορβοί ἱπποφορβία, καὶ ὡς Σοφοκλῆς ἱπποβουκόλοι, ἱπποφορβεῖς.

It has been suggested that an error has been made in the name of the poet, and that Pollux (or his authority) intended to refer to Eur. Phoen. 28 (n). However, fr. 659, 2 makes it quite likely that Sophocles used the word.
1058 Etym. Μ. p. 500, 55 κέκονα παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ, ἀπὸ τοῦ κτείνω. The same in Etym. Gud. p. 313, 14. Cf. Choerob. in Theodos. II p. 78, 1 Hilgard προστιθέασι τὸ κ καὶ φασὶ κέκονα.

From this gloss Cobet (V. L. p. 322) restored κατακεκονότες in Xen. anab. 7. 6. 36 (κατακεκανότες codd. ΑΒ, κατακανόντες vulg.). There is no difficulty in the vocalism καίνω: κέκονα, since καίνω is for km-ió: Brugmann, I 198, IV 246.
1059 Phot. lex. p. 151, 14 καῦρος (καυρός cod.)· κακός. οὕτως Σοφοκλής.

The accentuation of this word as properispomenon is attested by Arcad. p. 69, 21 τὰ εἰς ρος δισύλλαβα ἐπὶ ἐμψύχων τιθέμενα τῇ αν διφθόγγῳ παραληγόμενα βαρύνεται, φλαῦρος, σαῦρος, καῦρος ὁ κακός. For the meaning cf. Hesych. II p. 451 καῦρος· κακός. Etym. M. p. 530, 17 derives κορώνη from κρῴζω or alternatively from καῦρον ἢ γαῦρον, ὅπερ σημαίνει τὸ κακόν. The etymologer treated γαῦρος as a phonetic variation of καῦρος : ib. p. 493, 53 καῦρος· ὁ κοῦφος ταῖς φρεσί, πλεονασμῷ τοῦ κ, αὐρός τις ὤν· τὸν γὰρ κατὰ νοῦν ἐλαφρὸν καῦρον ἐπονομάζουσι. βέλτιον γαῦρον λέγειν κτέ. The explanation illustrates the familiar Greek confusion of foolishness with vice: see on fr. 925, and Eur. Hclid. 413. There is no probability in Nauck's proposal to substitute καῦρον for μοῦνον in Trach. 958.

1060 Etym. Μ. p. 513, 45 Κιμμερίους ...γράφεται δὲ καὶ Κερβερίων· καὶ ἔοικε καὶ Σοφοκλῆς περιπεπτωκέναι τῇ τοιαύτῃ γραφῇ. Cf. schol. PV Hom. λ 14 Κιμμερίων... ἔνιοι δὲ γράφουσι χειμερίων. οἳ δὲ Κερβερίων, ὡς Κράτης. Eustath. Od. p. 1671, 1.

Schol. H. on Hom. l.c. states that Aristarchus also read Κερβερίων in that passage, so that it was undoubtedly an old variant, which Sophocles may have found in his copy of Homer. That the name was familiar at Athens is shown by Ar. Ran. 186 τίς ἐς τὸ Λήθης πεδίον ἢ εἰς ὄνου πόκας | ἢ 'ς Κερβερίους; The name Κέρβερος was said to mean 'pallid' (Hesych. II p. 467), a derivation which Gruppe, p. 4082, supports by quoting Κέρβης, the name of a river in Euboea said to make the sheep which drank of it white ([Arist.] mir. ausc. 170). The Κερβέριοι would thus be a phantom race dwelling in the Arctic north, close to the entrance of Hades.

1061 Etym. Μ. p. 514, 27 κινάκης· ἀκινάκης (‘κινάκης addunt DEM, Nauck) παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ. τὸ μὲν γὰρ Ἀνακρεόντειον (fr. 136) χωρὶς τοῦ ἰῶτα γράφεται· γέγονεν ἔκθλιψις τοῦ ἰῶτα· καὶ κράσει τοῦ ωα τὠκινάκῃ, ὥσπερ ὦ Ἄπολλον ὦπολλον. The last words are perhaps a reference to Aesch. Ag. 1057, and the writer means that the apparent example of κινάκης in Anacreon is not such, but a regular Ionic crasis: see Weir Smyth, Ionic Dialect, p. 263.

H. remarks: ‘Before accepting κινάκης from Sophocles, I should like to know the word that came before it.’ There is a certain amount of evidence to confirm the authority of the Etym. Μ., but not of a very satisfactory character: Hesych. II p. 404 κάνακις· ξίφος, where M. Schmidt conjectured κινάκης. The Latin The- saurus I 413 quotes Gloss. IV 215, 32 canacem gladium, and V 494, 9 caucem gladium.
1062 Eustath. Od. p. 1761, 27 λέγει δὲ καὶ (sc. Ἀριστοφάνης ὁ γραμματικός) λαπίζειν παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ τὸ συρίζειν. Cf. Aristoph. Byz. ap. Miller, Mélanges, p. 427 λαπύζειν· τὸ συρίζειν.

There seems to be no other evidence for this use of λαπίζειν and Eustathius mentions it in a list of καινοφώνους λέξεις preserved by Aristophanes. But there was certainly a verb λαπίζειν or λαπίττειν which is glossed by ψεύδεσθαι, ἀλαζονεύεσθαι, and γαυροῦσθαι (Phot. lex. p. 208, 1; Bekk. anecd. p. 277, 27; Hesych. III p. 13), with derivatives λαπιστής and λάπισμα; and ἐλάπιζε, if it is the right reading, bears this sense in Cic. Att. 9. 13. 4. Hence Nauck at one time conjectured ὑβρίζειν for συρίζειν. The evidence of Aristophanes seems explicit enough, but it is worth remarking that Photius (l.c.) continues καὶ λαπήκτης (l. λαπίκτης) ὁ ψεύστης διὰ τοῦ κ ὡς σαλπίγκτης συρίγκτης. This may perhaps justify the guess that the grammarian's comment once ran: καὶ λαπίζειν τὸ ψεύδεσθαι διὰ τοῦ ζ ὡς σαλπίζειν συρίζειν, and that it was confused and corrupted by successive epitomizations. Mekler proposed to solve the difficulty by substituting τὸ Συρίζειν, for which he quoted Lucian de merc. cond. 10 ὑπὸ θυρωρῷ κακῶς Συρίζοντι ταττόμενον. But, if Συρίζειν is there rightly interpreted as equivalent to βαρβαρίζειν, it does not seem an appropriate gloss. Cohn in Jahrb. f. Philol. Suppl. XII 296 held that συρίζειν was ‘sine dubio corruptum.’
1063 Phot. lex. p. 219, 25 and Suid. s.v. ληκυθιστής· ὁ μικρόφωνος. οὕτως Σοφοκλῆς.

Meineke conjectured μακρόφωνος in place of μικρόφωνος, but it is not clear that he was right, or that L. and S. are correct in their rendering bawler. The origin of this view is to be found in schol. Ar. Ach. 589 κομπολακύθου]. . . ληκυθίζειν γὰρ τὸ μεῖζον βοᾶν καὶ ψοφεῖν. ἦχον γὰρ ἐπιτελεῖ καὶ ἡ λήκυθος, ἐπεὶ καὶ αὕτη πεφύσηται· πάντα γὰρ τὰ πεφυσημένα κόμπον ποιεῖ. But further search reveals that it was not so much the volume as the quality of the sound that was denoted by ληκυθίζειν etc., and that the central meaning is a hollow, false, affected sound. Hence Hesych. III p. 34 ληκυθιστής· κοιλόφωνος, explained by Phryn. praep. soph. p. 86, 9 (Bekk. anecd. p. 50, 8) ληκυθίζειν· ὁπόταν βούλωνται οἱ φωνασκοῦντες κοῖλον τὸ φθέγμα ποιεῖν, ὥσπερ εἰς ληκύθους προϊέμενοι. Cf. schol. Hephaest. p. 33, 10 G. (explaining ληκύθιον) ἢ διὰ τὸν βόμβον τὸν τραγικόν· βόμβος γὰρ γίνεται περὶ τὸ ληκύθιον ἐκ τοῦ ἐμπεριεχομένου αὐτῷ ἀέρος κινουμένου, ἢ ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἀνδρός, ἢ ὑπ᾿ ἄλλου· διὸ καὶ Καλλίμαχος (fr. 98c) μοῦσαν ληκύθειον τὴν τραγῳδίαν λέγει. So ληκυθισμός becomes a term of abuse for what is unreal and affected in speech: Plut. adu. Epic. 2, p. 1086 E. Anon. ap. Suid. s.v. ληκυθισμός· περιενεγκεῖν εὐστρόφως καὶ κεκλασμένως τὸν ληκυθισμὸν τῶν αἰσχρῶν καὶ γελοίων ᾀσμάτων. The application to the style of tragedy — or elevated literature — is familiar from Cic. Att. 1. 14. 3, Plin. ep. 1. 2, Hor. Α. Ρ. 97, Epist. 1. 3. 14. Strabo 609 contrasts θέσεις ληκυθίζειν with φιλοσοφεῖν πραγματικῶς, where the point is emptiness of substance. Thus it is by no means certain that the metaphor is derived from the laying on of colour taken from a paint-pot.
1064 Phryn. ecl. p. 187 (CLXIII R.) λίβανον λέγε τὸ δένδρον, τὸ δὲ θυμιώμενον λιβανωτόν, εἰ καὶ διὰ τὴν ποιητικὴν (ἄδειαν add. Lobeck) λίβανον καὶ τοῦτο Σοφοκλῆς λέγει.

λίβανος is used for frankincense (τὸ ποιούμενον ἀπὸ τοῦ ποιοῦντος) also in Eur. Bacch. 144 and other passages quoted in Lobeck's excellent note. So μέλισσα for μέλι in O.C. 481, fr. 155, ἐλέφας for ivory, πορφύρα for purple, χελώνη for tortoiseshell.

1065 Phot. lex. p. 227, 19 and Bachm. anecd. I p. 291, 20 λίτρα· ἦν μὲν καὶ νόμισμά τι. . . Σοφοκλῆς δὲ λιτροσκόπον φησὶ τὸν ἀργυραμοιβὸν ἀπὸ (ἐπὶ Bachm. anecd.) τοῦ νομίσματος. Cf. Hesych. III p. 45 λιτροσκόπους· ἀργυραμοιβούς, ἀπὸ τοῦ Σικελικοῦ νομίσματος, ὃ καλεῖται λίτρα.

The locus classicus for λίτρα is Pollux 4. 173 — 175, where Epicharmus and Sophron are quoted. It was a small silver coin current in Sicily, and said to be equivalent to an Aeginetan obol. It was also used as a weight, and corresponded to the Latin libra: see Dict. Ant. ΙΙ 69 a.
1066 Steph. Byz. p. 425, 3 Μαγνησία, πόλις παρὰ τῷ Μαιάνδρῳ καὶ χώρα · ...ὁ πολίτης Μάγνης...τὸ θηλυκὸν Μάγνησσα...καὶ Μαγνήτις παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ.
Besides λίθος μαγνήτις (fr. 800), ἵπποισι Μαγνητίδεσσιν occurs in Pind. Pyth. 2. 45, with reference to the Thessalian Magnesia.

1067 Phot. lex. p. 247, 17 μαρίλη (μαρινη cod.)· ἡ μεμαρασμένη ὕλη, καὶ <μαριλοκαύτας> τοὺς ἀνθρακευτάς. Σοφοκλῆς. μαριλοκαύτας was restored by Naber from Hesych. III p. 72 μαριλοκαυτῶν· ἀνθρακευτῶν· μαρίλη γὰρ τὸ ἀπόψημα τῶν ἀνθράκων.

The next gloss in Phot. is as follows: μαρίλη· ὁ χνοῦς τῶν ἀνθράκων· καὶ ἡ ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν ἀσβόλη. Similarly Suidas: μαρίλη. ἀμαυρὸν πῦρ· ὁ χνοῦς καὶ τὸ λεπτότατον τῶν ἀνθράκων. ῾χαλκεὺς οἷά τις | γέμων καπνοῦ <τε> καὶ μαρίλης᾿ (Com. fr. adesp. 443, III 492 Κ.). καὶ Κρατῖνος ἐν Ὥραις· (fr. 257, I 90 Κ.) ῾ἐφθάρη μαρίλης τὴν φάρυγα πλέαν ἔχων.᾿ ἡ ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνθράκων σποδιά. Then Suidas quotes Ar. Ach. 350, where the schol. explains μαρίλη as ἡ ἐξ ἀνθράκων τέφρα. Etym. Gud. p. 379, 35 betrays a later date: μαρίλη σημαίνει τὴν κόνιν τὴν γινομένην ἐκ τοῦ κατασβέννυσθαι τοὺς κάρβωνας. Themistius has appropriated the first quotation in Suidas: or. 21 p. 298, 10 ἀνθρακέως τινὸς ἢ σιδηρέως, καπνοῦ γέμοντος καὶ μαρίλης. It is clear from all this that μαρίλη means coal-dust, and it is difficult to resist the impression that μαριλοκαύτης, which is an inexact substitute for ἀνθρακεύς (ευτής), has a comic—or at least a contemptuous—innuendo. Cf. Ar. Ach. 609 ἐτεόν, ὦ Μαριλάδη—‘Coaly.’ μαρίλη also occurs in Hipponax fr. 59. Wilamowitz found a place for the word in the Ichneutae: see fr. 314, 34.

1068 Pollux 3. 45 ὁ δὲ μέλλων γαμεῖν μελλονύμφιος ὑπ᾽ ἐνίων ἐκλήθη... καὶ ἡ μέλλουσα γαμεῖσθαι μελλονύμφη. βέλτιον δ᾽ ὡς Σοφοκλῆς ὠνόμασεν, ῾τῆς μελλογάμου᾿ (Ant. 627)...μελλόποσιν δὲ τὸν ἄνδρα ὠνόμασεν. Cf. Hesych. III p. 88 μελλέποσις· ὁ μέλλων ἀνὴρ γίνεσθαι.

There is the same uncertainty as to the vowel in μελλόγαμος and μελλέγαμος, μελλόπταρμος and μελλέπταρμος, and there is no reason for regarding one form as more legitimate or earlier than the other. In Pollux I. 21 Bethe adopts βλεπεδαίμων, but the MSS vary between βλεπεδαίμων, βλεπιδαίμων, and βλεποδαίμων. Lobeck, Phryn. p. 768, holds that the form in ε ‘veluti longi temporis praescriptione possessionem obtinet,’ whereas that in ο ‘magis publica et praesente nota signata est.’ Jebb (on El. 72 at p. 207) distinguishes ἀρχε as a verbal stem from ἀρχο as a nominal; but this cannot apply to μελλε μελλο, and is not historically correct. According to Brugmann, wherever a real verbal stem appears as the first member of a compound, it is a new formation, called into existence by conscious association with the verbal stem of a nominal element in an old inherited compound. φιλόξενος, by association with φιλεῖν, produced μισόξενος. Thus, μελλε μελλο are analogues of ἀρχε ἀρχο, which are legitimate nominal components. Whether the ε was derived ultimately from an Indo-European stem, or was a Greek innovation when the first component was associated with a verb (ἀρχε from ἄρχει), has not been determined: see Brugmann, Comp. Gr. II pp. 46, 51 Eng. tr.

1069 Eustath. Il. p. 877, 59 Σοφοκλῆς δέ, φησί (sc. Aristophanes of Byzantium), δόξειεν ἄν που καὶ τὰ θηρία πάντα μῆλα καλεῖν· τὸν γοῦν Ἀχιλλέα τραφῆναί φησιν ἐν τῷ Πηλίῳ πᾶν μῆλον θηρῶντα. This is repeated by Eustath. Od. p. 1648 fin.

The suggestion that this fragment belongs to the Ἀχιλλέως Ἐρασταί seems to have been first made by Hartung: see on fr. 154. In the words immediately preceding Aristophanes was mentioned as attributing to Simonides (fr. 28) the use of μᾶλον (μῆλον) and πρόβατον to signify βοῦν ἄρρενα, and as quoting the line μῆλα, βόας κεραοὺς καὶ ὄϊς καὶ πίονας αἶγας. We are, therefore, justified in believing that the gloss which appears in Phot. lex. p. 265, 26, Etym. Μ. p. 584, 2, and Suid. μῆλα· πάντα τὰ τετράποδα· ὅθεν καὶ πᾶσα βύρσα μηλωτὴ καλεῖται goes back to an Alexandrian source. Similarly Hesych. III p. 103 μῆλα· κοινῶς μὲν πάντα τὰ τετράποδα· ... κατ᾿ ἐπικράτειαν δὲ τὰ πρόβατα καὶ αἶγες. Phryn. praep. soph. p. 27, 6, Apollon. lex. Hom. p. 458. The wider meaning which μῆλον sometimes bore (cf. the gradual restriction of our ‘cattle’) is not entirely unknown in extant literature (e.g. Pind. Ol. 7. 63). H. refers to Aesch. fr. 158 σπείρω δ’ ἄρουραν δώδεχ᾿ ἡμερῶν ὁδόν, | Βερέκυντα χῶρον, ἔνθ᾿ Ἀδραστείας ἕδος, | Ἴδης τε μυκηθμοῖσι καὶ βρυχήμασιν | ἕρπουσι μήλων πᾶν ὀρεχθεύει πέδον: see his explanation of this passage in C. R. XVI 435. It appears that μηλοσφαγεῖν was the generic term for sacrificing victims, whether sheep or oxen: Ar. Au. 1232 μηλοσφαγεῖν τε βουθύτοις ἐπ’ ἐσχάραις. Thus, Weil and Herwerden proposed to restore μηλοσφαγοῦντες for ταυροσφαγοῦντες in Aesch. Theb. 43 from the parody in Ar. Lys. 188 εἰς ἀσπίδ᾿ ὥσπερ φασὶν Αἰσχύλος ποτέ, | μηλοσφαγούσας, where the schol. remarks ἀντὶ τοῦ ταυροσφαγούσας μηλοσφαγούσας εἶπεν, εἰ μὴ ἄρα μῆλα πάντα τὰ τετράποδα. Similarly, it is no valid argument against the adoption of βούτας in Aesch. Ag. 718 ff. (ἔθρεψεν δὲ λέοντος ἶνιν δόμοις ἀγάλακτα βούτας ἀνὴρ φιλόμαστον) to call attention to μηλοφόνοισιν ἄταις in v. 731, although Wilamowitz in C.R. XX 446 speaks as if Headlam, in adopting it, had ignored this consideration. — Aristophanes quotes the substance of Sophocles' text without giving the actual words, and some might be inclined to add to the lemma at least as much as ἐν τῷ Πηλίῳ...πᾶν...θηρῶντα.
1070 Phot. lex. p. 269, 8 μιαίνεσθαι καὶ ἐκμιαίνεσθαι· τὸ ὀνειρώττειν· Σοφοκλῆς.

Naber concluded that the citation of Sophocles was an error, and that his name should be transferred to the preceding gloss μηχανορράφος (O.T. 387). This is a plausible conjecture, and Nauck in his second edition was persuaded by it to remove the present fragment from his collection (TGF2 p. xx). But we are hardly justified in rejecting the tradition, since Sophocles may have used μιαίνεσθαι in a satyr-play with the meaning stated. The explanation of the gloss will be found in Ar. Ran. 753 with the schol., or in Hor. Sat. 1. 5. 84. Inasmuch as Aristophanes employed the compound verb, it may be that we should refer μιαίνεσθαι (rather than ἐκμιαίνεσθαι) to Sophocles, and that Σοφοκλῆς <καὶ Ἀριστοφάνης> was in the original gloss.

1071 Pollux 3. 10 ὁμοίως δὲ μήτηρ ἡ τεκοῦσα, ἡ ὠδίνουσα, ἡ γεννησαμένη ὁ Πλάτων (Menex. 237 Ε), ἡ γεννήσασα ὡς Σοφοκλῆς, ἡ μαστὸν ἐπισχοῦσα, ἡ θηλάσασα. I have followed the text of Bethe, who in connecting the words ἡ γεννήσασα with Sophocles, adopts the reading of the codices FS, in preference to that of BC. The latter give the words in the order ἡ μαστὸν ἐπισχοῦσα ὡς Σοφοκλῆς, ἡ θηλάσασα. However that may be, the editors have made a strange mistake in citing the passage of Pollux as an authority for the use of μήτηρ by Sophocles in a particular sense, that of foster-mother, according to the reading which they adopted. For it is patent that Pollux compiled a list of expressions used by various authors which were synonymous with μήτηρ, and that ἡ γεννήσασα (or ἡ μαστὸν ἐπισχοῦσα) is to be attributed to Sophocles.
The only instance in tragedy of γεννᾶν applied to the mother is Aesch. Suppl. 48, but it is commonly so used in later Greek.

1072 Etym. Μ. p. 595, 1 μύνδος (μύνδιος Sorb.) ἰχθῦς, Σοφοκλῆς, ὁ μὴ αὐδῶν. ὅθεν καὶ ἔλλοψ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐλλιπῆ τὴν ὄπα ἔχειν. Cod. F has μῦνδος ὁ μὴ αὐδῶν, Σοφοκλῆς μῦνδος ἰχθύς. Etym. Gud. p. 400, 35 μῦνδος ὁ μὴ αὐδῶν· Σοφοκλῆς μύνδος ὁ μὴ αὐδῶν.

Sophocles is apparently quoted for the sense dumb, but some scholars consider that the etymologer cited him as using μυνδός = ἰχθύς. See Schneider on Callim. fr. 260 μυνδότεροι νεπόδων. Lycophr. 1375 ἔλλοπος μυνδοῦ δίκην. Bergk, on the strength of this evidence, wished to restore χορὸς δὲ μυνδῶν ἰχθύων in fr. 762, I. On the other hand, van Leeuwen suggested that the name of Sophocles was wrongly introduced into the text of the Etym. M. by someone who remembered Ai. 1297. For the accentuation see Chandler, § 367. Wecklein thinks that μυνδός is not a genuine word, but arose from a corruption of δ' ἀναύδων to δὲ μυνδῶν in fr. 762.
1073 Pollux 7. 30 καταξῆναι Πλάτων ὁ κωμικός (fr. 245, 1 664 Κ.), ὁ δὲ φιλόσοφος Πλάτων καὶ τέχνην ξαντικήν (polit. 282 A), Σοφοκλῆς δὲ ξάσμα.
Dindorf conjectured ξάσματι for φάσματι in Trach. 838, to which passage he thinks Pollux was alluding.
1074 Phot. lex. p. 312, 22 ξυνῶνα· τὸν κοινωνόν. Σοφοκλῆς.

H. writes: ‘This is the true Attic form, though occurring only here.’ He has discussed the type of formation in an article on τοκέων in C. R. XV 401 ff., where he gives a list of the dialectical varieties affecting the small class of words in question. These words are the representatives of an old formation (with
suffix ᾱƑον or ᾱƑων), which ceased at an early date to be productive. Its appearance in literature is rare, and apt to be due to deliberate archaism. Hence the occurrence of certain anomalies is not easy to explain. (1) The accentuation of λυμεών, ἀπατεών, πορθεών )( τοκέων, ξυνέων is treated by Postgate (in C. R. XV 403) as an Attic innovation on the analogy of the κενεών, οἰνεών class (Lobeck, Phryn. p. 166). (2) The vagaries of εων ων are puzzling. Certainly ων was not universal in Attic, for there is no trace of contraction in the three words which alone—proper names apart—can be described as current, viz. ὀργεών, λυμεών, ἀπατεών. On the other hand, εων was often merely graphic (εων: cf. ἅλα ξυνεῶνα of Alex. Aetolus [v. 15] ap. Parthen. 14) in Ionic (Weir Smyth, p. 258); and in Archil. fr. 86, 2 we actually find ξυνωνίην. Moreover in Doric contraction is attested by Pindar's κοινάν (Pyth. 3. 28) and ξυνάν (Nem. 5. 27); and κοινωνός and its derivatives (cf. κοινανέω) prove the antiquity of the contracting tendency. The evidence is not sufficiently uniform to condemn Scaliger's κοινεῶν᾿ ἐκλῄζομεν, adopted by Murray, in Eur. Her. 340: Euripides may have had literary reasons for introducing such a form, although we cannot identify them. Whether these variations are ultimately due to accent-position, producing doublets, one or the other of which, if not changed by analogy, survived in certain conditions, is a question for philologists to determine.
1075 Phot. lex. p. 326, 13 ὀκριάζων· τραχυνόμενος. Σοφοκλῆς. Also in Hesych. III p. 193, but without the author's name. M. Schmidt quotes from Theognostus p. 23, 25 the error οἱριάζων, τραχυνόμενος.

We may suppose that Sophocles copied Hom. σ 33 οὐδοῦ ἐπὶ ξεστοῦ πανθυμαδὸν ὀκριόωντο, explained by schol. BHQ ἐτραχύνοντο, ἠγριαίνοντο, and by schol. V ἐτραχύνοντο, διεφέροντο, διεπληκτίζοντο. Similarly Apollon. lex. p. 494 ὀκριόωντο. μεταφορικῶς ἐβαρύνοντο, ἐτραχύνοντο κατὰ τὴν ψυχήν.
1076 Phot. lex. p. 329, 15 ὁλοσπάδες· ὅλαι καταπινόμεναι καὶ κατασπώμεναι. Σοφοκλῆς. Cf. Hesych. III p. 199 ὁλοσπαδεῖς· ὅλαι κατασπώμεναι καὶ καταπινόμεναι.

ὁλοσπάς was perhaps an epithet of ἄμυστις (schol. Ar. Ach. 1229 τὴν ἀθρόαν πόσιν οὕτως ἔλεγον). For σπᾶν cf. Eur. Cycl. 417 ἐδέξατ᾿ ἔσπασέν τ᾿ ἄμυστιν ἑλκύσας, ib. 571 συνεκθανεῖν δὲ σπῶντα χρὴ τῷ πώματι. The metaphor is quite natural, as our draught shows: Paley on Cycl. 572 gives an absurd explanation, as if the verb was applied to the cup rather than to its contents.
1077 Phot. lex. p. 346, 23 ὀρθόφρων· ἀνατεταμένος καὶ μετέωρος ταῖς φρεσίν. οὕτως Σοφοκλῆς. Hesych. III p. 219 ὀρθόφρων· ἀνατεταμένας φρένας ἔχων, ἢ ὀρθάς. μετέωρος.

It appears that the meaning is ‘with spirit erect—excited.’ The evidence of the compound is interesting, for ὀρθός is not known to occur in this sense before the fourth century: Isocr. 5. 70 (οἵαν) αἰσθάνῃ δὲ τὴν Ἑλλάδα πᾶσαν ὀρθὴν οὖσαν ἐφ᾿ οἷς σὺ τυγχάνεις εἰσηγούμενος, 16. 7 ὀρθῆς δὲ τῆς
πόλεως γενομένης διὰ τὸ μέγεθος τῶν αἰτιῶν, Lycurg. 39 ὀρθὴ δ’ ἦν ἡ πόλις ἐπὶ τοῖς συμβεβηκόσιν, Hyperid. fr. 39 K. ὀρθῆς δὲ τῆς πόλεως οὔσης ἐπὶ τούτοις [= κεκινημένης]. Plut. Demosth. 18, 3 ὀρθὴν δὲ τὴν Ἑλλάδα γενέσθαι καὶ συνεξαναστῆναι πρὸς τὸ μέλλον. The similarity of these passages, and others quoted by the lexicons from Polyb. and Diod., is remarkable: slightly different is Polyb. 28. 17. 11 ὀρθοὶ καὶ μετέωροι ταῖς διανοίαις ἐγενήθησαν οἱ Ῥόδιοι πάντες. Philostr. vit. Apoll. 2. 36. Contrast Ο.Τ. 528.
1078 Phot. lex. p. 361, 16 οὐράν· αἰδοῖον. Σοφοκλῆς. Hesych. III p. 241 οὐρά· ἡ κέρκος, καὶ τὸ αἰδοῖον.
κέρκος is used similarly in Ar. Ach. 785, Lys. 239, and cauda in Cic. fam. 9. 22. 2, Hor. Sat. 1. 2. 45. See also Eustath. Od. p. 1968, 41.
1079 Phot. lex. p. 363, 19 ὄφελμα· αὔξημα. Σοφοκλῆς. Cf. Hesych. III p. 246 ὄφελμα· αὔξημα. κάλυμμα. κάλλυντρον.

The explanation κάλλυντρον refers to the fact that ὄφελμα is used by Hipponax in the sense of a broom (fr. 51 ἄνθρωπον εὗρε τὴν στέγην ὀφέλλοντα | —οὐ γὰρ παρῆν ὄφελμα—πυθμένι στοιβῆς); but κάλυμμα is obscure. Perhaps we should read κάλλυσμα, ‘sweepings’: see Herwerden, Lex. suppl. s.v.
1080 Pollux 10. 50 πέλλυτρα· οὕτω γὰρ τὰ ποδεῖα Σοφοκλῆς καλεῖ.

It is thought that Sophocles is here cited in error for Aeschylus, to whom Pollux twice elsewhere (2. 196, 7. 91) ascribes the word πέλλυτρα (fr. 259). A warm kind of sock or stocking is meant: see Dict. Ant. II 932 b.
1081 Pollux 7. 203 κυβεία...πεττεία ἢ πεσσεία, ὡς Σοφοκλῆς.
The word πεσσεία probably occurred in the Nauplius or the Palamedes. For the distinction between κυβεία and πεσσεία see on frs. 429 and 947.

1082 Phryn. praep. soph. p. 36, 1 (Bekk. anecd. p. 21, 27) αἰκάλλοντες· σημαίνει τὸ σαίνοντες, ὅπερ οἱ κύνες ποιοῦσιν. ὁ μέντοι Σοφοκλῆς καὶ προσσαίνειν. χρῶ οὖν, εἰ μὲν φιλοτίμως, τῷ αἰκάλλειν, εἰ δὲ πολιτικῶς, τῷ προσσαίνειν.

Wecklein thinks that Sophocles is mentioned in error for Aeschylus, by whom προσσαίνειν is used twice (Prom. 861, Ag. 1665). It occurs also in Eur. Hipp. 863. αἰκάλλω is only found in Eur. Andr. 630, unless Musgrave's correction is accepted in O. T. 597. In Athen. 99 Ε δέον αἰκάλλειν μᾶλλον καὶ προσσαίνειν τοῖς συνδείπνοις no distinction is apparent, but Phrynichus treats αἰκάλλειν as the more elevated and poetic word: for φιλοτίμως cf. schol. Ai. 701. It might be argued that αἰκάλλοντες is also quoted from Sophocles, or, at any rate, that he used αἰκάλλειν (so apparently de Borries) of human wheedling. But neither inference is necessary; for Phrynichus may have meant that though writing in the elevated style Sophocles nevertheless employed προσσαίνειν.
1083 Phot. lex. p. 470, 3 πτέρυγας· τὰ πηδάλια. Σοφοκλῆς.

The statement is confirmed by Hesych. III p. 403 πτέρυγες· εὐθυντῆρες, τὰ πηδάλια...δηλοῖ δὲ καὶ τῶν πηδαλίων τὰ πλατέα καὶ τὰ χείλη. Thus πτέρυξ was used specifically for the blade or tip of the paddle: Pollux 1. 90 τὸ δὲ τελευταῖον (τοῦ πηδαλίου) πτερύγιον. πτερόν was applied both to oars and sails, but not, so far as we know, to the rudder, although Pflugk suggested this interpretation for Eur. Hel. 147 νεὼς στείλαιμ᾽ ἂν οὔριον πτερόν.

1084 Eustath. Il. p. 948, 19 ὅτι δὲ τὸ πτύον καὶ πτέον ἔλεγον οἱ Ἀττικοὶ ὕστερον Αἴλιος Διονύσιός φησιν (fr. 288 Schw.). ἕτερος δέ τις λέγει· πτέον οἱ ἄλλοι, πτύον δὲ Σοφοκλῆς ἀκολουθῶν δηλαδὴ τῷ ποιητῇ (Ν 588).
That the later or Attic form was πτέον is recorded also by Phot. lex. p. 469, 22, Pollux 1. 245, 10. 128.
1085 Etym. Μ. p. 695, 50 πύγαργος· εἶδος ἀετοῦ· Σοφοκλῆς ἐπὶ τοῦ δειλοῦ, ἀπὸ τῆς λευκῆς πυγῆς, ὥσπερ ἐναντίως μελάμπυγος ἀπὸ τῆς ἰσχυρᾶς (leg. ἐπὶ τοῦ ἰσχυροῦ). See also schol. Lycophr. 91.

Sophocles seems to have applied the word metaphorically to a coward, and this sense probably arose without reference to any observation of the eagle's disposition, ὅτι τοὺς λευκοπύγους ὡς γυναικώδεις ἐκωμῴδουν, as the schol. on Ar. Lys. 802 remarks. In Aesch. Ag. 117 two eagles appeared, ὁ κελαινός, ὁ δ᾽ ἐξόπιν ἀργᾷς, and the latter was identified by Calchas with the craven-hearted Menelaus (see Headlam on 125 f.). Holzinger on Lycophr. 90 supposes that Paris is there called πύγαργος because of his μαχλοσύνη, but Paris also was taunted with cowardice (Hom. A 390). On the other hand for μελάμπυγος, the traditional epithet of Heracles, see Zenob. 5. 10 (Paroem. I 119) μὴ σύ γε μελαμπύγου τύχοις. Eubul. fr. 61, II 185 Κ. ἐγὼ δὲ γ᾽ εἰμὶ τῶν μελαμπύγων ἔτι. Additional evidence is collected by Blaydes on Ar. Lys. l.c. μελάμπυγος τε τοῖς ἐχθροῖς ἅπασιν.
1086 Strabo 364 Σοφοκλῆς δὲ καὶ Ἴων (fr. 66) τὸ ῥᾴδιον ῥᾴ (ῥᾶ A and Epit.), Ἐπίχαρμος δὲ τὸ λίαν λῖ (fr. 223 K.). Eustath. Il. p. 295, 5 καὶ Σοφοκλῆς τὸ ῥᾴδιον ῥᾴ.

Strabo introduces ῥᾴ as an illustration of apocope in the course of a list of similar examples. But several of these, such as the Homeric κρῖ and δῶ (for which see Brugmann, II 488, III 102), as well as ῥᾴ itself, are beside the mark. The grammarians attributed the invention of ἀπότρωκτον, as they called it, to Epicharmus (Hesych. I p. 135 ἄλφι etc.); and Philetas and Euphorion may have copied him. Nauck writes ῥᾶ, and regards it as a contraction of the Homeric ῥέα; but Bergk (PLG III 53), commenting on Alcm. fr. 42 τίς δ' ἄν, τίς ποκα ῥὰ ἄλλω νόον ἀνδρὸς ἐνίσποι; reverted to the traditional form, which he regarded as a neut. acc. of PAIC used adverbially. This would agree well enough with ῥηΐδιος, ῥᾷον, ῥηΐτερος etc. It should be added that the Alexandrian grammarians, although they wrongly treated ῥᾴ as shortened from ῥᾴδιον, deliberately rejected the derivation from ῥέα, because (1) the accentuation ought then to be, but was not, ῥᾶ; (2) tradition invariably supported the ι; (3) the Aeolic form would not then be βρᾴ. See Apollon. Dysc. ap. Bekk. anecd. p. 566 f., abbreviated in Etym. M. p. 700, 26 (cf. ib. p. 210, 43). The origin of the Homeric ῥέα is another matter. Leaf on P 462 says that the original forms of ῥέα and ῥεῖα were ϝρᾶ and ϝρεῖα (=ῥηια), but does not explain why ῥέα was written. Meyer wrote ϝρᾶ wherever the word was monosyllabic. Osthoff connected ῥᾴων (= ῥᾶσίων) with the Lat. rarior.

1087 Phot. lex. p. 480, 15 Ῥαικούς· οἱ βάρβαροι τοὺς Ἕλληνας. Σοφοκλῆς τῇ λέξει κέχρηται. But the testimony of Eustath. Il. p. 890, 14 is to the opposite effect: οὓς (sc. Γραικούς) ἡ μὲν συνήθεια καὶ Σοφοκλῆς δέ που κατὰ τοὺς παλαιοὺς καὶ ὁ Λυκόφρων δὲ διὰ τοῦ ἐν ἀρχῇ Γ προφέρουσιν ἐπὶ Ἑλλήνων, οἱ βάρβαροι δὲ Ῥαικοὺς φασὶ δίχα τοῦ Γ, ὡς ἐν παλαιῷ εὕρηται λεξικῷ ῥητορικῷ (Ael. et Paus. fr. 369 Schwabe). Probably Eustathius is nearer to the original statement than Photius. Suid. Ῥαικός· ὁ Ῥωμαῖος is still further degraded. However, even the statement as it appears in Eustathius is open to suspicion, and is possibly merely an echo of fr. 518, where see note. But though it is improbable that it was used by Sophocles, we should be wrong to deny altogether the existence of Ῥαικός. Cf. Hesych. III p. 419 Ῥαικός· Ἕλλην. Ῥωμαῖοι δὲ τὸ γ προσθέντες Γραικόν φασι, ib. p. 424 Ῥᾶχος· Ἕλλην, an error for Ῥαικός. Strabo 231 mentions Rhaeci as inhabitants of Latium. R. Schneider, Bodleiana, p. 6, restored it in Cramer, anecd. Oxon. I p. 11, 2. Etym. M. p. 239, 15 seeks a derivation from ῥαίω, — διὰ τὴν κατὰ πολὺ ἀνδρείαν; p. 701, 14. It is especially remarkable to find the word attributed to Epicharmus (fr. 184 Kaibel).
1088 Etym. M. p. 702, 54 = Etym. Gud. p. 491, 3 παρὰ δὲ Σοφοκλεῖ ῥαχία λέγεται ἡ τοῦ ὄρους.

Smyth, Ionic Dialect, p. 179, rejects the popular derivation of ῥηχίη (ῥαχία) from ῥήγνυμι on the ground that ῥήγνυμι has pan-Hellenic η, and connects it with ῥάχις. His argument is strengthened by
this use of ῥαχία which is identical with that of ῥάχις in Hdt. 3. 54 ἐπὶ τῆς ῥάχιος τοῦ οὔρεος. Smyth illustrates the application to natural objects of the names given to parts of the body by quoting arm of the sea, shoulder of the mountain, πολυδειρὰς Ὄλυμπος. Closer to the point is Choeril. fr. 2 (p. 719 N.2) <λίθοισι> γῆς ὀστοῖσιν ἐγχριμφθεὶς πόδα. The word arête is employed by mountaineers to describe a sharp edge of rock. Cf. Hesych. I p. 395 βρακίας· τραχεῖς τόπους.
1089 Phot. lex. p. 485, 10 Ῥειτά· ἐν Ἐλευσῖνι δύο ναμάτια φερόμενα ἐκ μιᾶς πηγῆς καλούμενα ῥειτά. οὕτως Σοφοκλῆς.

The following gloss is ῥειτῶν τόπος· ἱερῶν ῥευμάτων, which Wagner and Ellendt suppose to contain the words of Sophocles. Blaydes has a similar notion, that Sophocles wrote Ῥειτῶν ἱερῶν or Ῥειτῶν ῥευμάτων. The Gale ms points after ῥειτῶν: should we not read Ῥειτόν (or Ῥειτοί)· τόπος ἱερῶν ῥευμάτων? Anyhow, the natural inference is merely that Sophocles is quoted for the use of Ῥειτά. Elsewhere we find the form Ῥεῖτοι (or Ῥῖτοι), for which see M. Schmidt on Hesych. III p. 425. The description of Pausan. 1. 38. 1 is rendered by Frazer: 'What are called the Rhiti only resemble rivers in that they flow, for their water is salt. One might suppose that they flow underground from the Chalcidian Euripus, falling into a lower sea. The Rhiti are said to be sacred to the Maid and Demeter; and the priests alone are allowed to catch the fish in them.' See also Frazer's note in vol. II p. 486. The first skirmish in the Peloponnesian war, in which the Athenian cavalry was defeated, took place at Rhiti (Thuc. 2. 19). Welcker referred this fr. to the Triptolemus.
1090 Phot. lex. p. 488, 12 ῥήτωρ· συνήγορος, δικολόγος. καὶ ὁ τὴν ἰδίαν ἀποφαίνων γνώμην κριτής, παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ.

The same in Cramer, anecd. Par. IV p. 174, 25, Suid. s.v., and, without the reference to Sophocles, Hesych. III p. 428. This is one of the earliest occurrences of ῥήτωρ, which is used quite generally in Eur. Hec. 126 δισσῶν μύθων ῥήτορες ἦσαν. No doubt in Soph. also it bore the same meaning.
1091 Phot. lex. p. 488, 22 ῥικνός· ὁ πεφρικώς, παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ.

The ordinary meaning of ῥικνός is bent or shrivelled. Hesych. III p. 429 has the glosses ῥιγνόν· ῥιγεδανόν, φρικῶδες, and ῥικνὴν ὄψιν· φρικτήν, but without giving any authority. Naber conjectured that the latter gloss should be attributed to Sophocles; but, whereas Photius cites Sophocles for the sense shivering, Hesych. seems to understand ῥικνὴν ὄψιν as contorted and so terrible. There is no evidence to clear up the difficulty. For ῥικνοῦσθαι see on fr. 316.
1092 Apollon. lex. Hom. p. 140, 2 σάκος· ἀσπίς. ἀφ' οὗ καὶ οἱ νεώτεροι σακτὴν τὴν ὅλην πανοπλίαν λέγουσι, ὡς Σοφοκλῆς.

σάγη = harness; and the context would limit it to armour, as in Aesch. Pers. 243, Eur. Her. 188. Villoison's correction is confirmed by Hesych. IV p. 2 σάγη· ἡ ὅλη πανοπλία. Schol. Aesch. Theb. 117 δορυσσόοις σάγαις] πολεμικαῖς πανοπλίαις. Schol. ibid. 378 σάγαις] πανοπλίαις. Etym. M. p. 707, 23, 37 derives σάγμα and σάκος from σάγη τουτέστιν ἀσπίς. Sophocles employs πανσαγία in Ant. 106.

1093 Phot. lex. p. 497, 12 = Bachm. anecd. I p. 361, 20 σαλάβην· Σοφοκλῆς τὴν ὀπήν. Phot. lex. p. 497, 22 σαλάμβη· ὀπή, καπνοδόκη. οὕτως Σοφοκλῆς. Hesych. IV p. 5 σαλάμβη· ἡ ὀπή, δι᾿ ἧς τὸ σέλας βαίνει. ἢ πύλη, καπνοδόχη θυρίς. Μ. Schmidt was the first to connect with these glosses Eustath. Od. p. 1908, 40 (Ael. Dion. et Paus. fr. 431 Schw.) σέλας οὐ μόνον πυρός, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡλίου· ὅθεν παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ <σαλάμβη> ἡ ὀπή, ὡς ἐν ῥητορικῷ εὕρηται λεξικῷ, παρὰ τὸ σέλας, φασίν, ἐμβιβάζειν, where the word has been accidentally lost.

That σαλάμβη is the correct form of the word appears from Lycophr. 98 δισσὰς σαλάμβας κἀπὶ Γυθίου πλάκας, where Tzetzes says: σαλάμβαι αἱ θύραι λέγονται παρὰ τὸ ἐν σάλῳ βαίνειν, ἢ παρὰ τὸ σείειν καὶ λαμβάνειν τοὺς βαίνοντας. A similar note quoting Lycophron occurs in Etym. M. p. 707, 45. See also Etym. Gud. p. 267, 17 ἔνιοι δὲ τὰς θύρας σαλάμας (qu. σαλάμβας) καλοῦσιν, ἀπὸ τοῦ σέλας βάλλειν ἀνοιγομένας, ἢ δι' ὧν τὸ σέλας βαίνει. Orion p. 148, 1 σαλάμβη. ἡ θυρὶς ἡ ἐν σάλῳ οὖσα, ἢ παρὰ τὸ σέλας βαίνειν δι' αὐτῆς. The etymology of the word is unknown, but G. Meyer (Gr. Gram. 298) wished to connect it with the O.N. sváela 'smoke.' The nasal in the ending may be due to the analogy of ἴαμβος : ἰαίνω etc., just as χιλιόμβη follows ἑκατόμβη. So Sturtevant (Class. Phil. V 341 f.), who also points out that with certain exceptions nearly all the words with the suffix βη, βης, βος 'apply to persons or things of little worth or dignity, and more than half of them imply disapproval or contempt.'
1094 Phot. lex. p. 511, 15 = Bachm. anecd. I p. 364, 9 σίκλος (σίγλος Bachm. anecd.) καὶ τὸ ἐνώτιον, καὶ σταθμὸς βαρβαρικὸς δυνάμενος ὀκτὼ ὀβολοὺς Ἀττικούς. οὕτως Σοφοκλῆς.

σίκλος (or σίγλος) was a transliteration of the Hebrew shekel, which varied in weight in different localities. Naber and others consider that the reference to Sophocles is a mistake, and that Xen. anab. 1. 5. 6 was originally in its place. I agree with Ellendt that, if Sophocles used the word at all, it probably bore the sense 'ear-ring,' which seems rather to belong to the form σίγλης. Pollux 5. 97 calls σίγλης a Dorian word. The grammarians seem to have confused σίγλης and σίκλος (σίγλος). Cf. Hesych. s.vv. σίκλαι, σίγλαι, σίγλον.
1095 Steph. Byz. p. 9, 15 s.v. Ἄβροι· βαρύνεται δὲ ὡς Κίμβροι, οὕς τινες φασὶ Κιμμερίους, Σκόμβροι, καὶ οὗτοι ἔθνος, ὡς Σοφοκλῆς. Cf. Hesych. IV p. 48 Σκόμβροι· Θρᾴκιον ἔθνος.

Meineke in his index referred this statement to Sophocles the commentator on Apollonius Rhodius, but Lenz (Herodian, p. CCXXIV) agrees with Nauck on the ground that there is nothing about the Σκόμβροι in the scholia to Apollonius. For the mountain Σκόμβρος, part of the Balkan range to the south of Sofia, see Thuc. 2. 96.

1096 Schol. Hom. Φ 220 (Ox. Pap. II p. 66, col. xi 7) στεινόμενος νεκύεσσι] στενοχωρούμενος· παρὰ ταῦτα Ἀλκαῖος ῾στένω μὰν Ξάνθω ῥόος ἐς θάλασσαν ἵκανε,᾿ καὶ ἐν Ὀδυσσείᾳ (σ 385) ῾αἶψά κέ τοι τὰ θύρετρα καὶ εὐρέα περ μάλ᾿ ἐόντα στείνοιτο,᾿ οὐχ ὡς Σοφοκλῆς στενάζοι.

Grenfell and Hunt inferred that Sophocles must have paraphrased the passage in the Odyssey, and suggested that he did so in the Ἀχαιῶν σύλλογος. The latter view can no longer be supported (I p. 94, II p. 198), and it is by no means clear that the editors’ inference is correct. For the comment is too brief to be free from obscurity. Thus it might mean: (1) ‘In the Odyssey στείνοιτο is equivalent to στενοχωροῖτο, not, as in Sophocles, to στενάζοι.’ So Wilamowitz (GGA 1900 p. 42), who remarked that, in using στείνεσθαι for στένεσθαι, Sophocles gave yet another example of his tendency to Ionism. Or (2) ‘στείνοιτο be it observed — not στενάζοι, the word which Sophocles uses in a similar case.’ On the whole, I agree with Mekler (Jahresb. CXXIX 31) that this is the more natural interpretation of the scholium, and it is altogether unnecessary to conclude that Sophocles used the phrase θύρα στενάζει or the like in connexion with a reproduction of the scene from the Odyssey. There remains the question whether he meant by it is thronged, as the scholiast implies, or simply creaks (under the pressure of a crowd forcing its way through). The latter is to be preferred, and we should compare Hom. φ 48 τὰ δ’ ἀνέβραχεν ἠύτε ταῦρος | βοσκόμενος λειμῶνι· τόσ᾿ ἔβραχε καλὰ θύρετρα | πληγέντα κληῖδι, πετάσθησαν δέ οἱ ὦκα, or Ap. Rhod. 4. 42 θυρέων ὑπόειξαν ὀχῆες, | ὠκείαις ἄψορροι ἀναθρῴσκοντες ἀοιδαῖς. Ar. Ach. 548 στοᾶς στεναχούσης would be a closer parallel, if we could accept the scholiast's interpretation. I suspect that the author of [Theocr.] 25. 97 στείνοντο δὲ πίονες ἀγροὶ μυκηθμῷ purposely availed himself of the etymological association with στένω, as on the other hand Qu. 8. 88 ἐπέστενε δ᾿ αἶα νέκυσσι unquestionably uses ἐπιστένω in the sense of στείνεσθαι (cf. 7. 100, 9. 161).
1097 στιβάδα ποιούμενος Burges : στιβαδοποιούμενος L
1097 Schol. Soph. Phil. 1108 οὐ φορβὰν ἔτι προσφέρων] ἀντὶ προσφερόμενος. ἐνίοτε δὲ ἔμπαλίν φησι διακονούμενος ἀντὶ τοῦ διακονῶν καὶ στιβαδοποιούμενος ἀντὶ στιβάδα ποιῶν (στιβαδοποιῶν Lasc.).

If Sophocles used στιβαδοποιεῖσθαι, the schol. might have regarded it as improperly substituted for στιβαδοποιεῖν, since his parallels are equally unconvincing (for Phil. 1108 see Jebb's n.), and the fluctuation of voice can be illustrated by
the usage of παιδοποιεῖν. But στιβαδοποιεῖσθαι was a scholiastic word (schol. Theocr. 4. 25), and it is much more likely that Sophocles wrote στιβάδα ποιούμενος, as Burges suggested, more particularly since στιβάδα ποιῶν has been ascertained to be the reading of L. Lobeck, Phryn. p. 200, points out that Thuc. 7. 39 has ἀριστοποιεῖσθαι followed by ἄριστον ποιεῖσθαι in c. 40. For the use of the middle (‘to make for oneself’) cf. Ar. Pac. 288 ἐγὼ δὲ δοίδυκ᾿ εἰσιὼν ποήσομαι. The schol.'s διακονούμενος is generally supposed to be an inexact reference to Phil. 287, but the inference is far from certain.
1098 στομήρη FS Pollucis
1098 Pollux 2. 101 στομώδη δὲ τὰ εὔστομα καὶ εὔφημα Σοφοκλῆς.
The word was employed in the sense ‘clear-voiced.’ That εὔφημα is consistent with this interpretation appears (e.g.) from schol. O. T. 35 ὅτι τὸ ῾ἀοιδοῦ᾿ εὔφημόν ἐστιν.

1099 Pollux 2. 23 οὐλοκίκιννε δὲ Τελέσιλλα (fr. 8) εἴρηκεν. τὸν δὲ τοιοῦτον στραβαλοκόμαν Σοφοκλῆς ὠνόμασεν. μοχθηρὰ δὲ ἄμφω τὰ ὀνόματα. [στραβολοκόμαν in Bethe's text of Pollux appears to be a misprint: he quotes στραμβαλοκόμαν F, στραμβαλλοκόμαν S, as variants.]

στραβαλός was a secondary formation from στραβός, like ἡδύλος from ἡδύς, δριμύλος from δριμύς. See Brugmann, II p. 202. The disapproval of Pollux may be compared with the Atticist rejection of στραβός in place of στρεβλός: Phryn. praep. soph. p. 108, 4 (Bekk. anecd. p. 62, 23), Pollux 2. 51.

1100 Steph. Byz. p. 610, 16 Τεγέα, πόλις Ἀρκαδίας. . . ἔστι καὶ Τεγέα ἐν Κρήτῃ ὑπὸ Ταλθυβίου κτισθεῖσα. ὁ πολίτης Τεγεάτης ὡς Ἐλεάτης, καὶ θηλυκὸν Τεγεᾶτις . . . λέγεται καὶ Τεγεάς ὡς Ἰλιάς. ὀξύνεται. ὡς Σοφοκλῆς.
Meineke has suggested with much probability that the reference was to Auge in the Aleadae. For Τεγεᾶτις cf. fr. 142, ii 7.

1101 Suid. s.v. τέως. ἀντὶ τοῦ πρὸ τοῦ, πρίν, ἕως τινός, ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον ἕως. καὶ τέως τηνικαῦτα. ἢ τότε. Σοφοκλῆς δὲ ἀντὶ τοῦ πρότερον ἢ πρὸ μικροῦ. καὶ Ἀριστοφάνης ἀντὶ τοῦ πρότερον (Thesm. 449). ‘τέως μὲν οὖν ἀλλ᾽ ἡμικάκως ἐβοσκόμην.'

The various glosses are loose equivalents, not pointing to any sharp distinction of meaning: see also Phot. lex. p. 584, 12,
Bekk. anecd. p. 309, 23, Etym. Μ. p. 786, 2, and especially the elaborate schol. Plat. Hipparch. 229 D. πρότερον was a convenient paraphrase, when τέως was used, as in Thesm. l.c., with νῦν δὲ or the like following: see examples in Blaydes's n., and Blomfield on Aesch. Cho. 980. But an exactly similar instance in Nub. 66 is glossed by the schol. with μέχρι τινός. Where the contrast is not expressed by an adverb of time (νῦν, εἶτα or the like), it is given by implication in the context, as in Ar. Plut. 834 (gl. πρώην, πρότερον).
1102 Pollux 7. 32 τὰς δὲ ὁλοστημόνους ταινίας τολύπας Σοφοκλῆς ὠνόμασεν.

τολύπη is not only the ball of unspun wool, as explained in Dict. Ant. 1 897, but the prepared and twisted yarn produced by the operation of spinning; and it is in the latter sense that Sophocles is stated to have employed it. So exactly in Ar. Lys. 585 δεῦρο ξυνάγειν καὶ ξυναθροίζειν εἰς ἕν (sc. τὰ κατάγματα), κἄπειτα ποιῆσαι | τολύπην μεγάλην, κᾆτ᾽ ἐκ ταύτης τῷ δήμῳ χλαῖναν ὑφῆναι. Thus, τολύπη may be practically identical with νῆμα or στήμων (Plat. polit. 282 Ε τούτου δὴ τὸ μὲν ἀτράκτῳ τε στραφὲν καὶ στερεὸν νῆμα γενόμενον στήμονα μὲν φάθι τὸ νῆμα), with which it is contrasted in A. P. 6. 160 καλαθίσκον, | στάμονος ἀσκητοῦ καὶ τολύπας φύλακα.
1103 τριπαία (vel τρίπαια vel τριπαῖα) codd.: corr. post Sylburgium Brunck
1103 Bachm. anecd. I p. 390, 8 = Phot. lex. p. 602, 6 τριπαία (τρίπαια Phot.)· ἡ ἐναντία πνοή. οὕτως Σοφοκλῆς. Etym. M. p. 766, 40 τριπαῖα· ἡ ἐναντία πνοή. οὕτω Σοφοκλῆς εἴρηκε.

τροπαία is not a contrary wind, unless accidentally, but a wind blowing in the reverse direction, having shifted to the opposite quarter. It is used metaphorically by Aesch. Ag. 229 φρενὸς πνέων δυσσεβῆ τροπαίαν, Cho. 771 ἀλλ᾽ εἰ τροπαίαν Ζεὺς κακῶν θήσει ποτέ, Theb. 693. Cf. Eur. El. 1147 μετάτροποι πνέουσιν αὖραι δόμων. The word is becoming substantival, with an ellipse οἱ αὔρα (πνοή).
1104 Hesych. IV p. 188 Τυφῶ· ἀντὶ τοῦ Τυφῶνος. Σοφοκλῆς.

Moeris calls τυφώς the Attic form (p. 210, 23 τυφῶ Ἀττικοί, τυφῶνα Ἕλληνες), with this much of reason that τυφών regularly appears in Hellenistic Greek. Nauck, referring to Aesch. Theb. 504, Suppl. 569—to which he might have added Ag. 661—and Ar. Nub. 336, thinks that Sophocles has been substituted in error for Aeschylus or Aristophanes; but his suspicion seems unjustifiable.
1105 Eustath. Od. p. 1496, 35 ἀστείως δὲ καὶ Σοφοκλῆς ὃς λέγεται ὕπουλον εἰπεῖν τὸν δούρειον ἵππον.

For the word ὕπουλος see Jebb on Ο.Τ. 1396. It was applied commonly in late Greek to treacherous friends, as may be seen from the passages quoted by Wyttenbach on Plut. Mor. 44 A (VI p. 378). There may have been an allusion to the Wooden Horse in more than one of the Trojan plays: we might think of Αἰχμαλωτίδες, Ἀντηνορίδαι, Λαοκόων or Σίνων as among the likely sources.
1106 Phryn. praep. soph. p. 117, 13 (Bekk. anecd. p. 68, 4) ὑψαυχεῖν. Σοφοκλῆς. Hesych. IV p. 223 ὑψαυχεῖν· μεγαλαυχεῖν. Phot. lex. p. 635, 12 and Suid. s.v. ὑψαυχεῖν· ὑψηλοφρονεῖν.
The degradation of the metaphor is seen in A.P. 5. 250 ἀλλ᾽ οὐ σῆς κραδίης ὑψαύχενος ὤκλασεν ὄγκος.
1107 Phot. lex. p. 637, 1 φαικῷ· ἀκμάζοντι καὶ λαμπρῷ. οὕτως Σοφοκλῆς. Cf. Hesych. IV p. 227 φαικῷ· ἐνεργῷ ἀκμάζοντι, ἀπὸ τοῦ φαίνειν, οἷον λαμπρόν.

Curtius, G.E. II p. 303 E. tr., compared φαικός with φαίδιμος, φαιδρός, and Φαίδων, but the explanation of the presence of i is still to seek, unless φαικός arises from φαϝικος (like ἱππικός and the rest: Brugmann, II p. 260). Ellendt wrote φαϊκός. φαικάς (A.P. 6. 254), a white shoe, may be akin.
1108 φαρκίδα φαρμακίδα codd.: corr. Brunck et L. Dindorf
1108 Bachm. anecd. I p. 404, 1 = Phot. lex. p. 640, 18 φαρμακίδα· τὴν ἐκ τοῦ γήρως (γένους Phot.) ῥυτίδα. οὕτω Σοφοκλῆς.
For the word cf. Erotian gloss. Hippocr. p. 134, 10 φαρκιδῶδες· ῥυτιτῶδες· φαρκὶς γὰρ λέγεται ἡ ῥυτίς.
1109 Hesych. I p. 332 ἀφάρμακον χρῶμα Οἰδίποδος· ἄνευ ἄνθους· ἄνθη γὰρ τὰ φάρμακα. καὶ τὰ βαφεῖα φαρμακῶνας φαρμακῶντας cod.: corr. Musurus Σοφοκλῆς ἔφη.

The lemma of Hesychius is surely a tragic fragment, but Nauck does not include it, and ἀφάρμακος is absent from L. & S. Dindorf inclined to the view that ἀφάρμακον χρῶμα was the expression of Sophocles.
1110 Strabo 433 οὕτω καὶ Σοφοκλῆς τὴν Τραχῖνα Φθιώτιν εἴρηκεν.

Elmsley on Eur. Hclid. 194 restored Τραχῖνα for Τραχινίαν in the text of Strabo, and the context certainly favours his view, although for the present purpose the point is not of much importance. Welcker (p. 205) rightly resists Elmsley's inference that the quotation occurred in the Phthiotides, but why Ellendt rejects the fragment altogether is not easy to understand. Trachis was actually in Malis (Trach. 194), but in transferring it to Phthiotis Sophocles may have been influenced by Hom. B 682, where Trachis is included in the district of Achilles and closely connected with Phthia.
1111 Hermog. ap. Walz Rhet. Gr. ΙΙΙ Ρ. 324 καὶ ὁ Σοφοκλῆς δὲ φίλανδρον που τὴν Ἀταλάντην εἶπε διὰ τὸ ἀσπάζεσθαι σὺν ἀνδράσιν εἶναι, ἡμῶν πάλιν ἐπὶ ἄλλου πράγματος ταττόντων τοὔνομα τοῦτο.

φίλανδρος, like φιλάνωρ (Aesch. Ag. 420), is normally applied to a loving wife, but as epithet of the virgin Atalanta means masculine. We may compare φιλομεῖραξ, an ἐπίκλησις of Artemis at Elis, because her temple was in the neighbourhood of the gymnasium (Pausan. 6. 23. 6). Brunck was probably right in ascribing this fr. to the Meleager. For the character of Atalanta cf. Eur. fr. 525.

1112 Bachm. anecd. 1 p. 415, 5 χειμάμυνα· παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ, ἡ (ἢ cod.) παρ' Ὁμήρῳ (ξ 529) ἀλεξάνεμος. Pollux 7. 61 attributes the word to Aeschylus : τὸ μέντοι χειμερινὸν ἱμάτιον χείμαστρον ἂν λέγοις, καὶ χλαῖναν δὲ παχεῖαν, ἣν χειμάμυναν μὲν Αἰσχύλος (fr. 449), Ὅμηρος δὲ ἀλεξάνεμον κέκληκεν. The reference to Sophocles receives confirmation from a passage to which L. Cohn drew attention in Rh. Mus. XLIII 414, Herodian. Philetacr. from cod. Vat. 2226 suppl.: καὶ ἀμύνεσθαι λέγοντες οὐκέτι τὴν ἄμυναν <λέγουσιν>, εἰ μὴ Θεόπομπος ἅπαξ καὶ ἔχειν ἄμυναν, ὥσπερ καὶ Σοφοκλῆς. For ἔχειν ἄμυναν Papageorgius by a certain emendation restored χειμάμυναν. Whether he is right in inserting Αἰσχύλος after ὥσπερ is not so clear; and his change of ἀμύνεσθαι to ἄμυναν I do not understand.

Nauck, who in the addenda to TGF (p. xxv) treated this as a new fragment, afterwards (Index, p. XIV) accepted Papageorgius's emendations. Lobeck's statement (Phryn. p. 23) that ἄμυνα does not occur before the first century A.D. requires qualification, in view of pseudo-Herodian's citation of Theopompus. The word χειμάμυνα is further attested by Eustath. Od. p. 1767, 43 παχεῖαν χλαῖναν...ὁποία τις ἡ μὴ μόνον ἀλεξήνεμος λεγομένη, ἀλλὰ καὶ χειμάμυνα, ὡς ἐν ῥητορικῷ κεῖται λεξικῷ (Ael. et Paus. fr. 445 Schw.). Hesych. IV p. 277 χειμάμυνα· ἣν Ὅμηρος ἀλεξάνεμον λέγει. Cf. Hom. II 224 χλαινάων τ᾿ ἀνεμοσκεπέων. By the poets of the New Comedy χλαῖνα is mentioned as a winter wrap (Pollux 10. 123). See also fr. 117.

1113 Etym. Gud. p. 564, 25 χειροβοσκός· ὁ διὰ χειρὸς ζῶν, ὡς φησὶ Σοφοκλῆς. Pollux 7. 7 τὸ γὰρ ἀποχειροβίωτος καὶ χειρῶναξ καὶ χειρογάστωρ καὶ χειροβοσκὸς καὶ χειροβάναυσος ἦττον ἄν τις προσοῖτο. Hesych. IV p. 278 χειροβοσκόν (χειροβοσκῶν cod.)· τὸν διὰ χειρῶν ζῶντα.
For the contemptuous tone of -βοσκός see on fr. 140.
1114 Suid. s.v. χλωρανθείς· ἀντὶ τοῦ χλωρὸς γενηθείς. οὕτω Σοφοκλῆς.
This appears to be the only extant example of χλωραίνω.
1115 Herodian περὶ μον. λεξ. p. 14, 24 τὰ εἰς οῦς λήγοντα ὀνόματα μονοσύλλαβα ἀρσενικὰ πέφυκεν εἶναι, ἔσθ᾽ ὅτε δὲ καὶ κοινωνεῖ θηλυκῷ γένει.... Γλοῦς ὁ λῃστής, χνοῦς παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ.
1116 Schol. Ar. Ran. 1033 τὸν Μουσαῖον παῖδα Σελήνης καὶ Εὐμόλπου Φιλόχορος (FHG 1 416) φησίν...ὁ δὲ Σοφοκλῆς χρησμολόγον αὐτὸν φησί.

Aristophanes' words are Μουσαῖος δ' ἐξακέσεις τε νόσων καὶ χρησμούς. There was extant in the fifth century a collection of oracles which passed by the name of Musaeus: thus Hdt. 7. 6 relates how the Pisistratids had banished Onomacritus because he had been caught interpolating the oracles of Musaeus. Hence no doubt Clem. Alex. strom. I. 21, p. 397, says that according to some the oracles traditionally referred to Musaeus were actually the work of Onomacritus. Oracles belonging to his collection and referring to the battles of Salamis and Aegospotami are quoted by Herodotus (8. 96) and Pausanias (10. 9. 11); and the latter speaks of them as still extant in his time (10. 12. 11), although he did not believe in their genuineness (1. 22. 7). It was, in fact, on these that the fame of Musaeus principally rested: Plat. Prot. 316 D (sophists of old fearing to be so called) πρόσχημα ποιεῖσθαι καὶ προκαλύπτεσθαι, τοὺς μὲν ποίησιν...τοὺς δὲ αὖ τελετάς τε καὶ χρησμῳδίας, τοὺς ἀμφί τε Ὀρφέα καὶ Μουσαῖον, Philostr. heroic. 3. 38 Ὀρφέα δὲ ἐν πολλοῖς τῶν κατὰ θεολογίαν ὑπερῆρε (sc. Ὅμηρος), Μουσαῖον δ᾽ ἐν ᾠδαῖς χρησμῶν. Nauck justly remarks that χρησμῳδός might have been expected, and it is arguable that the schol. is giving the substance rather than the actual words of his quotation. [So also the editors of Steph. Thes.] Welcker assigns the fr. to the Triptolemus.
